name: ATSAML21E18B-MUT
title: SAM L21 ultra-low-power Arm Cortex-M0+ microcontrollers, 48 MHz, 32 to 256 KB Flash, up to 40 KB SRAM, full-speed USB, 1.62 V to 3.63 V
summary: A family of low-power 32-bit microcontrollers built on an Arm Cortex-M0+ at up to 48 MHz, with 32 to 256 KB of self-programmable Flash plus a read-while-write section, main SRAM and a separate low-power SRAM, in 32-, 48- and 64-pin packages. Power-domain gating, two performance levels, a buck or linear core regulator chosen at run time, battery backup and SleepWalking peripherals keep consumption down. Around the core sit a 16-channel DMA, a 12-channel event system, full-speed USB host and device, six SERCOMs, timers (TC and TCC), AES, a TRNG, custom logic, a 12-bit 1 Msps ADC, two DAC channels, two comparators, three op amps and a capacitive touch controller. ATSAML21E18B-MUT is the 32-pin QFN part with 256 KB Flash and 32 KB SRAM (plus 8 KB low-power SRAM) for -40 °C to 85 °C, with 25 GPIOs.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M0+ (r0p1), up to 48 MHz, 2.46 CoreMark/MHz, single-cycle multiplier, Micro Trace Buffer
256/128/64/32 KB plus an 8/4/2/1 KB read-while-write section; 256 KB on the E18B
32/16/8/4 KB main plus 8/8/4/2 KB low-power; 32 KB + 8 KB on the E18B
1.62 V to 3.63 V (VDDIN, VDDANA, VDDIO, VBAT)
12-bit, 1 Msps, up to 20 channels (10 on SAM L21E), oversampling to 16 bits
full-speed 12 Mbps, host and device, eight endpoints
two comparators, three op amps, touch controller with up to 169 mutual channels (42 on SAM L21E)
up to 51 GPIOs; 25 on the 32-pin SAM L21E
TQFP and QFN in 32, 48 and 64 pins; WLCSP64

notes: The code reads SAML 21, pin count (E 32, G 48, J 64), Flash density (15 32 KB, 16 64 KB, 17 128 KB, 18 256 KB), variant (A engineering samples only, B production), then package (A TQFP, M QFN, U WLCSP), grade (U -40 to 85 °C, N -40 to 105 °C, both matte tin) and T for tape and reel.
The variant letter marks functional differences; the die revision in DSU.DID.REVISION tracks changes to the die and is unrelated to it.
The SRAM column gives main SRAM only; low-power SRAM adds 8 KB (x18, x17), 4 KB (x16) or 2 KB (E15).

circuits.title: Power supply connection for linear mode only
circuits.description: A separate I/O rail feeds VDDIO; one main rail feeds VDDANA and VDDIN together, with a capacitor to ground. The core regulator runs linear, so VSW is left open and VDDCORE needs only its own capacitor to ground. GND and GNDANA meet at the board ground; VBAT (PB03) is unused.

circuits.title: Power supply connection for switching/linear mode
circuits.description: As for linear mode, but an inductor runs from VSW to VDDCORE so the regulator can be switched to its buck mode at run time; the VDDCORE capacitor sits at the inductor's output. VBAT (PB03) is unused.

circuits.title: Power supply connection for battery backup
circuits.description: The supply arrangement of the other two connections with a backup cell from VBAT (PB03) to ground; VBAT feeds the automatic power switch, which supplies VSWOUT from VDDIN or VBAT. The inductor from VSW to VDDCORE is optional and fitted for switching mode.

circuits.title: Power supply connection for switching/linear mode, with values
circuits.description: The full supply arrangement with values. The IO rail feeds VDDIO with 10 µF bulk and 100 nF at the pin. The main rail feeds VDDIN directly (10 µF bulk, 100 nF at the pin) and VDDANA through a ferrite bead with its own 10 µF and 100 nF, so digital noise stays out of the analog domain. A 10 µH inductor from VSW to VDDCORE lets the regulator run as a buck; VDDCORE has 1 µF and 100 nF to ground. GND and GNDANA share the ground. VBAT (PB03) is unused.

parts.note: ferrite bead from the main supply to VDDANA

circuits.title: Power supply connection for linear mode only, with values
circuits.description: As the switching arrangement but with no inductor: VSW is left open and the regulator runs linear, its VDDCORE output decoupled by 1 µF and 100 nF. VBAT (PB03) is unused.

parts.note: ferrite bead from the main supply to VDDANA

circuits.title: Power supply connection for battery backup, with values
circuits.description: The switching arrangement plus a backup cell from VBAT (PB03) to ground, so the backup domain keeps running when the main supply goes. The 10 µH VSW inductor is optional and fitted only for switching mode.

parts.note: ferrite bead from the main supply to VDDANA
buck inductor, fitted for switching mode

circuits.title: External analog references, two references
circuits.description: Two external references, one on VREFA (PA03) and one on VREFB (PA04). Each has 4.7 µF at the source and 100 nF close to its pin, both to ground.

circuits.title: External analog reference, one reference on both inputs
circuits.description: One external reference feeds both VREFA (PA03) and VREFB (PA04). It has 4.7 µF at the source, and each pin has its own 100 nF to ground close by.

circuits.title: External reset circuit
circuits.description: RESET has a 100 nF filter capacitor to ground and an optional 10 kΩ pull-up to VDD (the pin also has one inside). A push-button pulls RESET to ground through 330 Ω, which limits the discharge current of the capacitor.

circuits.title: External clock source
circuits.description: An external clock drives XIN (PA14); XOUT (PA15) is left open or used as an ordinary GPIO.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator
circuits.description: A 0.4 to 32 MHz crystal between XIN (PA14) and XOUT (PA15), with a load capacitor CLEXT from each pin to ground; CLEXT comes from the crystal load capacitance equation. The crystal sits as close to the pins as possible.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal without load capacitors
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal straight between XIN32 (PA00) and XOUT32 (PA01). With a crystal of under 12.5 pF load, the pin and PCB capacitance alone can be enough.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal with load capacitors
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal between XIN32 (PA00) and XOUT32 (PA01) with a load capacitor CLEXT from each pin to ground, for when the crystal maker asks for external capacitors.

circuits.title: SWCLK pull-up
circuits.description: A 1 kΩ pull-up from SWCLK (PA30) to VDD; SWCLK also goes on to the debug connector.

circuits.title: Cortex debug connector (10-pin)
circuits.description: The 10-pin Cortex debug header: pin 1 VTref senses VDD; SWDIO (pin 2) to PA31, SWDCLK (pin 4) to SWCLK on PA30, RESET (pin 10) to the RESET pin; pins 3 and 5 to ground; pins 6 to 9 unconnected.

circuits.title: 10-pin JTAGICE3 compatible serial wire debug header
circuits.description: The 10-pin header in the JTAGICE3 50-mil pinout: SWDCLK (pin 1) to SWCLK on PA30, SWDIO (pin 5) to PA31, RESET (pin 6) to the RESET pin, VTG (pin 4) senses VDD, pin 2 to ground; pins 3, 7, 8, 9 and 10 unconnected.

circuits.title: 20-pin IDC JTAG connector
circuits.description: The 20-pin IDC JTAG header used by SAM-ICE: VCC (pin 1) senses VDD; SWDIO (pin 7) to PA31, SWDCLK (pin 9) to SWCLK on PA30, RESET (pin 15) to the RESET pin; even pins 4 to 20 to ground (14 to 20 are the reserved GND* pins); pins 2, 3, 5, 11, 13, 17 and 19 unconnected.

circuits.title: Low-cost USB interface
circuits.description: The USB connector's D+ and D- run as a matched differential pair straight to USB D+ (PA25) and D- (PA24). VBUS is brought out, and the connector's GND and shield both go to board ground.

circuits.title: Protected USB interface
circuits.description: As the low-cost interface, with a transient-suppressor array near the connector and an RC filter between ground and shield. Two suppressors clamp D+ and D- up to VBUS and three clamp VBUS, D+ and D- down to the shield line. A 4.5 nF capacitor in parallel with 1 MΩ joins the connector shield to the connector GND, which goes to board ground, so the cable shield is not tied straight to ground.

operation.text: SAM L21 parts share one peripheral set, one linear address map, hex-compatible code and pin-compatible footprints from 32 to 64 pins; the family also migrates from SAM D. Each TC and TCC can generate frequencies and waveforms, time program execution or capture inputs to measure time and frequency. TCs run as 8-bit or 16-bit counters and pairs cascade into a 32-bit counter; two TCCs are 24-bit and the third 16-bit, with extras for motor, lighting and other control work. A SERCOM can be set up as USART, UART, SPI, LIN slave, SMBus, PMBus or I2C up to 3.4 MHz. The touch controller handles up to 192 touch buttons, sliders and wheels plus proximity sensing. Every oscillator can clock the system, and clock domains run at independent frequencies.

Four sleep modes are chosen in software: Idle stops the CPU while everything else may keep running; Standby stops every clock and function not chosen to stay on while keeping all RAM and logic state; Backup and Off are the other two. With SleepWalking a peripheral wakes on its own condition, so work such as a DMA transfer goes ahead and the CPU is woken only when needed, for instance on a crossed threshold or a finished conversion. Events between peripherals, synchronous or asynchronous, keep flowing in Standby.

Two performance levels, PL0 and PL2, set the lowest core voltage that supports the chosen frequency. To cut leakage further, hardware switches off logic areas with state retention, without software involvement.

The Flash is reprogrammed in-system through the two-pin SWD interface, which also gives non-intrusive on-chip debug. A bootloader in the device may use any communication interface to load new application code.
Members differ in their number of SERCOM and timer/counter instances and of PTC and ADC signals. The three TCC instances are configured differently, including how many waveform output lines each has.

Each pin defaults to general-purpose I/O under PORT control and can instead be handed to one of the peripheral functions A to I. Writing 1 to PINCFGn.PMUXEN (n = 0..31) enables the peripheral function and the odd and even fields of PMUXn (PMUXE/PMUXO) choose which one.

Crystal oscillator pins are not part of the PORT multiplexing; OSCCTRL and OSC32KCTRL control them. Of the debug pins only SWCLK goes through the PORT multiplexer; SWDIO switches to its debug role automatically when a debugger is plugged in, cold or hot. The SUPC outputs and VBAT pin are likewise outside the PORT functions and are run from SUPC registers.

The AC, ADC, DAC and op amps connect to one another internally (op amp outputs to ADC and AC inputs, DAC outputs to op amp and AC inputs, op amps cascaded through resistor ladders with taps). A peripheral may also reach another through a pad, in which case the pad loses its digital role and its set-up must not disturb the analog link. An enabled analog peripheral's output interferes with the other functions of its output pads, even when it is used only internally; analog inputs do not interfere.

Apart from external voltages such as VDDANA, a DETREF block supplies two internal references: BANDGAP, a fixed stable reference, and INTREF, set through SUPC.VREF. The ADC chooses its reference in ADC.REFCTRL, the DAC in DAC.CTRLB.REFSEL, and the AC is fixed to BANDGAP.

The ADC and AC can switch an op amp on when they need it. With OPAMPCTRLx.ONDEMAND = 1 the op amp starts on a request and acknowledges once fully running; with ONDEMAND = 0 a request is acknowledged at once if the op amp is already on and ignored if it is off. Requests are served only while the op amp output is active (OPAMPCTRLx.ANAOUT = 1). In Standby the on-demand behaviour continues when ONDEMAND = 1 and the op amp is off when ONDEMAND = 0. The op amp must be configured before it is requested. This mechanism is separate from the ONDEMAND bit of each clock source. The ADC issues requests when ADC.CTRLA.ONDEMAND = 1. The AC has no such bit: it requests whenever it runs single-shot or an event triggers a comparison, with the op amp already chosen as its input; setting AC.COMPCTRL1.MUXNEG = 0x7 (DAC/OPAMP) starts AC requests to the op amp.

If an op amp accepts requests but ADC.CTRLA.ONDEMAND = 0, the ADC sends continuous requests to whatever ADC.INPUTCTRL.MUXPOS selects: 0x1E reaches OPAMP0 and OPAMP1, 0x1F only OPAMP2. Likewise, with AC.CTRLA.ONDEMAND = 0 the AC requests continuously from the source chosen by AC.COMPCTRLx.MUXNEG: COMPCTRL1.MUXNEG = 0x7 reaches OPAMP2 and COMPCTRL0.MUXNEG = 0x7 reaches DAC0.

VDDCORE, VDDIO and VDDIN share GND; VDDANA returns to GNDANA. VDDANA and VDDIN must be fed from the same main supply, VDD. VDDCORE is the internal regulator output; it supplies the CPU, memories, peripherals and the two high-frequency sources DFLL48M and FDPLL96M. Two domains exist only inside, VSWOUT and VDDBU: VSWOUT is fed by the automatic power switch from VDDIN or VBAT and powers PB[3:0], PA[1:0], XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, POR and BOD33, and the backup domain PDBACKUP holds the RTC, PM, SUPC and RSTC. Logic is split into PDTOP, PD0, PD1 and PD2. On SAM L21E the VDDIO domain is tied to VDDANA inside the package and powered from it.

VDDIO (I/O lines and XOSC), VDDIN (I/O lines, OSC16M, the VDDCORE regulator and the automatic power switch), VDDANA (its I/O lines plus the analog blocks: ADC, AC, DAC, PTC, op amps) and VBAT (the automatic power switch) each take 1.62 V to 3.63 V. VDDCORE, the regulator output, sits at 0.9 V to 1.2 V typical. The automatic power switch picks VDDIN or VBAT to feed VSWOUT. VDDIN and VDDANA must carry the same voltage, called VDD. With the PTC in use VDDIO must equal VDD; without it VDDIO may be lower than VDD. Decoupling is given in the schematic checklist.

The core regulator has four modes, chosen through the Power Manager: linear, the default while running, needing no inductor; switching, the most efficient while running, selectable on the fly; low power, the default in Standby; and shutdown, in Backup mode, with the regulator off. The device runs from a single 1.62 V to 3.63 V supply.

VDDIN and VDDANA must come up together, ideally tied to each other. VDDIO may rise before or after them, but must be present before XOSC or any digital function on VDDIO pins is used. The POR circuits on VDDIN and VDDIO need a minimum supply rise rate, and no supply may rise faster than the maximum in the electrical characteristics.

After power-up the device stays in reset until power is stable throughout. It starts at performance level PL0 and the regulator delivers the matching VDDCORE; once VDDIN and VDDCORE are stable the internal reset releases. It then runs from a 4 MHz clock taken from OSC16M, enabled at 4 MHz by default after reset; this is the default source of generic clock generator 0, which drives GCLK_MAIN for the Power Manager. Some synchronous system clocks run from start-up on that 4 MHz clock so software can execute; other generic clocks are off. I/O pins come up tri-stated except PA30, an input with pull-up. The CPU then loads its stack pointer and program counter from address 0x00000000, the start of internal Flash.

POR watches VDDIN, VSWOUT and VDDIO in every mode, start-up and sleep included. VDDIN or VSWOUT falling below the threshold resets the whole chip; VDDIO falling below it resets the I/Os powered by VSWOUT. BOD33 watches VSWOUT or VBAT, as configured. BOD12, inside the regulator, watches VDDCORE once the device has started; it is calibrated in production, its calibration lives in the NVM user row, and that data should be kept unchanged whenever the user row is rewritten.

The device starts in PL0, which lowers consumption by capping logic speed and CPU frequency. In PL0 the USB and DFLL48M are unavailable; AHB and APB peripherals are bounded by the CPU frequency; FDPLL96M may make 48 MHz internally but logic cannot use it; GCLK, the SW interface, TC, TCC and SERCOM reach a quarter of their PL2 maximum. AC, ADC, DAC, EIC, OPAMP, OSC16M, PTC and every 32 kHz source and peripheral work fully in PL0. PL2 gives full capability, and SUPC ramps the voltage smoothly, with settings, between levels.

High-speed Flash with a read-while-write section, high-speed RAM and low-power RAM, both RAMs with single-cycle access at full speed. The high-speed bus is a bus matrix whose addresses are fixed and never remapped, not even at boot.

The user row at 0x00804000 holds settings loaded automatically at power-on (bootloader and EEPROM sizes, BOD33 and WDT start-up settings, region locks). It is written through NVMCTRL, and new values take effect only after a device reset.
Every device carries a 128-bit serial number made of four 32-bit words at 0x0080A00C, 0x0080A040, 0x0080A044 and 0x0080A048. It is unique only taken as all 128 bits.

ARMv6-M Cortex-M0+, revision r0p1, instruction-compatible with Cortex-M0 and upward-compatible with Cortex-M3 and M4. It has one 32-bit AMBA-3 AHB-Lite system interface to peripherals and all memory, and one 32-bit single-cycle I/O port to the PORT, used at the same time so the CPU fetches while it toggles pins. Core peripherals: SCS for debug, the NVIC, a 24-bit SysTick clocked by CLK_CPU, the SCB and the MTB.

When the CPU clock is far above the APB clock, placing a read barrier after every APB register write by the CPU avoids misbehaviour such as an interrupt handler being entered again right after it returns.

The NVIC takes 32 interrupt lines at four priority levels; 28 lines each serve one peripheral instance. A peripheral sets a flag in INTFLAG when an interrupt condition occurs; writing 1 to INTENSET enables it and 1 to INTENCLR disables it. A set and enabled flag raises the peripheral's request; all requests of one peripheral are ORed into one line that sets its NVIC pending bit (ISPR/ICPR). The NVIC acts on it once enabled in ISER/ICER, and IPR0-IPR7 hold each line's priority.

The CoreSight MTB-M0+ records program-flow changes into SRAM as pairs of 32-bit words, one pair for each non-sequential PC change (branches, exception entry). A debugger reads the trace back through the debug access port and rebuilds the flow. Trace writes take priority over CPU accesses to that SRAM, and the trace buffer's place and size in SRAM are set in software; the rest of the MTB SRAM is ordinary storage. Tracing runs while MASTER.EN = 1; it can stop automatically at a watermark, and without one the buffer wraps over older packets. Registers at 0x41006000 (also listed in the CoreSight ROM table): POSITION (write pointer and wrap bit), MASTER (enable and controls), FLOW (watermark, AUTOSTOP, AUTOHALT) and BASE (where the SRAM sits, for debugger discovery).

Two bus matrices, high-speed and low-power, each a symmetric 32-bit crossbar running at the clock of its masters and allowing concurrent accesses to different slaves, plus two unified FlexRAM areas. Two AHB-to-AHB bridges link them. H2LBRIDGE: LP clock division, a 3-word posted-write FIFO, a 1-cycle stall on a write when full and 2 stall cycles on a read with the LP clock undivided. L2HBRIDGE: the same with a 1-word FIFO. Both have an ultra-low-latency mode for HS clocks no higher than half the device maximum, which removes the bridge's own stall cycles (except those for LP clock ratio); a 32-bit write of 1 to 0x41008120 enables it.

Each master accessing RAM has its own QoS level, passed to the RAM with every access. Concurrent accesses are ordered by QoS first, then by port ID, the lowest port ID winning. The MTB is fixed at HIGH (0x3). The CPU's level is read and written with 32-bit accesses at 0x41008114 bits [1:0], reset value 0x3; USB and DMAC set theirs in their QOSCTRL registers.

The PAC locks and unlocks peripheral registers against writes and reports access violations: writes to protected registers, accesses to unimplemented registers, writes during an ongoing synchronisation, and writes while enable protection or a software reset is in progress, each in one interrupt flag per peripheral. It also reports bus-level errors when an address with no slave behind it is accessed (INTFLAGAHB). It works in every sleep mode where its clock runs, and its bus clock CLK_PAC_APB is gated in MCLK. The PAC is enabled after every reset and only a hardware reset resets it. With the CPU halted in debug, write protection is lifted; it never applies to an external debugger. WRCTRL, INTFLAGAHB and the INTFLAGn registers cannot themselves be protected.

A word write to WRCTRL with a peripheral ID (PERID) and a key (KEY) clears protection, sets it, or sets and locks it; a locked protection clears only on hardware reset. STATUSn shows the protection of each peripheral on bridge n, and INTFLAGn records violations on bridge n. Anything but a word write to WRCTRL is ignored and flagged as a PAC error in INTFLAGn.PAC. An error is also raised by setting protection on an already protected peripheral, clearing it twice, set-and-lock on a protected peripheral, or writing to a locked one. A handler that changes the protection of a peripheral also used elsewhere reads STATUS first, or interrupts are kept out while protection changes.

The ERR interrupt flags any peripheral access violation or bridge error and is a synchronous wake-up source; it is enabled in INTENSET, cleared in INTENCLR, and software reads INTFLAGAHB and INTFLAGn to find the cause. Writing 1 to EVCTRL.ERREO also makes any set flag issue an ERR event. In sleep the PAC stays enabled while a bus master (CPU or DMA) runs and keeps catching errors.

The DSU detects debugger probes, lets the debug access port take over the multiplexed debug pads and the CPU reset, and serves debug adapters with a CoreSight debug ROM for device and component identification. It also offers memory services for applications, such as tests for IEC 60730 Class B. Sitting on the high-speed bus matrix, it can be used by a debugger and the CPU at once. Some features are limited or absent while the NVMCTRL security bit protects the device. Features: CPU reset extension, cold- and hot-plug debugger detection, chip erase, CRC32 of any memory reachable through the bus matrix, CoreSight identification, two debug communication channels, a DAP security filter and memory built-in self-test.

SWCLK is assigned to the DSU by default so it can detect a probe and stretch the CPU reset. Changing the SWCLK pin function in PORT, or disabling its multiplexing, turns hot-plug detection off until a power or external reset. The DSU works in any sleep mode where its clock runs; MCLK gates its APB and AHB bus clocks (CLK_DSU_APB, CLK_DSU_AHB). It has no interrupts or events. All registers except DCC0 and DCC1 can be PAC-protected; protection is lifted while the CPU is halted in debug and never applies to an external debugger.

After an external reset releases, the CPU can be held in reset so it runs no code while a debugger connects. The DSU sees a debugger when RESET rises while SWCLK is low; SWCLK has an internal pull-up at start-up so an open pin is not mistaken for a probe. While held, STATUSA.CRSTEXT reads 1; writing 1 to it releases the CPU and clears it, writing 0 does nothing. On a protected device the release is refused and STATUSA.PERR is set.

Cold plugging is detection while the system is in reset, through the reset extension. Hot plugging is detection on a falling SWCLK edge while the system runs; it cannot happen during reset because POR and RESET reset the detector, and it needs SWCLK left on its debug function (STATUSB.HPE shows whether it is available). Either one sets STATUSB.DBGPRES. Hot plugging is unavailable on a protected device. Detection needs powered pads, so at cold start it waits for POR release; on a protected device cold plugging is the only route, so the external reset must outlast the POR time, and the attempt is repeated if RESET released before POR did.

Chip erase wipes all volatile memories and the Flash, including the EEPROM emulation area, and clears the NVMCTRL security bit; the auxiliary rows, user row included, are kept. On a protected device the debugger first resets the part to be detected. Writing 1 to CTRL.CE starts it (ignored if the DSU is PAC-protected); volatile memories are cleared before the Flash is erased, and STATUSA.DONE shows completion. Because the CPU can alter clocks and power settings, erase after a cold-plug: detect the probe with the CPU held in reset, write CTRL.CE, poll STATUSA.DONE, then reset so NVMCTRL reloads the fuses.

Flash and RAM can be programmed only when the security bit is clear. The debugger holds RESET low at power-up; POR holds the system until the supply passes the POR threshold and the regulated supplies are safe. The PM starts on the slow clock with internal resets held by the external reset. The debugger keeps SWCLK low and releases RESET (a cold plug), then clocks SWCLK so the DAP runs while the CPU stays in reset and the rest of the system starts. A chip erase precedes programming through the AHB-AP. Afterwards the part restarts by RESET, a power cycle or writing 1 to STATUSA.CRSTEXT; SWCLK must be high when RESET is released or the CPU reset is extended again.

Setting the NVMCTRL security bit restricts external tools from internal memories; a chip erase removes it. While protected, AHB-AP reads and writes are confined to the DSU range and DSU commands are limited; accesses elsewhere are dropped with an error that sets the AHB-AP sticky error bits. The CPU uses the DSU without restriction. The first 0x100 bytes of DSU registers are mirrored at offset 0x100: 0x0000-0x00FF is the internal range, closed to debuggers on a protected device, and 0x0100-0x01FF the external range, open with restrictions; the CoreSight ROM sits at 0x1000-0x1FFC. A protected device's DAP may issue MEM-AP accesses only in 0x0100-0x2000.

Identification follows the Arm CoreSight scheme: a system ROM table, whose address is in the DAP's MEM-AP BASE register, identifies the vendor and how to identify the chip, through a 64-bit ID built from PID0 to PID7. The DSU DID register then gives the processor, product family, product series and device selection.

CRC32 and MBIST share the ADDR, LENGTH and DATA registers, which are set before a command is written to CTRL. Further commands are ignored until STATUSA.DONE shows the current one finished. The DSU is enabled by enabling its clocks. Debug adapters should use the external range 0x100-0x2000 (on a protected device the first 0x100 bytes return an error); the CPU should use the internal range 0x0-0x100.

The DSU computes a CRC32 over any memory area, Flash and AHB RAM included, using the standard polynomial 0xEDB88320 (reversed form). ADDR takes the start and LENGTH the size, both word-aligned; DATA takes the initial value, normally 0xFFFFFFFF or a previous result to chain blocks. Writing 1 to CTRL.CRC starts it and writing 1 to CTRL.SWRST cancels it. The result is read from DATA and must be inverted to match the usual CRC32, or left as is to seed the next run. On completion STATUSA.DONE sets and STATUSA.BERR shows whether a bus error occurred. From the external range, and on a protected device, only the whole Flash array or the whole EEPROM area can be checked, with ADDR, LENGTH and DATA forced to fixed values, which lets the contents of a protected part be verified.

DCC0 and DCC1 are two registers with handshake logic, open to the CPU and the debugger even on a protected device, for exchanging data at run time or in debug and for building a custom debug protocol. STATUSB.DCC0D and DCC1D set when the matching register is written and clear when it is read. On a protected device a debugger cannot connect while the CPU runs. The registers are shared with MBIST and must not be used during an MBIST run.

MBIST runs the March LR algorithm, mainly for production test, in a time linear in memory size that depends on CPU clock and bytes tested. Steps: write all zeros; descending, read 0 write 1 bit by bit; ascending, read 1 write 0 read 0 write 1; ascending, read 1 write 0; ascending, read 0 write 1 read 1 write 0; then read all zeros ascending. It finds address decoder, stuck-at, transition, coupling and linked coupling faults. ADDR.ADDR takes the start and LENGTH the size; testing a whole physical block at once gives the best coverage. Writing 1 to CTRL.MBIST starts it and 1 to CTRL.SWRST cancels it. With ADDR.AMOD = 0 (default) it stops at the first fault or at the end, setting STATUSA.DONE, and STATUSA.FAIL if a fault was found; with AMOD = 1 it pauses on a fault with only FAIL set, and resumes when 1 is written to FAIL. On a fault ADDR holds the failing word's address and DATA gives the bit (bit_index, bits 4:0) and the phase (bits 10:8). It cannot run from the external range on a protected device; trying sets STATUSA.PERR.
An external access lands in DSU offsets 0x200-0x1FFF and an internal one in 0x0-0x100.

Clocks come from oscillators run by two controllers: OSCCTRL (XOSC, OSC16M, DFLL48M, FDPLL96M) and OSC32KCTRL (XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, each with 32 kHz and 1 kHz outputs). The GCLK turns any source into generic clocks: programmable dividers called generators feed peripheral channels, one channel per peripheral clock, and generator 0 always makes GCLK_MAIN. MCLK takes GCLK_MAIN and makes the synchronous clocks: CPU, AHB and APB bus clocks and the bus-side interface clock of each peripheral, with a mask bit per module and prescalers for CPU and buses. Generic clock channel 0 is the DFLL48M reference; channels 1 and 2 are the FDPLL96M reference and its 32 kHz clock. The RTC, WDT, EIC and OPAMP also take the 32 kHz and 1 kHz clocks straight from OSC32KCTRL.

To clock SERCOM0 from the DFLL48M in open loop: enable the DFLL48M, select it as source of generator 1, point peripheral channel 13 (GCLK_SERCOM0_CORE) at generator 1, and unmask CLK_SERCOM0_APB in the MCLK APBC mask. A generator's source is GCLK.GENCTRLn.SRC; a channel's generator is GCLK.PCHCTRLm.GEN, and the channel number m is fixed per peripheral. AHB clocks are switched in MCLK.AHBMASK and APB clocks in MCLK.APBxMASK.

Synchronous clocks are the CPU and bus clocks from MCLK; asynchronous clocks are the generic clocks from GCLK. Because the CPU and a peripheral may sit in different clock domains, some register accesses must cross between them, and such a peripheral has a SYNCBUSY register that shows a crossing in progress.

Each peripheral has a bus interface on an APB or AHB clock and a core on its generic clock. Interface registers need no synchronization. Core registers are synchronized on every write, and some also on read; the hardware does this even when both clocks share source and frequency. Each such register has its own synchronizer and SYNCBUSY bit (one shared bit when a register is both read- and write-synchronized). A write sets the bit until the value has crossed; another write to the same register meanwhile is dropped and flags an error, but different registers synchronize in parallel, so a 32-bit write covering three registers may land in each at a different moment. A read-synchronized register is refreshed whenever its value changes without setting SYNCBUSY, and a read returns the last refreshed value; after a wake from sleep these bits are set until the refresh is done. Completion is seen by polling SYNCBUSY or by the synchronization-ready interrupt where present, which fires when every bit is 0.

Writing CTRLA.ENABLE starts a synchronization and sets SYNCBUSY.ENABLE; CTRLA.ENABLE reads back the new value at once and the busy bit clears when done. Writing 1 to CTRLA.SWRST likewise sets SYNCBUSY.SWRST, reads 1 at once, and both clear when the peripheral has been reset; writing 0 does nothing. The ready interrupt cannot be used for either.

A peripheral on a generic clock needs: a running clock source; an enabled generator using it; its peripheral channel pointed at that generator and enabled; and its bus interface unmasked. Masked, its registers read 0 and writes are lost.

Every clock source can run on demand: it stays stopped until a peripheral asks for it, the request passing from the peripheral through the peripheral channel and generator to the source, and it stops again once no request remains. A request gets through only if the peripheral, its channel and the generator are all enabled. Clearing a source's ONDEMAND bit keeps it always running, which removes the start-up wait at the price of power. With the RUNSTDBY bits set on the modules along the path, requests also work in Standby.
A slow generic clock lowers a peripheral's active power, but synchronization to the CPU domain then takes longer, so response is slower and register accesses wait longer.

Every reset returns the synchronous clocks to OSC16M enabled at 4 MHz, generator 0 taking OSC16M to make GCLK_MAIN, and CPU and bus clocks undivided. A power-on reset also resets the 32 kHz sources and the whole GCLK: all generators off except generator 0 on OSC16M at 4 MHz, and all peripheral channels off. A user reset resets the GCLK except the generic clocks whose WRTLOCK was set before it.

The generic clock controller gives peripherals the clock frequencies they need: generators each take one internal or external source and may divide it, and their outputs feed peripheral channels that hand GCLK_PERIPH to the modules. The number of channels follows the number of peripherals, up to 64. Generator 0 is always the direct source of GCLK_MAIN. The GCLK works in every sleep mode if needed, keeps running when the CPU halts in debug, has no interrupts, events or DMA, and its bus clock CLK_GCLK_APB is switched in MCLK. Its writable registers may be PAC write-protected.

Enable the clock source first. Then enable the generator and set its division in one 32-bit write to GENCTRLn (GENEN, DIVSEL, DIV), and configure the peripheral clock by writing the generator number to PCHCTRLm.GEN. Each generator n has its own GENCTRLn and each channel m its own PCHCTRLm. The module has no global enable; CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except locked channels and the generators behind them.

Each generator can take any of nine sources, except generator 1, which has eight; generator 1 is the only one that can be the source of other generators. Each generator is tied to one GCLK_IO pin, which can be its input or show its output. GENCTRLn.GENEN=1 enables it and 0 stops and gates its clock. GENCTRLn.SRC picks the source and can be changed on the fly: the generator keeps the old source until the new one is ready, holding requests on both meanwhile, and SYNCBUSY.GENCTRLn stays 1 until the switch is done.

GENCTRLn.DIV sets the divider, read according to GENCTRLn.DIVSEL; with DIVSEL=0 a DIV of 0 or 1 leaves the clock undivided. The width of DIV differs between generators. An odd division gives an uneven duty cycle unless GENCTRLn.IDC is set, which makes it 50/50.

With GENCTRLn.OE=1 and the generator enabled, the generator requests its source and drives its clock on its GCLK_IO pin. With OE=0 the pin rests at GENCTRLn.OOV (0 low, 1 high). In Standby an output clock freezes at the OOV level unless GENCTRLn.RUNSTDBY=1, which keeps it running on the pin.

A channel takes any enabled generator through PCHCTRLm.GEN and is switched on by PCHCTRLm.CHEN=1; CHEN crosses into the generic clock domain and reads its old value until that is done, which is how completion is checked (a change during an ongoing crossing raises no error). Clearing CHEN gates the clock. To change a channel's generator without a glitch: clear CHEN, wait until it reads 0, write GEN, set CHEN again.

PCHCTRLm.WRTLOCK=1 ignores all later writes to that channel and also locks the GENCTRLn of its generator; only a power reset unlocks them, not CTRLA.SWRST. Generator 0 cannot be locked, as it makes GCLK_MAIN and restarts in a known state on every reset. After an external reset a locked channel's generator is disabled and its CHEN reads 0 until the generator is enabled again, when CHEN returns to 1.
GENCTRLn and CTRLA are synchronized when written. PCHCTRLm.CHEN is the exception: it is checked by reading it back.

When a peripheral needs its clock in a sleep mode with generic clocks stopped, it asks the GCLK, which wakes the right source and enables the generator and channel in turn to deliver the clock. GENCTRLn.RUNSTDBY decides whether a generator's output keeps reaching its pin in Standby. Entering Standby can be delayed while generators with RUNSTDBY=0 are checked to have stopped cleanly; how long depends on their frequency.
Some peripherals must have a generic clock right after reset, so the reset configuration of generators and channels is device-specific.

The main clock controller makes the synchronous clocks for the CPU and the AHB and APB modules from GCLK_MAIN through a common 8-bit prescaler dividing by 1 to 128. Clocks are grouped in domains that can run at different frequencies, and each module's clock can be masked. Clock switching at run time is safe. MCLK works in every sleep mode where a synchronous clock is needed and keeps running when the CPU halts in debug; in sleep its clocks then stay on for the debugger, so power readings are wrong while debugging. Its bus clock CLK_MCLK_APB, once disabled, comes back only with a reset. MCLK is always enabled and cannot be reset.

There are three synchronous domains: CPU (fCPU), low-power (fLP) and backup (fBUP). The bus clocks stay locked in step with the CPU clock, can be divided, and can run with the CPU clock stopped in sleep; a gate after the common APB clock switches each module's APB and AHB clock. CPU and LP domains can be retuned on the fly as long as fCPU ≥ fLP ≥ fBUP. Maximum frequencies per performance level are in the electrical characteristics.

After reset the default GCLK_MAIN source is started and calibrated before the CPU runs, and the main clock is used undivided with only the needed clocks on. CPUDIV sets the CPU domain division; LPDIV and BUPDIV set the others. Writing a forbidden value stores it but it is not used and the PAC is told of a violation. DIV fields can be written without stopping peripherals, and all clocks of a domain change together.

A new CPUDIV or LPDIV takes a moment to apply; meanwhile INTFLAG.CKRDY reads 0, and with INTENSET.CKRDY=1 an interrupt marks when the setting is in effect. CPUDIV, BUPDIV and LPDIV must not be written again while CKRDY is 0: the system may hang and a PAC violation is reported. CKRDY is the only MCLK interrupt and is a synchronous wake-up source. In Idle MCLK keeps running on the main clock; in Standby it is frozen unless a synchronous clock is needed.

Writing a module's bit in AHBMASK or APBxMASK to 0 or 1 stops or starts its bus clock; a module on several buses has several bits. Without its APB clock a module's registers cannot be read or written. Masking the NVMCTRL clock breaks Flash reads by the CPU, and masking MCLK itself or its APB bridge leaves the mask registers unwritable until a system reset.

The RSTC collects the reset sources, puts the device in its initial state according to the source, and records the latest cause in RCAUSE for software to read at boot. Sources are power-supply resets (POR, BOD12, BOD33), user resets (the RESET pin, the watchdog, and a system reset request from the CPU's SYSRESETREQ bit) and backup resets (a wake from Backup mode by the RTC, an EXTWAKE pin or the battery backup power switch). After power-on RCAUSE shows POR. The RSTC is always on and enabled, runs in every sleep mode and in debug halt, and its bus clock is CLK_RSTC_APB; it has no interrupts, events or DMA.

EXTWAKE pins work only in Backup mode and must be set as inputs in PORT before entering it. They cannot wake the device from battery backup mode, because the pin configuration is lost there. WKEN enables each pin and WKPOL sets its level (0, the default, active low; 1 active high). The enabled pins are ORed into a debounce counter set by WKDBCONF and clocked from OSCULP32K; it runs in Backup mode when at least one pin is enabled and WKDBCONF is not OFF (in other sleep modes it is stopped), and the debouncer needs the 32 kHz clock. A pin held active longer than the debounce time sets BKUPEXIT.EXTWAKE, stores the enabled pins' levels in WKCAUSE and applies a backup reset.

Pulling RESET low makes the external reset. POR, BOD12 and BOD33 resets come from the SUPC, the watchdog reset from the WDT. Backup mode ends on a BBPS wake when the 3.3 V VDDIO returns, on an EXTWAKE pin, or on an RTC interrupt; any of these sets RCAUSE.BACKUP and updates BKUPEXIT.

The PM runs the sleep modes (Idle, Standby, Backup, Off), the two performance levels (PL0, PL2) that scale the core regulator voltage on the fly, and power-domain gating, which switches unused domains off by hardware without software help, or under manual control in Standby. SleepWalking works in Standby, logic state is fully retained in Standby, and I/O pin states can be held through a Backup wake. Interrupts from enabled peripherals and any enabled reset bring the device back to Active. The PM is always enabled and cannot be reset; its bus clock CLK_PM_APB, once disabled, returns only with a system reset. After power-on the device is Active in PL0 with every power domain active.

The PM keeps running when the CPU halts. Standby requested while debugging leaves the power domains on, and Backup requested keeps the core domains and debug modules on; on the reset that ends Backup the core domains reset but the debug logic does not, so the session continues. Power readings in debug are therefore not meaningful. Hot plugging works in Standby unless PD2 is in retention; neither cold nor hot plugging works in Off or Backup.

PL0 gives the best energy efficiency and PL2 the highest operating frequency; each level has its own maximum frequency and µA/MHz figure in the electrical characteristics. Changing level moves the voltage on the whole logic area, and choosing it is up to the application.

Besides the supply domains (VDDIO, VDDIN, VDDANA) there are PD0, PD1, PD2, PDTOP and PDBACKUP. PD0, PD1 and PD2 are switchable: in Standby or Backup they can be off or in retention when none of their peripherals is needed, but a powered domain always powers the lower ones (PD1 active means PD0 active). PD0 holds the event system, GCLK, OSCCTRL, MCLK, SERCOM5, TC4, ADC, AC, OPAMP, CCL, PTC, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M. PD1 holds the DMAC, PAC, low-power bus matrix, TCCs, AES, TRNG, DAC, low-power SRAM, SERCOM0-4 and TC0-3. PD2 holds the Cortex-M0+, NVMCTRL, DSU, USB and the main SRAM. PDTOP holds the remaining core-domain controllers; it is on in Active, Idle and Standby, has no retention, and is fully off in Backup and Off. PDBACKUP, on in every mode but Off, holds the 32 kHz oscillators, SUPC, RSTC, RTC and the PM.

In Standby each switchable domain is active (powered at the performance level), in retention (main supply off, a small supply keeps the flip-flops, and the logic resumes on wake) or off (state lost). Idle stops the CPU while synchronous clocks run only on request and logic is kept; Standby also stops peripherals, keeps logic and allows domain gating; Backup powers only the backup domain (RTC, 32 kHz sources, wake pins); Off powers nothing.

A sleep mode is entered with WFI, at the depth set by SLEEPCFG.SLEEPMODE. The write to SLEEPCFG reaches the register late through the bridges, so software must read back the intended value before WFI.

Idle wakes fastest: the CPU stops but peripherals keep working and still get their bus clocks on request, and the main clock keeps running. Select IDLE in SLEEPCFG, then WFI; with SLEEPONEXIT set in the Cortex SCR, Idle is also entered on return from the lowest-priority ISR, for code that runs only on interrupts. Any unmasked interrupt of enough priority to be taken wakes the CPU back to Active. Generic clocks, regulators and RAM are unaffected.

Standby is the lowest-power mode that keeps logic state and RAM. All clocks stop except those serving SleepWalking, or those kept on by their ONDEMAND and RUNSTDBY settings (for example a SERCOM with RUNSTDBY=1), synchronous or generic. Enter with SLEEPCFG=STANDBY and WFI (SLEEPONEXIT works too). Any peripheral able to raise an asynchronous interrupt wakes it; the CPU then runs the handler or carries on depending on PRIMASK. The regulator runs in low-power mode and switches itself to normal mode when a SleepWalking task needs more power, then back.

Backup is the lowest-power mode short of Off: only the backup domain is powered and its peripherals keep running, for instance the RTC on a 32.768 kHz oscillator. All PM registers reset except CTRLA.IORET. Enter with SLEEPCFG=BACKUP and WFI; it ends on a backup reset seen by the RSTC. Off powers the whole device down; enter with SLEEPCFG=OFF and WFI, and leave by pulling RESET low or by a power reset.

In Backup the PORT is off but pin configuration is held. On exit, CTRLA.IORET=0 releases the pins to the PORT reset state; IORET=1 keeps them as they were until software writes IORET to 0, giving time to set up the PORT.

PLCFG.PLSEL changes the level on the fly, only in Active mode. Going down, lower the bus frequency first so the new level's limit is not exceeded; going up, raise the frequency only once INTFLAG.PLRDY reads 1. The device starts in the lowest level after reset. PLCFG.PLDIS=1 freezes the device in PL0, which lowers power and shortens wake-up from Standby; PLDIS may only be changed while in PL0, and changing it elsewhere, or selecting a higher level while it is 1, is ignored and reported to the PAC. PLRDY is the PM's only interrupt and is a synchronous wake-up source.

With all peripherals idle, Standby puts PD0, PD1 and PD2 in retention and wakes them all to active on exit. Static SleepWalking: a peripheral that must keep running in Standby (a SleepWalking task or RUNSTDBY=1) keeps its domain and the domains below it active, and when the task ends the device may wake or stay asleep. Dynamic SleepWalking: an active domain can bring a higher domain out of retention for a task and let it fall back afterwards. Both are automatic; the domains can also be set by hand.

operation.topic: RAM, NVM and regulators in sleep
operation.text: By default Standby and Backup put RAM, NVM and regulators in low-power mode. RAM goes low-power when its domain is in retention or off in Standby. The NVM, in PD2, goes low-power when PD2 is in retention or off, and in Standby or Idle whenever it is not being read; NVMCTRL CTRLB.SLEEPPRM changes this. In Standby the PM picks the main or low-power regulator for VDDCORE from device activity. Idle changes none of this.

STDBYCFG.PDCFG overrides the automatic choice, for example keeping every domain active in Standby for a faster wake. STDBYCFG.LINKPD links domains: while PDn (n = 0 or 1) is active, the linked higher domains stay active even with nothing to do; with PD1 linked to PD0 (PD01), a static task in PD0 keeps both active, and under dynamic SleepWalking PD1 follows PD0.

By default RAM is back-biased (low-power) when its domain is in retention in Standby; the STDBYCFG.BBIASxx fields change this. In Standby the DMAC can reach the LP SRAM only while PD1 is out of retention and BBIASLP=0x0, and the main SRAM only while PD2 is out of retention and BBIASHS=0x0.

In Standby the low-power regulator feeds VDDCORE when every switchable domain is in retention; a SleepWalking task on generic or bus clocks brings in the main regulator. STDBYCFG.VREGSMOD changes this.

SleepWalking briefly starts a peripheral's clocks for a task while the CPU stays in Standby; afterwards an interrupt from that peripheral wakes the device or it returns to Standby. On this device it works only on generic clocks, through on-demand clock sources. The task runs at the performance level set for Active mode and on the main regulator chosen for Active mode (LDO or buck).

Wake from Standby adds up: bringing domains out of retention (zero if they stayed active, which PDCFG or LINKPD can force); the main regulator rising from the lower ULP-regulator voltage back to the level of the performance level, for example PL2; the start-up of the CPU clock source; the first NVM access; and, with back-bias on, the regulator settling after retention. Times are in the electrical characteristics.

All peripherals support SleepWalking with static domain gating; some need CTRLA.RUNSTDBY=1. An AC in continuous measurement with RUNSTDBY=1 keeps PD0 active while PD2 and PD1 go to retention; its interrupt brings PD1 then PD2 back before the CPU runs the handler, and since the main regulator stayed on only the domain wake adds to the time. A TC0 counting with RUNSTDBY=1 keeps PD1 (and PD0 with the clock generator) active and only PD2 retires. An EIC filtering a pin with CLK_ULP32K needs no GCLK and sits in PDTOP, which is never switched and has no RUNSTDBY: all switchable domains retire and the low-power regulator feeds VDDCORE, so the wake adds both domain and main-regulator start-up time.

With dynamic domain gating a domain moves between retention and active by itself. A DMAC AHB transfer aimed at PD2 brings PD2 out of retention for the transfer and lets it fall back afterwards, the CPU still asleep; for example a DMAC with RUNSTDBY moving data from a PD1 peripheral to SRAM on each periodic request, waking the device at the end of a block.

Needs STDBYCFG.DPGPD0 and DPGPD1 set to 1. An event aimed at a domain in retention makes it active; the event users concerned are in PD0 and PD1. With PD0, PD1 and PD2 all in retention the trigger can be an AC output event, an RTC output event or an EIC output event when the EIC runs on CLK_ULP32K. With PD0 active and PD1, PD2 in retention: the RTC or EIC (on CLK_ULP32K) events, or any event-capable PD0 peripheral (all of PD0 can), with the EVSYS generator on the synchronous or resynchronized path. With PD0 and PD1 both in retention it is of no use. Example: the AC in single shot with RUNSTDBY=1, GCLK_AC from a 32.768 kHz oscillator (OSCULP32K for low power) and periodic RTC events through EVSYS; PD0 rises with the main regulator for each measurement and falls back unless the result calls for an interrupt, which wakes PD1 and PD2.

Needs STDBYCFG.DPGPD0 and DPGPD1 set to 1. A valid DMA trigger from a PD0 peripheral (its DMAC channel enabled with RUNSTDBY=1) brings PD1, holding the DMAC, out of retention. Example: the ADC on GCLK_ADC from OSCULP32K, triggered by periodic RTC events through EVSYS, with ADC, DMAC and the channel all set to run in Standby; each conversion lifts PD0, its result-ready request lifts PD1 so the DMAC moves the sample to LP SRAM, and then both fall back, until the DMAC's block-done interrupt wakes the device after N samples. A PD1 peripheral woken by a PD0 event keeps PD1 active until its follow-up task ends if it supports SleepWalking, and stays active with PD1 afterwards if it does not.

OSCCTRL is the interface to four sources for the GCLK: XOSC, a 0.4-32 MHz crystal oscillator with tunable gain, programmable start-up and crystal or external clock on XIN; OSC16M, a fast-starting internal oscillator at 4, 8, 12 or 16 MHz; DFLL48M, a 48 MHz internal oscillator needing no external parts, free-running in open loop or locked to a known clock as a multiplier in closed loop; and FDPLL96M, a fractional PLL giving 48 to 96 MHz from a 32 kHz to 2 MHz reference of several possible sources, with an adjustable PI controller and 1/16 fractional steps. Status bits are gathered in STATUS and can interrupt. OSCCTRL works in any sleep mode where its source runs, its interrupts can wake the device, and it keeps running in debug halt. Its bus clock is CLK_OSCCTRL_APB.

A 0.4-32 MHz crystal goes between XIN and XOUT with whatever load capacitors it needs, or an external clock drives XIN. At reset XOSC is off and both pins are GPIO. XOSCCTRL.ENABLE=1 starts it; XTALEN=1 selects the crystal, which takes both pins, and XTALEN=0 the external clock on XIN, leaving XOUT free as GPIO. In crystal mode XOSCCTRL.GAIN must match the crystal frequency; AMPGC=1 adjusts amplitude automatically, usually lowering current. After reset or a sleep where it was off, the output is masked for the start-up time set in XOSCCTRL.STARTUP; STATUS.XOSCRDY then sets, with an interrupt if enabled.

An open-loop internal oscillator at 4, 8, 12 or 16 MHz chosen by OSC16MCTRL.FSEL, which may only change while the oscillator is off. OSC16MCTRL.ENABLE starts and stops it; its clock is passed on once STATUS.OSC16MRDY is 1, and before enabling it again software must see OSC16MRDY at 0. After reset it is on at 4 MHz as the default clock.

Every reset selects open loop. The output frequency is then set by DFLLVAL.COARSE and DFLLVAL.FINE, which may be changed while the DFLL runs. Writing COARSE with the factory 'DFLL48M COARSE CAL' word, kept in the NVM software calibration area, puts the output near 48 MHz.

Closed loop keeps the output locked to an accurate low-frequency reference, CLK_DFLL48M_REF, which is generic clock channel 0. Before setting DFLLCTRL.MODE=1: enable the reference; choose the largest coarse and fine steps the tuner may take in DFLLMUL.CSTEP and FSTEP (small steps overshoot less but lock more slowly; keep each at no more than half the maximum of COARSE and FINE); and set the multiplier DFLLMUL.MUL so the output stays under the device maximum (a target below the DFLL minimum gives the minimum).

Locking starts from the current COARSE and FINE (read-only in closed loop) in two stages: coarse lock finds COARSE and sets STATUS.DFLLLCKC; fine lock tunes FINE and sets STATUS.DFLLLCKF; each can interrupt. Accuracy depends on which locks are held. Starting COARSE near its final value shortens coarse lock; for 48 MHz the procedure is to load 'DFLL48M COARSE CAL' into COARSE, set DFLLCTRL.BPLCKC=1 to skip coarse lock, and set MODE=1, leaving only the fine lock time.

With DFLLCTRL.STABLE=0 the tuner follows drift without losing lock, so FINE may change after every measurement. Large drift or an unstable reference can push FINE past its range, setting STATUS.DFLLOOB (with an interrupt if enabled, also raised when coarse lock fails); MUL must then be written again. A stable reference such as the XOSC32K avoids this. If the reference stops or falls below CLK_DFLL48M/(2 × MULMAX), STATUS.DFLLRCS sets, which can take a long time to detect, on the order of 217 CLK_DFLL48M cycles; the DFLL then runs as in open loop and closed loop resumes by itself when the reference returns.

operation.topic: DFLL48M settling, chill cycles and quick lock
operation.text: A new output frequency can take several microseconds to appear, and a small MUL can make locking unstable. Chill cycles, on by default and turned off by DFLLCTRL.CCDIS=1, skip the frequency measurement for a cycle and may double the lock time. Quick lock, also on by default and turned off by DFLLCTRL.QLDIS=1, relaxes the lock criteria, giving more spread in frequency but the same average.

With DFLLCTRL.USBCRM and MODE both 1 the DFLL locks to the USB start-of-frame, one every 1 ms, instead of its generic clock reference; a multiplier of 0xBB80 gives 48 MHz. BPLCKC is ignored and the COARSE value, which software can load from the NVM calibration row, is taken as final, so locking goes straight to the fine search. QLDIS must be 0 and CCDIS should be 1 for a faster lock; STABLE is ignored and an automatic jitter reduction is used instead.

operation.topic: DFLL48M wake from sleep and accuracy
operation.text: With DFLLCTRL.LLAW=0 the DFLL restarts after being disabled with its previous settings and locks, even without the reference, and fine tracking then corrects any drift once the reference is back (with STABLE=0). With LLAW=1 it loses its locks when disabled and must lock again from the start. Accuracy at fine lock depends on the fine step size (relatively smaller at higher output frequencies), on the measurement resolution (a small output-to-reference ratio can lock below target, so a reference of 32 kHz or lower is advised for low targets) and on the reference's own accuracy.

The DPLL keeps its output CLK_DPLL in phase with a reference: XOSC32K, XOSC (through a divider) or a generic clock, chosen by DPLLCTRLB.REFCLK. Disabled, its output is low. DPLLRATIO.LDRFRAC=0 gives integer mode; otherwise fractional mode, which adds jitter. Examples: 32 kHz in and 48 MHz out is a ratio of 1500, so LDR=1499; 48.006 MHz out is 1500.1875 (1500 + 3/16), so LDR=1499 and LDRFRAC=3.

DPLLCTRLA.ENABLE starts and stops it; DPLLSYNCBUSY.ENABLE sets on any change and clears once the output CK has seen the enable (or, on disable, once CK has stopped). The output is stable when enabled and DPLLSTATUS.LOCK is set. With DPLLCTRLB.LTIME non-zero a fixed, user-set lock time validates the lock; with LTIME=0 the lock follows the DPLL's own status and its time depends on filter and target frequency. DPLLCTRLB.WUF=1 opens the clock gate at the end of start-up before the frequency has settled, saving several milliseconds. After the first edge, DPLLCTRLB.LBYPASS=1 keeps CLK_DPLL running regardless of lock.

operation.topic: FDPLL96M reference switching, prescaler, ratio and filter
operation.text: To change reference, put the DPLL in standby, change DPLLCTRLB.REFCLK, then activate it again. The output prescaler DPLLPRESC.PRESC selects CK, CK/2 or CK/4, and DPLLSYNCBUSY.DPLLPRESC is set until the change is synchronized. DPLLRATIO can be rewritten while running: STATUS.DPLLLDRTO sets once the new ratio is taken, LOCK clears and sets again when the frequency settles. The PI loop filter adjusts itself between stability and jitter, but DPLLCTRLB.FILTER can override it, and DPLLCTRLB.LPEN bypasses the time-to-digital converter.

Interrupts, all synchronous wake-up sources on one shared line, flag a 0-to-1 change of XOSCRDY, OSC16MRDY, DFLLRDY, DFLLOOB, DFLLLCKF, DFLLLCKC, DFLLRCS, DPLLLCKR, DPLLLCKF, DPLLLTTO and DPLLLDRTO. Once the DFLL is enabled every access to its registers needs STATUS.DFLLRDY=1; writes while it is 0 are ignored, and in on-demand mode it stays 0 until a peripheral asks for the DFLL. DFLLCTRL, DFLLVAL and DFLLMUL are write-synchronized. To read DFLLVAL in closed loop, first write DFLLSYNC.READREQ=1, since the tuner may be changing it; a read during an update, or during any ongoing write synchronization, returns 0. For the DPLL, DPLLCTRLA.ENABLE, DPLLRATIO and DPLLPRESC are synchronized on write, with their DPLLSYNCBUSY bit set until done.

OSC32KCTRL runs three 32.768 kHz sources for the GCLK, RTC and WDT: XOSC32K, a crystal oscillator or external clock on XIN32 with programmable start-up; OSC32K, a high-accuracy internal oscillator with fine tuning and programmable start-up; and OSCULP32K, an ultra-low-power, always-on internal oscillator with fine tuning. Calibration is loaded from Flash at reset and 1.024 kHz outputs are available. It works in any sleep mode where a 32 kHz source runs, its interrupts can wake the device, and it runs in debug halt. Its bus clock is CLK_OSC32KCTRL_APB.

The production calibration of OSC32K is not loaded by hardware: software copies it from the NVM software calibration area into OSC32K.CALIB to reach the specified accuracy. Before USB is used, PADCAL must likewise be loaded from that area.

A 32.768 kHz crystal goes between XIN32 and XOUT32 with any load capacitors it needs (values in the electrical characteristics), or an external clock drives XIN32. At reset it is off and both pins are GPIO. XOSC32K.ENABLE starts it; XTALEN=1 selects the crystal, taking both pins, and XTALEN=0 the external clock, leaving XOUT32 as GPIO. EN32K enables the 32.768 kHz output and EN1K the 1.024 kHz output, which only the RTC can use; the output must be enabled before the GCLK or RTC using it is enabled, and those must be disabled before changing their clock selection. WRTLOCK=1 freezes the configuration until a POR. Because a crystal starts slowly, with ONDEMAND=0 it keeps running through every reset except POR. After reset or a sleep where it was off, its output is masked for the time set in XOSC32K.STARTUP, then STATUS.XOSC32KRDY sets, with an interrupt if enabled.

A tunable low-speed, low-power internal source, off at reset and switched by OSC32K.ENABLE. Its frequency is set by OSC32K.CALIB, which must hold the production value; after writing CALIB, wait for STATUS.OSC32KRDY before the value takes effect. EN32K enables its 32.768 kHz output and EN1K the 1.024 kHz output for the RTC; outputs must be enabled before the GCLK or RTC using them, which must be disabled before their clock selection changes. WRTLOCK=1 freezes the configuration until a POR. With ONDEMAND=0 it keeps running through every reset except POR. After reset or a sleep where it was off, its output is masked for the time set in OSC32K.STARTUP, then STATUS.OSC32KRDY sets.

A tunable ultra-low-power source, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature; the choice over OSC32K when power matters more than frequency stability and accuracy. It is on after POR and runs at all times except during POR. OSCULP32K.CALIB, which corrects process spread, is loaded from Flash at start-up and may be overwritten by software. WRTLOCK=1 freezes the configuration until a POR. It can clock the GCLK or the RTC, which must be disabled before their clock selection changes.

The WDT runs on the 1.024 kHz output of OSCULP32K, which always runs and is enabled internally when the WDT asks. The RTC clock is chosen in RTCCTRL before the RTC is enabled; any oscillator output can serve, and the RTC should be disabled before the choice changes.
XOSC32KRDY and OSC32KRDY flag a 0-to-1 change of the matching STATUS bit; both are synchronous wake-up sources on one shared interrupt line.

The SUPC manages the core (VDDCORE) and backup (VDDBU) regulators, voltage references, supply monitoring and two output pins. Regulators: the main regulator, an LDO or a buck converter switchable in Active mode (MAINVREG); a low-power regulator for Standby (LPVREG); and a backup regulator, with a controlled VDDCORE slope on each change. A battery on VBAT backs the backup domain with automatic switching both ways, optional automatic entry to and exit from Backup mode, and a request for main power on Backup wake-up sources. It provides references for ADC and DAC and a temperature sensor. BOD33 watches VDD or VBAT with a programmable threshold, continuous or sampled, its threshold, action (reset, interrupt or battery switch) and hysteresis loaded from Flash at start-up; BOD12, internal and not configurable, watches VDDCORE. The outputs can toggle on RTC events. The SUPC works in every sleep mode except Backup, where BOD33 and the battery switch still run. Its bus clock is CLK_SUPC_APB, and sampled BOD mode needs a 32 kHz clock.
When a debugger cold-plug is detected, BOD33 and BOD12 resets are masked, so a BOD33 level set too high for the supply can be corrected; under hot plugging the BOD resets stay active.

The LDO feeds VDDCORE after any reset. VREG.ENABLE=0 disables the main regulator, whose output level follows the sleep mode chosen in the PM. In Active mode VREG.SEL switches between LDO and buck on the fly: STATUS.VREGRDY drops to 0 when the switch starts and returns to 1 when it is done, which the VREGRDY interrupt can signal.

VDDCORE changes on a new performance level, on entering or leaving Standby, and on a SleepWalking request in Standby. To limit peak supply current it moves in steps of VREG.VSVSTEP every VREG.VSPER until it reaches the target; VSVSTEP at its maximum makes the change in one step. STATUS.VCORERDY reads 0 during the change and 1 at the target, with a VCORERDY interrupt. Entering Standby with no SleepWalking request does not use this scaling.
In Standby LPVREG feeds VDDCORE. With VREG.RUNSTDBY=1 the main regulator does instead, at PL0 when VREG.STDBYPL0=1 or at the current level otherwise.

DETREF in the SUPC makes a fixed BANDGAP of 1.1 V and an adjustable INTREF whose level, set by VREF.SEL, goes to analog modules such as the ADC. The reference output (VREF.VREFOE) and temperature sensor (VREF.TSEN) are off after any reset. With VREF.ONDEMAND=0, enabling both at once is advised against: only the reference output then appears on both ADC inputs. VREF.RUNSTDBY and VREF.ONDEMAND set their behaviour in sleep.

The BBPS is off at power-up and the backup domain runs from main power. BBPS.CONF=0x2 (FORCED) always feeds it from VBAT. Otherwise switching to VBAT is automatic, by the automatic power switch (CONF=APWS; STATUS.APWSRDY and INTFLAG.APWSRDY set when it is ready) or by BOD33 (CONF=BOD33: VDD below the BOD33 threshold moves the backup domain to VBAT). Switching back to VDD is by the APWS, or, when CONF is not APWS and BBPS.PSOKEN=1, by a rising edge on the PSOK pin as VDD returns; with PSOKEN=0 and CONF not APWS the device cannot restart. STATUS.BBPS shows whether VDD or VBAT feeds the backup domain. The switch runs in every sleep mode.

operation.topic: Entering and leaving battery backup mode
operation.text: Backup mode is entered by WFI, by the APWS detecting loss of main power, or by BOD33 detecting it with BOD33.ACTION=BKUP, BOD33.VMON=VDD and BBPS.CONF=BOD33; in the last two the backup domain moves to the battery. It is left on RTC requests or external RSTC requests, whether the backup domain is on main power with the switch not forced, or the switch is forced; on battery the device stays in backup mode until main power returns and takes over the backup domain. With CONF=APWS, the return of main power wakes the device if BBPS.WAKEEN=1, or only moves the backup domain to main power with WAKEEN=0. A rising PSOK edge wakes it if PSOKEN=1, WAKEEN=1 and CONF is not APWS; with WAKEEN=0 it only restores main power to the backup domain.
BKOUT.EN hands an OUTx pin to the SUPC; BKOUT.SETx drives it high and BKOUT.CLRx low, and with BKOUT.RTCTGLx=1 it toggles on each RTC event.

Before enabling BOD33, set its threshold (BOD33.LEVEL), its configuration in Active, Standby and Backup, the prescaler for sampled mode (PSEL), and the action and hysteresis. The BOD33 register is enable-protected: it can be written only while ENABLE=0 and SYNCBUSY.BOD33EN=0, other writes are dropped with an APB error, and the enable bit itself is exempt. BOD33 and BOD12 settings are loaded from the NVM user row after power-on or user reset.

BOD33.VMON chooses VDD or VBAT to watch in Active and Standby; in Backup it always watches whichever feeds the backup domain. VDD is compared with BOD33.LEVEL in every mode except Backup, which uses BOD33.BKUPLEVEL; crossing below it raises an interrupt, a reset or the battery switch, as BOD33.ACTION says. VBAT is compared with BKUPLEVEL, and crossing below gives an interrupt or a reset. STATUS.BOD33DET shows the detection. Continuous mode is the default (ACTCFG=0 in Active, STDBYCFG=0 in Standby). Sampled mode (ACTCFG=1 or STDBYCFG=1) powers the detector only briefly on each tick of a sampling clock derived from the 1 kHz OSCULP32K output, staying off in between; the clock domains then need synchronization. BOD33.HYST=1 adds hysteresis, separating the falling (VBOD-) and rising (VBOD+) thresholds so ripple does not toggle the reset, in either mode.

BOD12 is calibrated in production with its setting kept in the NVM user row, which must not be changed. It resets the device when VDDCORE falls below its level, is always off in Standby, and is turned off automatically in Backup.

In Standby BOD33 works when enabled with BOD33.RUNSTDBY=1, continuous or sampled as set by STDBYCFG. In Backup, with BOD33.RUNBKUP=1, it runs in sampled mode on the supply of the backup domain, VDD or VBAT.

Interrupts on one shared line: VCORERDY, APWSRDY, VREGRDY and BOD33DET are asynchronous wake-up sources; BOD33RDY and B33SRDY are synchronous. BOD33.ENABLE crosses into the asynchronous prescaler domain on write: STATUS.B33SRDY clears when it starts and sets when it ends, and writing the register meanwhile gives an error without stalling the APB.

The watchdog is a timer that, once enabled, runs all the time and resets the system unless software clears it within a set time-out. An early-warning interrupt can fire before the time-out. In window mode the clear must also not come too early: a clear before the window opens resets the system as well, which catches code that clears the watchdog too often. It runs in Active and in the sleep modes from its own clock, independent of the CPU, so it still resets or interrupts if the main clocks fail.

Reset on missed clear; early-warning interrupt; asynchronous operation from a dedicated oscillator; Normal and Window modes; time-out from 8 to 16,384 cycles in Normal mode and from 16 to 32,768 cycles in Window mode; Always-On option.

The bus clock CLK_WDT_APB is masked in MCLK. The counter runs from a 1 kHz clock, CLK_WDT_OSC, which must be set up and enabled in OSC32KCTRL first; it normally comes from the ultra-low-power OSCULP32K, whose accuracy is low, so the real time-out differs between devices and software must allow for the spread. Because CLK_WDT_OSC and the bus clock are unrelated, some register writes are synchronized. The WDT keeps running in any sleep mode whose clock runs, and its interrupt can wake the device. It has no I/O lines, DMA or events. It halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger. Every writable register except INTFLAG can be write-protected by the PAC; debugger accesses are not protected.

CTRLA (except ENABLE), CONFIG and EWCTRL are enable-protected: they can be written only while CTRLA.ENABLE=0. Protected CTRLA bits may be written in the same write that sets ENABLE to 1, not in the one that clears it. Set the time-out in CONFIG.PER; for Window mode also set CTRLA.WEN=1 and the closed-window length in CONFIG.WINDOW.

operation.topic: WDT reset values from the user row
operation.text: After a power-on reset, CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLA.ALWAYSON, CTRLA.WEN, CONFIG.WINDOW, CONFIG.PER and EWCTRL.EWOFFSET are loaded from the NVM user row.
Writing CTRLA.ENABLE=1 starts the watchdog and writing 0 stops it, but it can be stopped only while CTRLA.ALWAYSON=0.

CONFIG.PER sets the time-out (TOWDT). Writing 0xA5 to CLEAR restarts the period; writing any other value to CLEAR resets the system at once. There are 12 time-out settings, from 8 ms to 16 s. The early-warning interrupt is off by default; INTENSET.EW=1 turns it on and INTENCLR.EW=1 off. In Normal mode EWCTRL.EWOFFSET sets when it fires.

Two periods follow each other: a closed window TOWDTW set by CONFIG.WINDOW, then an open window TOWDT set by CONFIG.PER. Writing 0xA5 to CLEAR is accepted only in the open window; a clear during the closed window resets the system. Each period ranges from 8 ms to 16 s, and the full time-out is their sum. With the early-warning interrupt enabled, it fires as the open window starts, after TOWDTW.

One source, Early Warning (EW), raised as the counter nears time-out; it is an asynchronous wake-up source. The flag is in INTFLAG, enabled through INTENSET and disabled through INTENCLR; the request stays active until the flag clears, the source is turned off or the WDT resets. All WDT requests share one NVIC line.

The WDT runs in every sleep mode whose clock is active except Backup, and its interrupt can wake the device; without an enabled interrupt in the NVIC the CPU simply resumes after the sleep instruction. Writes to CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLA.WEN, CTRLA.ALWAYSON and CLEAR are synchronized.

Setting CTRLA.ALWAYSON=1 keeps the watchdog running whatever CTRLA.ENABLE says; only a power-on reset clears the bit. While it is set, CONFIG and EWCTRL are read-only, so PER, WINDOW and EWOFFSET are fixed. CTRLA.WEN may still be changed to enter or leave Window mode, and the early-warning interrupt may still be enabled or disabled through INTENSET and INTENCLR.

In Normal mode EWCTRL.EWOFFSET gives the number of CLK_WDT_OSC cycles from the start of the period to the early-warning interrupt. An offset longer than the time-out means the reset comes first and the interrupt never fires. In Window mode the interrupt fires as the open window starts, which lets a sleeping system wake, clear the watchdog and go back to sleep. Example: with CONFIG.PER=0x2 and EWCTRL.EWOFFSET=0x1, Normal mode gives the interrupt 16 CLK_WDT_OSC cycles into the period and the reset 32 cycles in.

The real-time counter is a 32-bit counter behind a 10-bit programmable prescaler, normally left running to keep time. It can wake the device from sleep on an alarm or compare match, on a periodic tick or on overflow. Prescaler outputs give periodic events; compare and alarm matches give interrupts and events at any count; overflow gives an interrupt and event; and the counter can clear itself on a match, so long and accurate periodic intervals are possible. From a 32.768 kHz source the shortest tick is 30.5 µs and time-outs reach 36 hours; with a 1 s tick the longest time-out is over 136 years.

A 32-bit counter fed by a 10-bit prescaler, clocked from a choice of sources and usable whole or as a 16-bit counter, compared against a single 32-bit value or a pair of 16-bit values; a calendar mode with seconds, minutes, hours (12 or 24 hour), day, month, year and leap-year correction; digital prescaler correction for accuracy; overflow, alarm/compare and prescaler interrupts and events, with optional clear on match; two general-purpose registers.

The RTC keeps running in any sleep mode whose clock runs; its interrupts can wake the device and its events can act on other peripherals without waking it. It is reset only by power-on or by CTRLA.SWRST=1. The bus clock CLK_RTC_APB is masked in MCLK. The counter needs a 32 kHz or 1 kHz clock, CLK_RTC_OSC, set up and enabled in OSC32KCTRL first; it is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes are synchronized. The RTC halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL forces it to run. All writable registers except INTFLAG and the GPx registers can be write-protected by the PAC. A 32.768 kHz crystal with its load capacitors goes on XIN32 and XOUT32.
CTRLA.MODE selects Mode 0 (COUNT32, a 32-bit counter), Mode 1 (COUNT16, a 16-bit counter) or Mode 2 (CLOCK, a clock/calendar with alarm).

CTRLA.MODE, CTRLA.PRESCALER, CTRLA.MATCHCLR, CTRLA.CLKREP and the EVCTRL register are enable-protected. To change them on a running RTC, write CTRLA.ENABLE=0, wait for its synchronization to finish, then write the field. Protected bits can be written with the write that sets ENABLE, not with the one that clears it. The prescaler divides CLK_RTC_OSC to give the counter clock CLK_RTC_CNT; in Clock/Calendar mode it must give 1 Hz.
CTRLA.ENABLE=1 starts the RTC and 0 stops it. CTRLA.SWRST=1 returns every register except DEBUG to its reset value and disables the RTC; the RTC must be disabled first.

With CTRLA.MODE=0x0 the counter counts up on each rising edge of CLK_RTC_CNT to 0xFFFFFFFF, then wraps to 0 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. COUNT is read and written as 32 bits. It is compared with the 32-bit COMP register continuously; a match sets INTFLAG.CMP0 on the next rising edge of CLK_RTC_CNT. With CTRLA.MATCHCLR=1 the counter clears on the cycle after a match, giving periodic interrupts or events longer than the prescaler can make; CMP0 and OVF are then set together on the match.

With CTRLA.MODE=0x1 the counter counts up on each rising edge of CLK_RTC_CNT to the value in the 16-bit PER register, then wraps to 0 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. COUNT is read and written as 16 bits. It is compared with the two 16-bit registers COMP0 and COMP1; a match sets INTFLAG.CMPn on the next rising edge of CLK_RTC_CNT.

With CTRLA.MODE=0x2 the counter advances on each rising edge of CLK_RTC_CNT, which must be 1 Hz. CLOCK holds time and date in one 32-bit word: seconds, minutes and hours, in 12- or 24-hour form chosen by CTRLA.CLKREP (changeable only while disabled); day of month from 1; month from 1 (January); and a year value from 0x00 to 0x3F that is added to a reference year of the user's choosing, which must be a leap year (2016, 2020 ...): year value 0x2D on reference 2016 is 2061. After 23:59:59 on December 31 of year 0x3F the clock wraps to 00:00:00 January 1 of year 0x00 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. CLOCK is compared with the 32-bit ALARM0 register; a match sets INTFLAG.ALARM0 on the next rising edge of CLK_RTC_CNT, so with a 1 Hz clock the flag comes 1 s after the match.

operation.topic: RTC alarm mask and clear on match
operation.text: MASK.SEL chooses which time and date fields take part in the alarm comparison and which are ignored. With CTRLA.MATCHCLR=1 the clock clears on the cycle after an alarm match, for periodic interrupts or events longer than the prescaler can make; ALARM0 and OVF are then set together on the match.

Sources: Overflow (OVF), the counter wrapped from its top value to zero; Compare (CMPn), counter equals a compare register; Alarm (ALARM), clock equals an alarm register; Period n (PERn), a prescaler bit toggled. Each has a flag in INTFLAG, enabled through INTENSET and disabled through INTENCLR; a request stays active until its flag clears, the source is turned off or the RTC resets. All share one NVIC line.
Output events OVF, CMPn, ALARM and PERn, with the same meanings as the interrupts, each turned on by its EVCTRL.xxxEO bit.

The RTC runs in any sleep mode whose clock is active; its interrupts wake the device and its events can act on other peripherals without waking it. Without an enabled interrupt in the NVIC the CPU resumes after the sleep instruction.

Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, and the COUNT, CLOCK, PER, COMPn, ALARMn, FREQCORR and MASKn registers. Synchronized on read: COUNT when CTRLA.COUNTSYNC=1, and CLOCK when CTRLA.CLOCKSYNC=1.

Any of prescaler bits 2 to 9 can raise an interrupt or event. With EVCTRL.PEREOn=1 (n = 0 to 7) an event comes on each rising edge of the matching prescaler bit: PER0 every 8 CLK_RTC_OSC cycles, PER1 every 16, and so on. These events do not depend on the counter's prescaler setting, except that with CTRLA.PRESCALER=0 none are produced.

Digital correction compensates an oscillator that runs slow or fast, and needs CTRLA.PRESCALER greater than 1. Once every 4096 CLK_RTC_OSC cycles the prescaler gains or skips one count; FREQCORR.VALUE says how many times this is done in 240 such periods, giving steps of about 1 ppm (1.017 ppm resolution). FREQCORR.SIGN picks the direction: positive adds counts, lengthening the period and lowering the frequency; negative removes counts and raises it. The correction also moves the periodic events: the interval in which it lands is lengthened or shortened.
Two registers, GPn, are reset only with the RTC and stay powered as long as the RTC is, so they hold user values while the rest of the system is powered off.

The DMAC holds a DMA engine and a CRC engine. The DMA moves data between memories and peripherals without the CPU, reaching every peripheral. Its channels each take triggers and send transfer requests to an arbiter, which grants one active channel at a time. The fetch engine loads the granted channel's transfer descriptor from the low-power SRAM into the active channel's internal memory, and the transfer runs from there. A higher-priority channel can interrupt a transfer: the updated descriptor is written back to LP SRAM and the other channel takes over. A finished channel can raise interrupts and events. The DMAC has four bus interfaces: data transfer, descriptor fetch and write-back, all AHB masters, and the register interface through the AHB/APB bridge, an APB slave. The CRC engine checks data for accidental errors.

Transfers between any mix of memory and peripherals, either one as source and either one as destination. Triggers from software, from the event system, or from dedicated peripheral requests. Transfer descriptors in SRAM: one descriptor for a single transfer, or linked descriptors for multi-buffer or circular buffers. Up to 16 channels, each with its own descriptor fetch and suspend/resume. Four priority levels per channel, with fixed or round-robin order within a level. 1 to 256 KB in one block transfer.
