Static or incrementing addresses with configurable step. Interrupts on block complete, error and channel suspend. Four event inputs and four event outputs, one each on the four lowest channels; inputs can trigger normal, periodic or conditional transfers or suspend and resume a channel; outputs can mark AHB, block or transaction completion. A write-back section per channel stores the ongoing descriptor for error handling. CRC polynomial selectable between CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) and CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3).

The DMAC runs in any sleep mode whose clock runs; its interrupts can wake the device and its events act without waking it. Hardware or software reset returns all registers to reset values. The bus clock CLK_DMAC_APB must be enabled first; it keeps in step with the module clock CLK_DMAC_AHB, yet can be divided down and can keep running while the module clock is stopped. The DMAC halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL forces it to run. All writable registers except INTPEND, CHID and CHINTFLAG can be write-protected by the PAC.

A beat is one access of the data transfer bus, sized by BTCTRL.BEATSIZE. A block is what one descriptor moves, 1 to 64k beats, and it can be interrupted. A transaction is the whole list of linked descriptors, each pointing to the next. Descriptors must stay in LP SRAM.

A software, event or peripheral trigger on a channel sends a request to the arbiter, which picks the active channel when several are pending. A higher-priority channel can interrupt a transaction, which resumes when its channel is granted again. Each beat can give an output event; each block can give interrupts and an output event. At the end of a transaction the channel is suspended or disabled, as configured.
Two polynomials, CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) and CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3), computed on the data of a chosen DMA channel or on data written through the I/O interface.

BASEADDR and WRBADDR can be written only while CTRL.DMAENABLE=0. CTRL.SWRST only while both DMAENABLE and CRCENABLE are 0. A channel's CHCTRLB (except CMD and LVL) and CHCTRLA.SWRST only while that channel is disabled (CHCTRLA.ENABLE=0). CRCCTRL and CRCCHKSUM only while CTRL.CRCENABLE=0.

Before enabling the DMAC: write the LP SRAM address of the descriptor section to BASEADDR and of the write-back section to WRBADDR, and enable each priority level wanted with CTRL.LVLENx=1. Before enabling a channel: write its number to CHID, choose the trigger action in CHCTRLB.TRIGACT and the trigger source in CHCTRLB.TRIGSRC; in its first descriptor set BTCTRL.BEATSIZE, set BTCTRL.VALID=1, and write BTCNT (beats), SRCADDR and DSTADDR. Before enabling the CRC: choose its input in CRCCTRL.CRCSRC and the polynomial in CRCCTRL.CRCPOLY, and for I/O input the beat size in CRCCTRL.CRCBEATSIZE.

CTRL.DMAENABLE turns the DMAC on and off. A channel is turned on or off with CHCTRLA.ENABLE after writing its number to CHID.ID. CTRL.CRCENABLE turns the CRC on and off. CTRL.SWRST, written while DMAC and CRC are disabled, resets every register except DBGCTRL. CHCTRLA.SWRST, after selecting the channel in CHID.ID, resets that channel's registers, and takes effect only while the channel is disabled.

A channel's first descriptor must be set up and valid (BTCTRL.VALID) before the channel is enabled and triggered; it describes the first block of the transaction. All descriptors live in LP SRAM. BASEADDR points at the descriptor section, which holds the first descriptor of every channel in one contiguous run ordered by channel number, starting with channel 0. WRBADDR points at the write-back section, where the DMAC keeps the ongoing descriptor of each channel, likewise contiguous and in channel order. Each descriptor holds BTCTRL, BTCNT, SRCADDR, DSTADDR and DESCADDR, the address of the next descriptor.
The descriptor and write-back sections may be separate or the same (BASEADDR=WRBADDR). Kept separate, a channel's transaction can be run again without rewriting its first descriptor.

An enabled, unsuspended channel that receives a trigger sends a request; the arbiter queues it and sets PENDCH.PENDCHx, which clears when the channel is granted. On the first granted transfer of a request BUSYCH.BUSYCHx sets and stays set through later grants. After its granted transfers a channel goes back in the queue (BUSYCHx stays 1), or waits for a trigger, is suspended or is disabled (BUSYCHx clears). Suspending a pending channel removes it from the queue but leaves PENDCHx set, and resuming puts it back; disabling a pending channel removes it and clears PENDCHx.

ACTIVE.LVLEXx is set while a level has a pending or transferring channel. CHCTRLB.LVL gives each channel one of four levels; with all levels enabled, a higher level number wins. Each level is enabled by CTRL.LVLENx=1. Within a level, PRICTRL0.RRLVLENx=0 selects static order, where the lower channel number wins and high channels may never be served. PRICTRL0.RRLVLENx=1 selects round-robin: the last channel granted drops to lowest priority for the next grant, and its number is kept in PRICTRL0.LVLPRIx.

Once granted, the channel's descriptor is fetched over the fetch bus from the descriptor section for a new block or from the write-back section for an ongoing one, and data move over the data transfer bus from the current source to the current destination. Arbitration runs after every transfer. If the same channel wins again, BTCNT drops by the beats moved, the beat event fires if enabled, and the next transfer starts; if another wins, BTCNT is written back before the other descriptor is fetched. When BTCNT reaches zero, BTCTRL.VALID is cleared and the descriptor is written back; the transfer-complete and suspend interrupts and the block event follow if enabled. After the last block DESCADDR is 0x00000000 and the channel is suspended or disabled per BTCTRL.BLOCKACT; otherwise DESCADDR points to the next descriptor, which is fetched and copied to the write-back section before the next arbitration.

A transfer starts only when a request is seen and the channel is granted. Triggers come from software, a peripheral or an event, each channel choosing its source in CHCTRLB.TRIGSRC. CHCTRLB.TRIGACT sets what one trigger moves: a block (0x0, the default), a beat (0x2) or a whole transaction (0x3). With block triggers, a single-descriptor channel disables itself after its block, and a linked list disables after its last descriptor, otherwise waiting for the next trigger.

A trigger arriving during a transfer is held as pending (CHSTATUS.PEND=1) and served afterwards; only one can be held per channel and further triggers are lost. CHSTATUS.BUSY is set while the trigger action runs. All channels' pending and busy flags are also in PENDCH and BUSYCH.

Each block has a source address (SRCADDR) and a destination address (DSTADDR); each may be static or incrementing. BTCTRL.SRCINC=1 increments the source and BTCTRL.DSTINC=1 the destination. BTCTRL.STEPSEL picks which side uses the step size in BTCTRL.STEPSIZE: STEPSEL=1 applies it to the source, STEPSEL=0 to the destination; the other side steps by one beat.

Channel 0 with SRCINC=1 steps its source by one beat per beat; channel 1 with SRCINC=1, STEPSEL=1 and STEPSIZE=0x1 steps by two beats, both writing to fixed peripheral addresses (DSTINC=0). Likewise for destinations: DSTINC=1 steps by one beat, and DSTINC=1 with STEPSEL=0 and STEPSIZE=0x1 by two, from a fixed peripheral source.

An AHB bus error during a transfer disables the active channel and sets CHINTFLAG.TERR, with an interrupt if enabled; BTCNT is not decremented and its value is written back before the channel stops. Fetching an invalid descriptor (BTCTRL.VALID=0), or resuming into a null next address (DESCADDR=0x00000000), suspends the channel, sets CHINTFLAG.SUSP and CHSTATUS.FERR, with the suspend interrupt if enabled.

A transaction of several blocks is a chain of descriptors. After each block the DMAC fetches the descriptor at DESCADDR, until a block whose DESCADDR is 0x00000000 ends the transaction. To append a descriptor, build it in LP SRAM with DESCADDR=0 and point the old last descriptor's DESCADDR at it.

Enable the channel's suspend interrupt and the channel; reserve LP SRAM and build the new descriptor (DESCADDR, DSTADDR, SRCADDR, BTCTRL with VALID set and optionally the suspend block action); clear VALID on the existing list and on the descriptor to change; then read the write-back copy of DESCADDR. When the DMA has not yet fetched the descriptor to change, update its DESCADDR in the list, optionally clear its suspend action, set VALID and optionally issue Resume. If the DMA is running that very descriptor, issue Suspend; once the suspend interrupt arrives, change the next address held in write-back memory, clear the interrupt and issue Resume, then update the list entry, optionally clear the suspend action and set VALID. Repeat from building a descriptor as needed.

To put descriptor C between A and B: if the DMA is executing B, C cannot be inserted. If it has not started A, clear A's VALID, point A's DESCADDR at C and C's at B, then set A's VALID. If it is executing A, suspend the channel, do the same four steps, then resume it.

Writing the Suspend command to CHCTRLB.CMD suspends the channel after the current burst; the command clears itself, CHINTFLAG.SUSP is set and the suspend interrupt fires if enabled. BTCTRL.BLOCKACT = 0x2 or 0x3 suspends the channel after each block: it stays enabled and still takes triggers but leaves arbitration. Fetching an invalid descriptor also suspends it and sets CHSTATUS.FERR. Only enabled channels can be suspended; a suspend on a disabled channel is ignored.
The Resume command in CHCTRLB.CMD restarts a suspended channel where it stopped. Issued before the channel is suspended, it makes the channel skip its next suspend and carry on.

Event input actions exist only on the lowest-numbered channels. Each action is chosen by CHCTRLB.EVACT, with CHCTRLB.TRIGSRC set to DISABLE for a normal transfer and to a peripheral for the others, and is enabled by CHCTRLB.EVIE=1.
The event triggers a beat or burst transfer. It is acknowledged on arrival and sets CHSTATUS.PEND and PENDCH.PENDCHn; an event arriving while the channel is already pending is lost.

A transfer happens only when a peripheral trigger coincides with an event, for timed protocols or periodic transfers between peripherals. The event is acknowledged on arrival. The peripheral request is registered only when the channel is not pending and an event is active; an active peripheral trigger waits for an event. With both present, CHSTATUS.PEND and PENDCH.PENDCHn are set, and a software trigger then also starts a transfer.

Each peripheral trigger is registered when an event arrives, for example a peripheral-to-peripheral transfer where one peripheral gives the event and the other the trigger. Registering sets CHSTATUS.PEND and PENDCH.PENDCHn and acknowledges the event; a software trigger then starts a transfer.
An event must arrive before transfers within a block start; it is acknowledged when the block completes. A software trigger starts a transfer.

operation.topic: DMA suspend, resume and skip on event
operation.text: Channel Suspend: the event suspends the channel and is acknowledged when the current AHB access ends. Channel Resume: the event resumes a suspended channel, is acknowledged on arrival and clears CHINTFLAG.SUSP. Skip Next Block Suspend: a channel already suspended resumes, with the event acknowledged; an event that arrives first is kept until the next block suspend, which is then skipped, and acknowledged when that block completes.

Event outputs exist only on the lowest-numbered channels; each pulse lasts one AHB clock cycle. CHCTRLB.EVOE=1 enables the output and BTCTRL.EVOSEL picks the cause: after each block (0x1) or each beat (0x3). For an event at the end of a transaction, select the block event in the last descriptor only.

Disabling a channel aborts its transfers, and disabling the DMAC aborts all. The active channel stops after its current beat and once write-back memory is updated, so no data is corrupted; other enabled channels stop on the next clock cycle. CHCTRLA.ENABLE clears when the channel has stopped, and CTRL.DMAENABLE when the whole DMAC has.

The CRC produces a 16- or 32-bit checksum of a data stream or block. CRC-n on a block of any length detects every single error burst of n bits or fewer and the fraction 1-2^-n of longer bursts. CRCCTRL.CRCSRC chooses one DMA channel or the APB interface as input, and CRCCHKSUM holds the result; with CRC-32 the value read is bit-reversed and complemented. CRCCTRL.CRCPOLY picks the polynomial, CRC-16 by default. The engine works a byte at a time: from a DMA channel it uses that channel's beat size, and from the APB interface the beat size in CRCCTRL.CRCBEATSIZE (8, 16 or 32 bits), the bytes going through CRCDATAIN.

operation.topic: CRC on DMA data and through the I/O interface
operation.text: With a DMA channel as source, the CRC runs on all data passing through it, and the checksum can be read once the transaction completes or is aborted; SRAM, Flash or I/O memory can be checked by passing it through a DMA channel, with CRCDATAIN as the destination. Through the I/O interface the CPU writes any number of bytes to CRCDATAIN, after setting CRCCTRL.CRCBEATSIZE; a 32-bit write takes four cycles to process. CRCSTATUS.CRCBUSY signals completion, and new data may be written only while CRCBUSY is not set.

Per channel: Transfer Complete (TCMPL), a block finished; Transfer Error (TERR), a bus error during a burst or an invalid descriptor fetched; Channel Suspend (SUSP), the channel was suspended. Flags are in CHINTFLAG, enabled with CHINTENSET and disabled with CHINTENCLR; a request stays active until its flag clears, the source is turned off, or the DMAC or the channel resets. All share one NVIC line. INTSTATUS shows which channels have pending interrupts, and INTPEND gives the lowest channel with one and its flags.

Output event CH, on block completion or on beat completion within a block, enabled by CHCTRLB.EVOE=1 with the cause in BTCTRL.EVOSEL. Input actions, enabled by CHCTRLB.EVIE=1: TRIG (normal or periodic transfer), CTRIG (conditional transfer), CBLOCK (conditional block transfer), SUSPEND, RESUME, SSKIP (skip next block suspend) and INCPRI (raise channel priority). With several events connected, any enabled action is taken for any incoming event.

Each channel can work in any sleep mode; to run in Standby it needs CHCTRLA.RUNSTDBY=1. The DMAC can wake the device with interrupts from any sleep mode or act through the event system. For channels with RUNSTDBY=0, software must stop them before Standby: suspend those channels, check the SYNCBUSY bits of the registers they access, sleep, and resume them on wake-up. In Standby the DMAC can use LP SRAM only with PD1 out of retention and PM.STDBYCFG.BBIASLP at 0x0, and main SRAM only with PD2 out of retention and PM.STDBYCFG.BBIASHS at 0x0. The DMAC needs no register synchronization.

The external interrupt controller turns pins into interrupt lines, each separately maskable, sensing rising, falling or both edges, or high or low level. Each pin has a spike filter, can be made asynchronous to wake the device from sleep with all clocks stopped, and can raise an event. A separate non-maskable interrupt pin works the same way but drives the CPU's NMI.

At most 16 external interrupt pins and a separate NMI pin; a maskable interrupt per pin; rising, falling or both edges, detected synchronously or asynchronously; high or low level; asynchronous interrupts for clockless sleep modes; filtering; event generation.

The pins must be configured in PORT. Every interrupt works in every sleep mode, but some can be masked automatically to keep them from waking the device. The EIC runs in any sleep mode whose clock runs; its interrupts wake the device and its events act without waking it. The bus clock CLK_EIC_APB is masked in MCLK. Some functions need a peripheral clock: GCLK_EIC from GCLK for a wider choice of frequency, or CLK_ULP32K from OSCULP32K for the lowest power; both are asynchronous to CLK_EIC_APB, so some writes are synchronized. There are two interrupt lines, EXTINT and NMI; the NMI line needs no interrupt-controller setup. The EIC keeps running while the CPU is halted by a debugger. All writable registers except INTFLAG and NMIFLAG can be write-protected by the PAC.

In order: enable CLK_EIC_APB; set up the NMI in NMICTRL if used; if the NMI, synchronous edge detection or filtering is used, enable GCLK_EIC or CLK_ULP32K (GCLK_EIC for filter clocks above 32 kHz, CLK_ULP32K, chosen by CTRLA.CKSEL=1, for lowest power), and optionally asynchronous mode; set sense and filter in CONFIGn; enable the EIC. CTRLA.CKSEL and the EVCTRL, CONFIGn and ASYNCH registers can be written only while CTRLA.ENABLE=0; protected CTRLA bits can be written with the write that sets ENABLE, not the one that clears it.
CTRLA.ENABLE turns the EIC on and off. CTRLA.SWRST resets every register and disables the EIC.

CONFIGn.SENSEx sets each pin's sense: rising, falling or both edges, high or low level. A met condition sets INTFLAG.EXTINT[x]. After clearing in edge mode the flag sets again only on a new edge; in level mode it sets again at once if the pin still matches. CONFIGn.FILTENx=1 enables a majority-vote filter: it takes three samples of the pin, clocked by GCLK_EIC or CLK_ULP32K, and passes on whichever value at least two of them share.

operation.topic: EIC asynchronous level detection and clock request
operation.text: Level detection with the filter off is asynchronous and needs neither GCLK_EIC nor CLK_ULP32K, yet still gives interrupts and events. With filtering or edge detection on, the EIC requests the clock chosen by CTRLA.CKSEL by itself; GCLK_EIC must be enabled in GCLK.

The NMI pin senses edges or levels too, set in NMICTRL.NMISENSE, with its filter enabled by NMICTRL.NMIFILTEN=1. Edge detection or filtering needs GCLK_EIC or CLK_ULP32K. NMISENSE alone enables detection; the EIC itself need not be enabled. After reset the NMI detects nothing. A detection sets NMIFLAG.NMI, which always raises an interrupt.

ASYNCH.ASYNCH[x] chooses synchronous (0, default) or asynchronous (1) edge detection for pin x. Synchronously, the pin is sampled on the EIC clock chosen by CTRLA.CKSEL and the flag sets when two samples differ; the clock is required. Asynchronously, the pin sets INTFLAG.EXTINT[x] or NMIFLAG directly with no clock requested, with no debouncing, and this works in every sleep mode.

Sources: the external pins (EXTINTx) and the NMI pin. Flags are in INTFLAG (NMIFLAG for the NMI); every source except the NMI is enabled with INTENSET and disabled with INTENCLR. A request stays active until its flag clears, the source is turned off or the EIC resets. One line is shared by the external pins and one serves the NMI. When one EXTINT number is routed to two or more pins, only the first one programmed is active.
Each EXTINTx can give an output event, enabled in EVCTRL.EXTINTEO, generated when the pin meets its CONFIGn condition.
In sleep, an EXTINTx pin wakes the device when it meets its CONFIGn condition and its INTENSET bit is 1. Writes to CTRLA.SWRST and CTRLA.ENABLE are synchronized.

The Flash holds a main array and a smaller read-while-write array for EEPROM emulation (RWWEE), which can be programmed while the main array is read. The NVM controller sits on the AHB, for reads and writes to the Flash, and on the APB, for commands and configuration.

32-bit AHB interface for reads and writes; RWW EEPROM emulation area; every NVM section, calibration and system configuration included, mapped on the AHB; 32-bit APB interface carrying commands and control; read wait states that can be programmed; 16 regions that can each be locked; extra protection for a boot loader; device protection by a security bit; power-down of Flash blocks in sleep via the power manager, waking on sleep exit or on first access; direct-mapped cache. A register marked enable-protected may hold bits that are not.

The controller runs in any sleep mode whose clock runs and its interrupt can wake the device. On entering sleep the power manager puts the Flash in a low-power state as CTRLB.SLEEPPRM sets. It uses two synchronous clocks, CLK_NVMCTRL_AHB and CLK_NVMCTRL_APB. At higher system frequencies read wait states are needed; when the AHB frequency changes, the wait states must be set to match the electrical characteristics. It keeps running while a debugger halts the CPU; with the security bit set the Flash cannot be reached. All writable registers except INTFLAG and STATUS can be write-protected by the PAC.
After power-up the controller runs a power-up sequence during which AHB access is held off; it then works with no configuration needed.

The Flash is made of rows of four pages: erase is by row, write by page, so one row erase clears four pages and four page writes fill a row. Row n holds pages 4n to 4n+3. The calibration and auxiliary space (factory calibration and system configuration) and the RWWEE space are memory mapped and read over the AHB like the main space: main space from the NVM base address to base + NVM size, RWWEE from base + 0x00400000, calibration and auxiliary from base + 0x00800000. A boot loader section can be set aside at the bottom of the main space with the BOOTPROT fuses, and EEPROM rows at the top: the boot section runs from the base address to base + BOOTPROT size, the EEPROM from base + NVM size - EEPROM size to base + NVM size. The boot section is protected by its region lock bits and by BOOTPROT[2:0]; EEPROM rows can be written whatever the region lock state.

The Flash is split into 16 equal regions, each with a lock bit that blocks writing and erasing its pages; all are unlocked when shipped. The Lock Region and Unlock Region commands act on the region holding the address in ADDR (written by software or left by the last write) until the next reset or the next such command; LOCK shows the current state. The default lock state is set in the user configuration of the auxiliary space with the Write Auxiliary Page command, and takes effect after the next reset.

Reads and automatic page writes address the main or RWWEE space directly over the AHB; manual page writes, row erases and other operations are commands given through the controller. A command is CTRLA.CMD written together with the key in CTRLA.CMDEX. INTFLAG.READY stays low until it completes, and commands written meanwhile are ignored. CTRLB sets the power reduction mode, read wait states and write mode.

Main or auxiliary space is read directly over the AHB, data arriving after the wait states in CTRLB.RWS. Reading the main array while it is being programmed or erased stalls the AHB until the operation ends; programming or erasing the RWWEE array does not stall reads of the main array.

RWWEE space is read directly over the AHB, with the same timing as main reads for byte and half-word accesses and a data phase twice as long for word accesses. No RWWEE read is possible during a main-array write or erase, whereas RWWEE writes and erases may go on during main-array reads. RWWEE space is not cached.

Flash must be erased before it is programmed. A debugger Chip Erase clears the whole main and RWWEE space; Erase Row and RWWEE Erase Row clear single rows. After programming, a page's region can be locked against stray writes and erases; locking covers the whole region. Data first goes into a buffer one page long, shared by main and RWWEE arrays, by AHB writes of 16 or 32 bits; an 8-bit write to it causes a system exception. Each AHB write stores its address in ADDR. Once the buffer is filled, the Write Page command (main array) or RWWEE Write Page command (RWWEE array) in CTRLA.CMD, with the key in CMDEX, programs it. STATUS.LOAD shows whether the buffer holds data. A row has to be erased before any of its pages is programmed.

operation.topic: NVM automatic and manual page writes
operation.text: With CTRLB.MANW=0, filling the last location of the buffer programs whichever page ADDR points to at once; since ADDR holds the last written address it need not be loaded unless another page is meant. The row must be erased before the last buffer write, and partly filled pages need a manual write. With CTRLB.MANW=1, erase the row, fill the buffer by writing the main space, then issue Write Page with CMDEX. In both cases INTFLAG.READY is low and AHB access stalls while programming runs.
After each page write the buffer is set back to all ones. To empty a partly written buffer, issue Page Buffer Clear.

Before any page is written, its row must be erased; Erase Row works on the main space and RWWEE Erase Row on the RWWEE array, setting every bit to 1. Write any address in the row to ADDR, then issue the command. A row in a locked region is not erased and STATUS.LOCKE is set. ADDR.ADDR uses 16-bit addressing.

operation.topic: NVM lock, unlock and power reduction commands
operation.text: The lock and unlock commands act on regions as given for the lock bits. The Set Power Reduction Mode command puts the controller and Flash into power reduction mode and the Clear Power Reduction Mode command takes them out; STATUS.PRM shows the state.

The user configuration lives in the auxiliary space. The boot loader sits at offset zero of the main array and its section is write-protected. The EEPROM[2:0] bits give the EEPROM size; it occupies the top rows of the main space and can be written whatever the region lock state.

The security bit locks the whole chip against external access. It is set by the Set Security Bit (SSB) command and cleared only by a debugger Chip Erase; STATUS.PROGE can be checked after SSB. Enabling BOD33 while the security bit is set is recommended for higher security.

The cache cuts power and raises performance when wait states are needed. Only the main array is cached. It is direct-mapped, 64 lines of 64 bits (512 bytes), enabled by CTRLB.CACHEDIS=0, with three modes chosen by CTRLB.READMODE. The INVALL command (CTRLA.CMD=INVALL) invalidates every line, and commands that change NVM content invalidate lines automatically.

PORT controls the I/O pins, arranged in groups of up to 32 pins each, configurable one by one or together; the number of groups depends on the package. Each pin is either general-purpose I/O or handed to a peripheral. As GPIO a pin can be input or output with configurable drive and pull. Direction and output value can be set, cleared or toggled for any pins of a group in one atomic 8-, 16- or 32-bit write without touching the others. PORT sits on the bus matrix through an AHB/APB bridge, and DIR, OUT and IN are also reachable over the single-cycle CPU local bus (IOBUS).

Input or output per pin; software-selected peripheral multiplexing; a configuration register per pin; push-pull output with pull and drive-strength settings; input with internal pull-up or pull-down, selectable sampling, and an input buffer that can be turned off to save power; up to four input event pins per group with SET, CLEAR and TOGGLE actions on a pin's output value, which can be output to the pin; in Standby no access to the configuration registers but possible access to DIR, OUT and IN.

Each bundle of up to 32 lines is named by a letter x (A, B, C ...) and a two-digit number y (00 to 31), and the pin is Pxy, for example PA24 or PC03. A pin can be routed by the peripheral multiplexer to a peripheral, which then drives the pad and reads its state. Pins may be secured or non-secured, secured pins answering only secure accesses. Some lines may not exist on a given device.

During reset every pin is an input with input buffer, output buffer and pull all disabled. In Backup mode the PORT configuration registers and input synchronizers lose their contents and are not restored at power-up, but the pad latches keep their state, such as output value and pull. PORT runs in any sleep mode whose clock runs.

CLK_PORT_APB is masked in MCLK. PORT takes the CPU main clock, for CPU access over IOBUS, and the APB clock, a divided main clock, for register access through the bus matrix and AHB/APB bridge. IOBUS accesses have priority over event and APB accesses, which get wait states when they collide. The input synchronizers run on the CPU main clock to keep resynchronization delay low.

PORT keeps running while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL halts it. Every writable register can be write-protected by the PAC; protection is lifted automatically while the CPU is halted in debug and never applies to debugger accesses.

operation.topic: PORT analog connections and CPU local bus
operation.text: Analog functions connect straight from the analog blocks to the pads over analog buses; choosing an analog function on a pin disables its digital features. IOBUS is a single-cycle interface from the CPU to PORT with no wait states, taking 8-, 16- and 32-bit accesses: DIR and OUT can be read, written, set, cleared or toggled and IN read. Since IOBUS cannot wait for IN to resynchronize, pins read over it need continuous sampling set in CTRL, or stale data is read.

Each pad has a push-pull driver controlled by OUT and DIR (output enable), a pull resistor enabled by PULLEN, drive strength set by DRIVE, an input buffer enabled by INEN feeding a two-stage synchronizer to IN and to other modules, and a direct analog input/output. The back-up I/O pins have no ESD diode to VDDIO, only the one to ground.

Each group has its own copy of the PORT registers at increasing base addresses. A '1' in DIR makes a pin an output, and OUT then sets its level ('1' high, '0' low); a '0' in DIR makes it an input. PINCFGy holds the rest of pin y's configuration. IN reads the pin, resynchronized to the PORT clock, whether input or output; the synchronizers are clocked only when a read needs them, and with PINCFGy.INEN=0 the pin is not sampled. PINCFGy.PMUXEN=1 hands the pin to the peripheral chosen in PMUXn, replacing the PORT connection.
After reset each standard pad is connected to PORT, its output in high impedance and its input buffer turned off, even with no clock running; special pins such as debugger pins may start otherwise.

Each group has its own PORT register set; for pin y it is at byte address PORT + y × 0x4, indexed by y. Make pin y an output with DIR bit y = 1, or DIRSET bit y = 1 to leave the others alone, and set OUT bit y. OUTSET, OUTCLR and OUTTGL set, clear or toggle OUT bits. Make it an input with DIR bit y = 0 or DIRCLR bit y = 1; IN bit y is valid once PINCFGy.INEN=1. On-demand sampling delays a read by two CLK_PORT cycles; the CTRL.SAMPLINGn bit for a group of eight pins keeps their synchronizers always on, removing the delay at the cost of power. For a peripheral function set PINCFGy.PMUXEN (PINCFGy at byte offset PINCFG0 + y) and choose PMUXO or PMUXE in PMUXn (byte offset PMUX0 + y/2); the peripheral must also be set up and enabled.

PINCFGy sets push-pull or pull configuration. Because the pull is set there, no intermediate states appear while direction and value change. With pull enabled, OUT chooses pull-up or pull-down. A push-pull output drives the pin low or high per OUT with no limit beyond the pin's own capability; an input with no external pull floats. Enabling the output driver disables the pull. With input and output both off, the pin is in its reset or analog state.

Input events from EVSYS, possibly from another clock domain, can drive single pins. Actions: OUT, the pin follows the event level; SET, CLR and TGL, the pin is set, cleared or toggled on each event. OUT reaches the pin with no internal latency; SET, CLR and TGL take effect within three clock cycles of a rising edge. In Standby only OUT works. EVCTRL.EVACTm sets each input's action and EVCTRL.PORTEIm enables it; with several events connected, any enabled action is taken for any of them. Each input addresses one pin, chosen in EVCTRL.PIDn, and a single pin may be the target of as many as four inputs; simultaneous SET, CLR and TGL actions on one pin resolve to a single action: SET when all are SET, CLR when all are CLR, TGL otherwise. Events reach the pin asynchronously, so a pin driven by events can show unpredictable levels depending on timing; when several events output to one pin, the lowest event line wins and the others are ignored.

PORT is reached by the CPU over IOBUS, by the CPU over the bus matrix and AHB/APB bridge (APB), and by EVSYS through four asynchronous input events, in that order of priority: IOBUS first (it tolerates no wait), then APB, then events.

The event system lets peripherals signal each other directly, with low latency and no CPU, bus or RAM bandwidth. Generators raise events on conditions of their own; users take actions of their own on receiving them. A peripheral may hold several generators and several users.

12 channels, each connectable to any generator and each offering a synchronous, resynchronized or asynchronous path; 82 generators and 42 users of events; a configurable edge detector; peripherals as generators, users or both; SleepWalking and an interrupt for work in sleep modes; software events; each user picks its channel, and several users can share one channel.

The event system can wake the CPU from every sleep mode even with its channel clock and bus clock off: some generators raise events with their clocks stopped, and a channel on a synchronous or resynchronized path restarts its generic clock GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n without waking the system. The bus clock CLK_EVSYS_APB is masked in MCLK. Each channel has its own generic clock GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n for detection and propagation, which must be set up in GCLK first. It keeps running while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL halts it. All writable registers except CHSTATUS and INTFLAG can be write-protected by the PAC.

Channels carry events from generators to peripherals or pins (users). A generator can feed several channels, but a channel takes one generator. Each channel runs asynchronous, synchronous or resynchronized; the last two can pass events on rising, falling or both edges of the generator.

Enable the event output in the generator (its EVCTRL EO bit, for example TCC.EVCTRL.MCEO1, AC.EVCTRL.WINEO0 or RTC.EVCTRL.OVFEO); set the user multiplexer in EVSYS.USERm, then the channel in EVSYS.CHANNELn; set the user's action in its EVACT bits where it has them; enable the event input in the user (its EVCTRL EI bit, for example AC.EVCTRL.IVEI0 or ADC.EVCTRL.STARTEI).
The event system is always on. CTRLA.SWRST resets every register and cancels events in progress.

Each user has its own multiplexer that sees every channel and selects one in USERm.CHANNEL; set it before the channel. A channel selects one generator in CHANNELn.EVGEN (0, no generator, by default) and sends its events synchronized, resynchronized or asynchronously; synchronized and resynchronized channels include an edge detector. A channel can also send software events.

CHANNELn.PATH selects the path. Asynchronous: the event goes from generator to user with no involvement and no clock latency, the channel clock is not needed, the channel gives no interrupts, CHSTATUS reads zero, edge detection must be turned off, and each user chooses its own triggering edge. Synchronous: for a generator on the same generic clock generator as the channel; with different clocks a change can be missed and the event lost. Resynchronized: for a generator on a different clock generator, the channel resynchronizes the event. Synchronous and resynchronized channels give interrupts and update CHSTATUS.CHBUSYn.
Synchronous and resynchronized paths need edge detection, set in CHANNELn.EDGSEL: an event on rising edges only, on falling edges only, or on both.

Asynchronous path: maximum routing latency set by internal routing, device dependent. Synchronous path: at most one GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n cycle. Resynchronized path: at most three GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n cycles. Passing a user event into the peripheral's clock domain takes at most three peripheral clock cycles. The generator, channel and user clocks must be chosen to meet these latencies, or events and actions may be lost.

operation.topic: EVSYS overrun and event detected interrupts
operation.text: INTFLAG.OVRn sets, with an optional interrupt, when a user on channel n is not ready for a new event, or when an event arrives before every user has handled the previous one. INTFLAG.EVDn sets when channel n's generator raises an event. Both work only on synchronous or resynchronized paths and read zero on the asynchronous path.
On synchronous and resynchronized paths, CHSTATUS.CHBUSYn is 1 while some user of channel n still has an event to deal with, and CHSTATUS.USRRDYn is set when all its users are ready for a new event.
Writing 1 to SWEVT.CHANNELn raises an event on channel n, handled like any generator's.

Sources OVRn and EVDn, both asynchronous wake-up sources. Flags are in INTFLAG, enabled with INTENSET and disabled with INTENCLR; a request stays active until its flag clears, the source is turned off or the event system resets. All share one NVIC line.

The event system can wake the device from any sleep mode by interrupt. A channel runs in Standby with CHANNELn.RUNSTDBY=1. With CHANNELn.ONDEMAND=1 the channel requests GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNEL_n when its generator fires, adding two clock cycles to a resynchronized path (up to five in all).

There are up to six SERCOM instances. SERCOM0 to SERCOM4 (as many as the device has) sit in power domain PD1; SERCOM5 is on every device and sits in PD0. Each instance is set up as one of USART, SPI or I2C, and once enabled all of its resources serve that mode. Its serial engine holds a transmitter, a receiver, a baud-rate generator and address matching, and runs from its generic clock or an external clock in every sleep mode.
I2C (SMBus compatible), SPI or USART; one transmit buffer and a two-deep receive buffer; baud-rate generator; address match and mask; works in all sleep modes; DMA capable.

Because it sits in PD0, SERCOM5 lacks: DMA; on USART, fractional baud generation, 3x and 8x oversampling, RTS/CTS flow control, IrDA, EN54 single-wire UART and start/end-of-frame detection; on I2C, Fm+ and Hs modes, the SMBus SCL low time-out, 10-bit addressing and PMBus group command; on SPI, hardware chip select and wake on SS.

Each SERCOM has four internal pads, PAD[3:0], and its I2C, SPI or USART signals reach them through a multiplexer set from the mode's own pinout fields. The pins must also be given to the SERCOM in PORT.

The bus clock CLK_SERCOMx_APB is on after reset and is gated in MCLK. Two generic clocks serve the SERCOM: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE, needed when it acts as master, and GCLK_SERCOMx_SLOW, needed only by some functions. Both are set up in GCLK before use. They are asynchronous to the bus clock, so some register writes are synchronized.

operation.topic: SERCOM sleep, DMA, interrupts and debug
operation.text: The SERCOM works in any sleep mode whose clock runs, and its interrupts can wake the device. DMA requests go to the DMAC and the interrupt line to the NVIC, each configured first. The SERCOM has no events. It keeps running while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL makes it halt.
Every writable register can be write-protected by the PAC except INTFLAG, STATUS, DATA and ADDR. Debugger accesses are not protected.

The transmitter is one write buffer plus a shift register; the receiver is a two-level buffer plus a shift register. The baud-rate generator runs from GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE or an external clock. Address matching serves SPI and I2C.
CTRLA.ENABLE=1 turns the SERCOM on and 0 turns it off. CTRLA.SWRST=1 returns every register but DBGCTRL to its reset value and leaves the SERCOM disabled.

From the baud reference clock fref (the serial engine clock, internal or external) and the BAUD register the generator makes fBAUD. Asynchronous modes send with the divide-by-16 output and receive with the divide-by-1 output; synchronous modes use the divide-by-2 output; the choice follows the mode. In asynchronous arithmetic mode BAUD is 16 bits (0 to 65,535). In asynchronous fractional mode BAUD is 13 bits plus a 3-bit fractional part FP, and BAUD must be 1 or more; this mode serves auto-baud detection. In synchronous modes BAUD is 8 bits (0 to 255).

Address matching compares 7 or 8 bits, depending on the mode, in one of three ways. Address with mask: ADDR.ADDR is compared with the received address, ignoring every bit set in ADDR.ADDRMASK; a mask of all zeros matches one address and all ones matches every address. Two unique addresses: a match on either ADDR.ADDR or ADDR.ADDRMASK. Address range: any address from ADDR.ADDRMASK (lower limit) up to ADDR.ADDR (upper limit), both included.

Interrupt sources depend on the mode, each with its own flag in INTFLAG, enabled through INTENSET and disabled through INTENCLR. A request stays active until its flag clears, the source is disabled or the SERCOM resets. All sources share one NVIC line, and INTFLAG tells which fired. The SERCOM runs in any sleep mode whose serial clock (external, or from the baud-rate generator) runs. Registers marked write- or read-synchronized cross between the bus and core clock domains.

USART is a SERCOM mode built on its transmitter and receiver. The transmitter has one write buffer, so frames can follow each other with no gap; the receiver has a two-level buffer, status bits for error checking, and clock and data recovery that synchronize to the incoming stream and filter noise.

Full duplex; asynchronous with clock recovery, or synchronous; internal or external clock in either case; frames of 5 to 9 data bits with 1 or 2 stop bits; odd or even parity; LSB or MSB first; overflow and frame-error detection; false-start-bit detection and a digital low-pass filter; collision detection; works in all sleep modes; up to half the system clock with an internal clock and up to the system clock with an external one; RTS/CTS flow control; IrDA modulation up to 115.2 kbps; start-of-frame detection; DMA.

In USART mode the SERCOM sets the direction and level of its pins. PINCFGn.DRVSTR still acts on the output pins; PINCFGn.PULLEN still acts on the input pins but can only switch a pull-down, never a pull-up. With the receiver or transmitter disabled, its pin is free for other uses. PORT together with CTRLA.TXPO and CTRLA.RXPO places TxD, RxD and XCK on the pads.

operation.topic: USART clocks, DMA, interrupts and protection
operation.text: CLK_SERCOMx_APB is on after reset and gated in MCLK. GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE must be set up in GCLK first; it is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes are synchronized. DMA requests go to the DMAC and the interrupt line to the NVIC. No events. The USART keeps running under a debugger halt unless DBGCTRL stops it. The PAC can write-protect every writable register except INTFLAG, STATUS and DATA; debugger accesses are not protected.

Data move in frames: one start bit (low), 5 to 9 data bits sent MSB or LSB first, an optional even or odd parity bit after the data, and 1 or 2 stop bits (high). After the stop bits either the next frame starts at once or the line idles high.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except RXEN and TXEN) and BAUD are enable-protected: writes are dropped while CTRLA.ENABLE=1 and, during disable, take effect once disabling completes. Set-up order: CTRLA.MODE for external (0x0) or internal (0x1) clock; CTRLA.CMODE for asynchronous (0) or synchronous (1); CTRLA.RXPO for the receive pad; CTRLA.TXPO for the transmit and clock pads; CTRLB.CHSIZE for character size; CTRLA.DORD for bit order; for parity, CTRLA.FORM=0x1 and CTRLB.PMODE for even or odd; CTRLB.SBMODE for stop bits; BAUD when the clock is internal; then CTRLB.RXEN and CTRLB.TXEN.
CTRLA.ENABLE=1 turns the USART on and 0 off. CTRLA.SWRST=1 resets every register but DBGCTRL and leaves it disabled.

In both synchronous (CTRLA.CMODE=1) and asynchronous (CMODE=0) modes the shift clock comes either from the baud-rate generator (CTRLA.MODE=0x1) or from the XCK pin (CTRLA.MODE=0x0). Asynchronous mode uses the full 16-bit BAUD value, synchronous mode only its eight low bits.

In synchronous mode CTRLA.MODE makes XCK an input or an output; edge timing is the same either way. RxD is sampled on the XCK edge opposite the one that changes TxD. CTRLA.CPOL=0: data change on the rising edge and are sampled on the falling edge. CPOL=1: change on falling, sample on rising. With XCK as clock input (CTRLA.MODE=0x0) the shift registers run straight from XCK, unsynchronized to the system clock, up to the system frequency.

TxDATA and RxDATA share one address, DATA: a write fills TxDATA and a read returns RxDATA. A write to DATA starts a transmission; the byte moves to the shift register once it is empty. INTFLAG.DRE says DATA can take a new byte, and DATA should be written only then. INTFLAG.TXC is set when a whole frame with its stop bits has gone and nothing new waits. Writing CTRLB.TXEN=0 disables the transmitter only after the shift register and TxDATA are both empty.

A valid start bit starts reception; the bits are sampled at the baud rate or on XCK until the first stop bit, and a second stop bit is ignored. The frame then moves into the two-level buffer and INTFLAG.RXC is set; read DATA then. Writing CTRLB.RXEN=0 disables the receiver, empties the buffer and loses any frame in progress.

STATUS holds three receive errors: FERR (frame error), BUFOVF (buffer overflow) and PERR (parity error). Each stays set until 1 is written to it, and all clear when the receiver is disabled. With CTRLA.IBON=1, BUFOVF is raised the moment the buffer overflows, and software can empty the buffer by reading until RXC clears. With IBON=0 the overflow travels through the buffer with the data and BUFOVF appears with RXC when that data is read.

Clock recovery locks incoming frames to the internal baud clock and data recovery samples and low-pass filters each bit. How far the incoming rate may differ from the internal rate depends on the frame length and on the accuracy of the internal rate, which suffers from reference clock drift and from BAUD not dividing exactly; BAUD should be chosen for least error. Too large a difference and the receiver cannot lock to the start bit.

operation.topic: USART receiver error example at 3 Mbps
operation.text: With 16x sampling, 10 data bits, no parity, one start and one stop bit, and fBAUD = 48 MHz / 16 with BAUD=0 (no baud generator offset), the receiver accepts +3.3 % to -4.35 %. A DFLL source at 3 MHz with ±0.3 % error narrows that to +3.0 % to -4.05 %. A recommended receiver error of ±1.5 % then leaves a margin; the external transmitter should stay within ±1.5 %, and larger transmitter errors are tolerated as long as they stay inside the accepted window.

CTRLA.FORM=0x1 enables a parity bit. Even parity (CTRLB.PMODE=0) sets it so the number of ones in data plus parity is even; odd parity (PMODE=1) makes it odd. On reception the parity is recomputed and a mismatch sets STATUS.PERR.

RTS and CTS give out-of-band flow control with the remote device (TXD to its RXD, RXD to its TXD, CTS to its RTS, RTS to its CTS). It needs CTRLA.MODE=1 (internal clock), CTRLA.CMODE=0 (asynchronous) and CTRLA.TXPO=2 (the flow-control pinout). The receiver drives RTS high when it is disabled or its buffer is full, telling the remote to stop after the current frame; CTRLB.RXEN changes RTS after a synchronization delay, while a full buffer raises RTS at once and the frame being received waits in the shift register. STATUS.CTS shows the CTS input; a frame starts only while CTS=0, and when CTS goes high the frame in progress completes and transmission stops.

IrDA encoding up to 115.2 kb/s needs CTRLB.ENC=1, asynchronous mode (CTRLA.CMODE=0) and 16x sampling (CTRLA.SAMPR[0]=0). Each low bit is sent as a high pulse 3/16 of a bit period wide. The decoder resynchronizes its baud counter at the start of each zero pulse and accepts a pulse at least as long as set in RXPL.RXPL, passing it to the receiver at mid-bit. Transmit and receive polarity are opposite: a 0 goes out as a 1 pulse, and an accepted 0 pulse comes in as a 0 bit. Example: RXPL.RXPL=19 asks for pulses of at least 20 serial engine clocks, which with BAUD=0xE666 (160 clocks per bit) is 2/16 of a bit; a shorter low pulse is rejected.

Needs CTRLA.FORM=0x04 or 0x05 (auto-baud frames), CTRLA.CMODE=0 (asynchronous) and CTRLA.SAMPR=1 (16x sampling with fractional baud generation). It follows LIN: a frame opens with a break field and a sync field. More than 11 consecutive dominant bits at the set baud rate count as a break and set INTFLAG.RXBRK; the next character must be the sync byte 0x55. A counter runs over the 8 bit times of the sync field; its top 13 bits (count divided by 8) become BAUD.BAUD and its low 3 bits BAUD.FP, applied after a synchronization delay. A sync byte other than 0x55 sets STATUS.ISF and INTFLAG.ERROR and leaves the baud rate as it was.

With the receiver and transmitter both enabled and joined, by pin configuration or outside, CTRLB.COLDEN=1 compares each transmitted bit with the received one; characters received while the transmitter is idle cause no collision. On a collision the USART aborts the transfer, flushes the transmit buffer, clears CTRLB.TXEN after a synchronization delay (SYNCBUSY.CTRLB is set meanwhile, and TxD then floats), sets STATUS.COLL with INTFLAG.ERROR, and sets INTFLAG.TXC because nothing is left to send. Software re-enables the transmitter once SYNCBUSY.CTRLB has cleared.
Pointing CTRLA.RXPO and CTRLA.TXPO at the same pad loops transmit to receive at the pad, and the pin carries the looped signal too.

With CTRLB.SFDE=1 a start bit can wake the CPU, in asynchronous and synchronous modes. In Standby the fast-startup internal oscillator must be the GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE source: a falling edge on RxD powers up the 8 MHz internal oscillator and enables the USART clock, and the frame is received if the baud rate is slow enough for that oscillator's start-up time, which varies with supply and temperature. With INTENSET.RXS=1 the Receive Start interrupt fires as the start bit is seen; without it the oscillator and clock stay on through the frame and the CPU wakes only on Receive Complete.
In asynchronous mode the bit value is a majority vote of three middle samples, chosen by CTRLA.SAMPA. With SAMPA=0 these are samples 7, 8 and 9 at 16x oversampling and 3, 4 and 5 at 8x.
RX is raised while the receive buffer holds data and cleared by reading DATA. TX is raised while the transmit buffer is empty and cleared by writing DATA.

Sources DRE, RXC, TXC, RXS, CTSIC, RXBRK and ERROR, all asynchronous and able to wake the device from any sleep mode. Flags are in INTFLAG, enabled through INTENSET and disabled through INTENCLR; a request stays active until its flag clears, the source is disabled or the USART resets. One NVIC line serves them all.

Internal clock with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY=1: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE can run in every sleep mode and any interrupt can wake the device. External clock with RUNSTDBY=1: Receive Start and Receive Complete can wake it. Internal clock with RUNSTDBY=0: the clock stops once any transfer in progress ends, and Receive Start and Receive Complete can wake it. External clock with RUNSTDBY=0: the external clock is disconnected after the transfer in progress and all reception is lost.
Writes to CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLB.RXEN and CTRLB.TXEN are synchronized; CTRLB.RXEN synchronizes in its own way, set out in the CTRLB description.
SPI is a SERCOM mode. Host and client each have a shift register, one transmit buffer and two receive buffers; the host uses the baud-rate generator and the client may use the address match logic.

Four wires (MISO, MOSI, SCK, SS) carrying data both ways at once; one transmit buffer and two receive buffers; all four SPI modes; one-direction use frees MISO or MOSI for another function; LSB or MSB first; DMA. Host: SCK frequency 1/tSCK, an 8-bit clock generator and SS driven by hardware. Client: SCK frequency 1/tSSCK, optional 8-bit address match, works in all sleep modes, wakes on SS.

In SPI mode the SERCOM sets pin direction and level. PINCFGn.DRVSTR acts on output pins; PINCFGn.PULLEN acts on input pins but only as a pull-down. With the receiver disabled the data input pin is free for other uses. In host mode SS is driven by hardware when CTRLB.MSSEN=1. PORT together with CTRLA.DIPO and CTRLA.DOPO places the signals.

operation.topic: SPI clocks, DMA, interrupts and protection
operation.text: CLK_SERCOMx_APB is on after reset and gated in MCLK. GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE must be set up in GCLK first; it is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes are synchronized. DMA requests go to the DMAC and the interrupt line to the NVIC. No events. The SPI keeps running under a debugger halt unless DBGCTRL stops it. The PAC can write-protect every writable register except INTFLAG, STATUS and DATA; debugger accesses are not protected.

The SPI acts as host, which starts and clocks every transaction, or as client. The next character can be written to DATA while the current one shifts out, and received characters go to the two-level buffer. A transaction holds one or more characters of 8 or 9 bits. The host pulls the chosen client's SS low, drives SCK, sends on MOSI and receives on MISO, one character in for each out, and raises SS to end the transaction.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except RXEN), BAUD and ADDR are enable-protected: writes are dropped while CTRLA.ENABLE=1 and, during disable, take effect once disabling completes. Set-up order: CTRLA.MODE 0x2 (client) or 0x3 (host); CTRLA.CPOL and CTRLA.CPHA; CTRLA.FORM; CTRLA.DIPO for the receive pad; CTRLA.DOPO for the transmit pads; CTRLB.CHSIZE; CTRLA.DORD; in host mode BAUD and, for hardware SS, CTRLB.MSSEN=1; then CTRLB.RXEN=1.

CTRLA.ENABLE turns the SPI on and off; CTRLA.SWRST=1 resets every register but DBGCTRL and leaves it disabled. As host (CTRLA.MODE=0x3) the baud-rate generator in synchronous mode makes SCK from the 8-bit BAUD value. As client (MODE=0x2) the external host's SCK clocks the shift register directly. TxDATA and RxDATA share the DATA address: writes go to TxDATA and reads come from RxDATA.
CTRLA.CPHA sets SCK phase and CTRLA.CPOL its polarity, giving four modes. Data are shifted out on one SCK edge and latched on the other, which gives them time to settle.

In host mode (CTRLA.MODE=0x3) hardware drives SS when CTRLB.MSSEN=1. With MSSEN=0, SS is any GPIO configured as an output, pulled low by software before a transaction and high after it. A character written to DATA moves to the shift register and INTFLAG.DRE is set, ready for the next. With the receiver on, each character shifted in goes to the receive buffer on the clock cycle of its last bit and INTFLAG.RXC is set. INTFLAG.TXC is set when the last character has gone and DATA is empty.

In client mode (CTRLA.MODE=0x2) the interface idles with MISO floating while SS is high, and DATA may be written whenever INTFLAG.DRE is set. With SS low and SCK running, data are sampled and shifted out in the chosen mode; DRE is set as TxDATA loads into the shift register. Each character received goes to the buffer on its last bit, with INTFLAG.RXC. When the host raises SS, INTFLAG.TXC is set. A write to DATA needs up to three SCK cycles to be ready for the shift register at the next character boundary, so the first character of a transaction is not DATA unless preloading is used, and in a multi-character transaction DATA must be written with at least three SCK cycles of the current character left, or the previous received character is sent again. INTFLAG.DRE sets three CLK_SERCOM_APB cycles after DATA empties.

The only receive error is STATUS.BUFOVF, kept until 1 is written to it and cleared when the receiver is disabled. With CTRLA.IBON=1 it is raised as the overflow happens, and reading until INTFLAG.RXC clears empties the buffer. With IBON=0 the overflow travels through the buffer, and when that data is read BUFOVF and INTFLAG.ERROR are set with INTFLAG.RXC and RxDATA reads zero.

As client (CTRLA.MODE=0x2) with CTRLA.FORM=0x2, the first character of each transaction is checked by the address match logic. On a match INTFLAG.RXC is set, MISO is enabled and the transaction proceeds, and in sleep the match can wake the device; with no match the whole transaction is ignored. With 9-bit characters only the low 8 bits are compared with ADDR. Preload must be off (CTRLB.PLOADEN=0).

At the start of a transaction a client first sends what is in its shift register: the reset value, or the last character of the previous transaction. With CTRLB.PLOADEN=1 one character written while SS is high is preloaded into the shift register, so no dummy character is sent; a second character written before SS falls waits in DATA. Enough time must pass between SS falling and the first SCK sampling edge: the SS synchronization to the system clock plus the MISO-to-SCK setup time.

Clients in parallel need CTRLB.MSSEN=0: the host drives one SS line per client from GPIO pins, and only the selected client drives the shared MISO. Clients in series share one SS, are all enabled together, and the host shifts n characters for n clients; SS can then be hardware or software controlled. Loop-back: pointing CTRLA.DIPO and CTRLA.DOPO at the same pad loops data through the pad, so it also appears on the pin.

In host mode with CTRLB.MSSEN=1 the SERCOM drives one SS: low at least one baud cycle before the transfer and at least one after it, and high at least one baud cycle between back-to-back frames. Each of these gaps, T, is one to two baud cycles depending on the transfer mode. With MSSEN=0 the SS pins are software-driven GPIO.
As client, CTRLB.SSDE=1 makes a falling edge on SS set INTFLAG.SSL and wake the device where enabled.

DMA: RX is raised while the receive buffer holds data and cleared by reading DATA; TX is raised while the transmit buffer is empty and cleared by writing DATA. Interrupt sources DRE, RXC, TXC, SSL and ERROR are asynchronous and can wake the device from any sleep mode; flags in INTFLAG, enable through INTENSET, disable through INTENCLR; a request lasts until its flag clears, the source is disabled or the SPI resets. One NVIC line serves them all.

Host with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY=1: GCLK_SERCOM_CORE keeps running in Idle and Standby and any interrupt can wake the device. Host with RUNSTDBY=0: the clock stops after the transaction in progress and any interrupt can wake it. Client with RUNSTDBY=1: Receive Complete can wake it. Client with RUNSTDBY=0: all reception, including the transaction in progress, is lost. Writes to CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE and CTRLB.RXEN are synchronized; CTRLB.RXEN in its own way, set out in the CTRLB description.
I2C is a SERCOM mode. Host and client each hold one shift register, one transmit buffer and one receive buffer; the host uses the baud-rate generator and the client the address match logic.

Host or client; DMA; compatible with Philips I2C, SMBus and PMBus; 100 kHz, 400 kHz, 1 MHz and 3.4 MHz modes with low system clock frequencies; slew-rate-limited outputs and filtered inputs. Client: works in all sleep modes, wakes on address match, hardware 7-bit and 10-bit address match for a unique address and/or the 7-bit general call address, an address range, or two unique addresses usable with DMA.

In I2C mode the SERCOM sets pin direction and level; PINCFGn.PULLEN and PINCFGn.DRVSTR still act. With the receiver or transmitter disabled the pins are free for other uses. CLK_SERCOMx_APB is on after reset and gated in MCLK and the Power Manager. GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE clocks the I2C as host; GCLK_SERCOM_SLOW is needed only for some functions such as SMBus timing. Both are set up in GCLK first and are asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes are synchronized.

operation.topic: I2C DMA, interrupts, debug and protection
operation.text: DMA requests go to the DMAC and the interrupt line to the NVIC. No events. The I2C keeps running under a debugger halt unless DBGCTRL stops it. The PAC can write-protect every writable register except INTFLAG, STATUS, DATA and ADDR; debugger accesses are not protected.

SDA carries data and SCL the clock. The host sends a start condition, a 7-bit address and a direction bit; the addressed client acknowledges, and 9-bit data packets follow, each 8 data bits and an acknowledge bit. On a NACK, from client or host, the host ends with a stop condition or sends a repeated start to carry on. Read is direction bit 1 and write 0; ACK is 0 and NACK 1.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except ACKACT and CMD), BAUD, and ADDR in client mode are enable-protected: writes are dropped while CTRLA.ENABLE=1 and, during disable, take effect once disabling completes. Set-up: CTRLA.MODE=0x5 for host or 0x4 for client; optionally CTRLA.SDAHOLD, CTRLB.SMEN for smart mode and CTRLA.LOWTOUT for the SCL low time-out. Host: CTRLA.INACTOUT for the inactive-bus time-out and BAUD for the bit rate. Client: CTRLB.AMODE for address matching and ADDR.ADDR with ADDR.ADDRMASK to suit.

Start and stop detectors and a bit counter watch the bus in all sleep modes, and STATUS.BUSSTATE reports the state; the state machine runs while the host is enabled. After enable the state is UNKNOWN (0b00). It moves to IDLE (0b01) when software writes 0b01 to BUSSTATE, when a stop is seen, or on an SMBus inactive-bus time-out if CTRLA.INACTOUT is set; it never returns to UNKNOWN. From IDLE, another host's start makes it BUSY (0b11) until a stop or time-out. Writing ADDR.ADDR while IDLE issues a start and makes it OWNER (0b10); a stop at the end returns it to IDLE. A collision while OWNER loses arbitration and makes it BUSY until a stop. A repeated start changes the state only if arbitration is lost during it. The whole address is always sent; after losing arbitration only ones are driven. A protocol violation can hang the I2C; CTRLA.SWRST=1 recovers it.

The host works byte by byte from interrupts, handling most events itself; auto-triggered operations and smart mode (CTRLB.SMEN) cut driver code. With CTRLA.SCLSM=0 the host holds SCL low on either side of the acknowledge bit; with SCLSM=1, interrupts come only after the acknowledge, useful when DATA need not be checked before acknowledging. High-speed mode needs SCLSM=1.

operation.topic: I2C host clock, Sm, Fm and Fm+
operation.text: Supported modes: Standard up to 100 kHz, Fast up to 400 kHz, Fast-mode Plus up to 1 MHz and High-speed up to 3.4 MHz. In Sm, Fm and Fm+ the BAUD register sets SCL low and high times while the bus sets rise and fall times; fall time counts within TLOW and rise time lasts until a high level is seen. TLOW, TSU;STO, TBUF, THD;STA and TSU;STA are timed by BAUD.BAUDLOW, or by BAUD.BAUD when BAUDLOW=0; THIGH by BAUD.BAUD. TRISE depends on bus impedance and TFALL on bus impedance and the open-drain current limit, and is usually taken as zero. Fm+ wants SCL high to low in the ratio 1:2, and at least one of BAUD.BAUD and BAUD.BAUDLOW has to be above zero.

When DATA is written in smart mode, at least 6 APB cycles pass between an SDA change and the next SCL rising edge. Where long rise times need more, software must time the gap between the DATA write and the flag clear, and smart mode cannot then be used.

In Hs mode SCL is not synchronized; its frequency comes from fGCLK and BAUD.HSBAUD, with HSBAUD timing both halves when BAUD.HSBAUDLOW=0. Hs wants SCL high to low in the ratio 1:2, and at least one of HSBAUD and HSBAUDLOW has to be above zero.

Writing the client address and direction bit to ADDR.ADDR starts a transaction: the host waits for an idle bus, sends a start, then the address. Four outcomes follow. Arbitration lost or bus error: INTFLAG.MB and STATUS.ARBLOST are set (with STATUS.BUSERR on a bus error), SDA output stops and SCL is released, and the host stays off the bus until it is idle; clearing the interrupt flag is enough, since the other flags clear at the next ADDR.ADDR write. STATUS.RXNACK always holds the last acknowledge received. No ACK: INTFLAG.MB and STATUS.RXNACK are set and SCL is held; the client may be busy or asleep, and a stop (preferred) or a repeated start follows; under SMBus a client must acknowledge its address, so no answer means it is absent. ACK on a write: INTFLAG.MB set, RXNACK cleared, SCL held; software writes DATA.DATA to send, writes ADDR.ADDR for a repeated start and new address, or issues a stop. ACK on a read: the first data byte is received, then INTFLAG.SB is set, RXNACK cleared and SCL held; software acknowledges to read on (by hand, or automatically in smart mode per CTRLB.ACKACT), sends a new address, or stops.

After a successful write address, writing DATA.DATA sends a byte while the host watches for collisions. A collision loses arbitration and sets STATUS.ARBLOST; success brings an ACK and clears STATUS.RXNACK; INTFLAG.MB is set either way, so ARBLOST is best checked first in the MB handler. RXNACK must be checked after every byte, and the host may not send more after a NACK. Reading with SCLSM=0: when INTFLAG.SB is set one byte has arrived and the host must send ACK or NACK; if arbitration is lost while sending a NACK, SB is not set and MB reports the change instead. Reading with SCLSM=1: when SB is set the byte has arrived and been acknowledged per CTRLB.ACKACT; set ACKACT for the next acknowledge, then read DATA and, outside smart mode, issue a command.

A host code 0b00001nnn is sent at full speed with ADDR.HS=0 and draws a NACK, since no client acknowledges it; arbitration happens only in this phase. Once the host-write interrupt arrives, the client address is written to ADDR.ADDR with ADDR.HS=1; the host sends a repeated start and the address with direction at high speed and stays in Hs mode until a stop. Each further repeated start needs ADDR.HS=1 written again with the new address. Hs transmission needs CTRLA.SPEED=0x2 and CTRLA.SCLSM=1.

With ADDR.TENBITEN=1, writing ADDR.ADDR sends two address bytes, which the client acknowledges. The 10-bit address always goes first with direction bit ADDR.ADDR[0]=0. A NACK on the first byte raises the write interrupt with STATUS.RXNACK set; otherwise the write interrupt comes after the second byte. For a read: write the 10-bit address to ADDR.ADDR[10:1] with TENBITEN=1 and ADDR.ADDR[0]=0; when the Host on Bus interrupt arrives, write ADDR[7:0] as '11110 address[9:8] 1' with TENBITEN cleared, which sends a repeated start and the first 7 address bits with read direction; then transfer data.

The client also works byte by byte from interrupts, with auto-triggered operations and smart mode (CTRLB.SMEN). With CTRLA.SCLSM=0 the client holds SCL low on either side of the acknowledge. With SCLSM=1, interrupts come only after the acknowledge is sent: for a host read the address and data interrupts arrive together after the address acknowledge, and for a host write the first data interrupt comes after the first byte has been received and acknowledged. Hs mode needs SCLSM=1.

After a start the address is checked by the match logic; a mismatch is ignored until the next start. With SCLSM=0, a match sets INTFLAG.AMATCH and SCL is held low until AMATCH is cleared, giving software unlimited time. With SCLSM=1, the acknowledge set by CTRLB.ACKACT is sent first, then AMATCH is set and SCL held. STATUS.DIR, updated only on a valid address, gives the direction. STATUS.COLL set means the previous packet to this client collided; a collision releases SDA and SCL silently, so the next AMATCH is the first sign. Collisions follow the SMBus Address Resolution Protocol. On a host read (DIR=1) an ACK sets INTFLAG.DRDY to ask for data; on a host write (DIR=0) an ACK makes the client wait for data, a repeated start or a stop; after a NACK the client waits for a new start and match. CTRLB.CMD=0x3 serves both directions, acting on STATUS.DIR, and writing 1 to INTFLAG.AMATCH also sends the acknowledge set by CTRLB.ACKACT.

After its address the client either waits for data or sends by writing DATA.DATA; INTFLAG.DRDY is set on each byte received or sent, and received bytes are acknowledged per CTRLB.ACKACT. On receive, SCL is held low until software acts. On send, a NACK (STATUS.RXNACK=1) means a stop or repeated start comes next: the client releases SDA, and a stop sets INTFLAG.PREC and returns it to idle.

In Hs mode (CTRLA.SPEED=0x2) with CTRLA.SCLSM=1 the client switches speed by itself: a start, host code and NACK put it in Hs mode and set STATUS.HS until the next stop. With ADDR.TENBITEN=1 the two address bytes after a start are matched against the 10-bit address; the first byte is always acknowledged and the second raises the address interrupt. A write then carries N data bytes. A read continues with a repeated start and '11110 ADDR[9:8] 1', which raises a second address interrupt with DIR set; the client treats it as addressed by the earlier 10-bit address.

With CTRLB.GCMD=1 and 7-bit addressing, INTFLAG.PREC is set by any stop on the bus; with GCMD=0 a stop without an address match does not set it. In a group command the host addresses several clients in one transmission, each after a repeated start, ending with one stop; at that stop every addressed client starts its command, and this client gets its stop interrupt.

Three hardware SCL-low time-outs, timed by GCLK_SERCOM_SLOW, which must come from a 32.768 kHz oscillator: TTIMEOUT, a single SCL low period of 25 to 35 ms (CTRLA.LOWTOUTEN); TLOW:SEXT, a client's total clock-low extension of 25 ms from start to stop of one message (CTRLA.SEXTTOEN); TLOW:MEXT, the host's total clock-low extension of 10 ms within one byte, measured between start, ACK and stop boundaries (CTRLA.MEXTTOEN). An SMBus-compatible SDA hold time is also available.
In smart mode, reading DATA.DATA by itself sends the acknowledge, ACK or NACK as CTRLB.ACKACT says, saving software steps.
CTRLA.PINOUT=1 bypasses the internal I2C drivers: SCL and SDA in and out use separate pads, and the bus then needs an outside tri-state driver that meets the I2C standard.
With CTRLB.QCEN=1, INTFLAG.SB or INTFLAG.MB is set right after the client acknowledges the address, and software then issues a stop or a repeated start through CTRLB.CMD or ADDR.ADDR.

DMA needs smart mode (CTRLB.SMEN=1). Client: an address match raises the address interrupt, and once it is serviced the data move by DMA; RX is raised when host write data arrive and cleared by reading DATA, TX when data are needed for a host read and cleared by writing DATA. Host: write ADDR with the address, ADDR.LEN and ADDR.LENEN=1; ADDR.LEN gives 0 to 255 data bytes, which DMA moves before an automatic NACK (on reads) and stop. If the client NACKs a host write before LEN bytes, a stop is sent and STATUS.LENERR is raised with INTFLAG.ERROR. Host RX is raised when read data arrive (cleared by reading DATA), TX when write data are needed (cleared by writing DATA).

Client sources ERROR, DRDY, AMATCH and PREC; host sources ERROR, SB and MB. All are asynchronous and can wake the device from any sleep mode. Flags in INTFLAG, enable through INTENSET, disable through INTENCLR; a request lasts until its flag clears, the source is disabled or the I2C resets. One NVIC line serves them all.

Host: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE keeps running in Idle, and in Standby too with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY=1; with RUNSTDBY=0 it stops after the transaction in progress; any interrupt can wake the device. Client: RUNSTDBY=1 lets Address Match wake the device; with RUNSTDBY=0 all reception is lost. Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, STATUS.BUSSTATE, and in host mode ADDR.ADDR and the DATA register.

There are up to five TC instances: TC0 to TC3 (as many as the device has) in PD1, and TC4, on every device, in PD0. Each is built from a counter with its prescaler, compare/capture channels and control logic. It counts clock pulses or events, time-stamps events or pin edges to measure frequency and pulse width, and generates frequencies and PWM.

8-, 16- or 32-bit operation; two compare/capture channels, with a double-buffered period (8-bit mode only) and double-buffered compare values; frequency generation and single-slope PWM; capture of events or pin edges, of frequency, of pulse width and of time stamps; one input event; interrupts and output events on overflow/underflow and on compare match or capture; internal prescaler; DMA.

Pins are assigned in PORT. The TC runs in any sleep mode whose clock runs; interrupts wake the device and events act on other peripherals without waking it. CLK_TCx_APB is gated in MCLK. GCLK_TCx is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some register accesses are synchronized. TC0 and TC1 share one generic clock channel, as do TC2 and TC3, so each pair runs at one frequency. DMA requests go to the DMAC, the interrupt line to the NVIC, events to EVSYS. The TC halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL keeps it running.

The PAC can write-protect every writable register except INTFLAG, STATUS, COUNT, PER, PERBUF, CCx and CCBUFx. While the CPU is halted in debug, all write protection is off, and debugger accesses are never protected.

A TC carries two compare/capture channels at most, CC0 and CC1. Its counter counts EVSYS events or GCLK_TCx ticks, optionally prescaled, and its value feeds the channels for comparison or capture. COUNT, CCx and CCBUFx are 8, 16 or 32 bits wide, with MAX to match; each buffer has a valid flag (BUFV) set when it holds a new value. PER and PERBUF exist in 8-bit mode only. Counter range and clock rate set the time resolution. The counter counts up or down and is compared with TOP or ZERO, and on a match can request DMA or raise interrupts and events; compare matches on CCx do the same and, in waveform modes, set period or pulse width. Capture measures period and pulse width or time-stamps pin edges or events.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), DRVCTRL, WAVE and EVCTRL are enable-protected; protected CTRLA bits may be written in the same write that sets ENABLE, not the one that clears it. Set-up: enable CLK_TCx_APB; CTRLA.MODE for 8, 16 (the default) or 32 bits; WAVE.WAVEGEN; optionally CTRLA.PRESCALER and, with a prescaler, CTRLA.PRESYNC; optionally CTRLBSET.ONESHOT=1 for one-shot and CTRLBSET.DIR=1 to count down from TOP; CTRLA.CAPTEN for capture channels; DRVCTRL.INVENx to invert an output or pin input.

CTRLA.ENABLE turns the TC on and off. CTRLA.SWRST=1 resets every register but DBGCTRL; disable the TC first or the result is undefined. The prescaler counts GCLK_TCx up to the chosen value and toggles its output, dividing by 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 256 or 1024. Above divide-by-1, CTRLA.PRESYNC chooses whether the counter acts on the next GCLK_TCx edge or the next prescaled edge. Counting events bypasses the prescaler. Prescaled ticks and event ticks together form CLK_TC_CNT.

CTRLA.MODE selects COUNT8, with its own PER and PERBUF; COUNT16, the default, with no period register; or COUNT32, made by pairing two TCs: TC0 with TC1 and TC2 with TC3 (TC4 cannot run 32-bit). A pair is controlled through the even TC's registers; the odd one becomes slave, sets STATUS.SLAVE, and its own registers neither show nor change the 32-bit counter, and its COUNT and CCx may not be accessed.

Each CLK_TC_CNT tick clears, reloads, increments or decrements the counter; a clear or reload ends one cycle and starts the next. CTRLB.DIR=0 counts up and 1 down. Counting up, the tick after TOP sets the counter to zero (overflow); counting down, ZERO reloads TOP (underflow); either sets INTFLAG.OVF, which can raise an interrupt, an event or a DMA request, and stops the counter when CTRLBSET.ONESHOT is set. COUNT may be written while running, and the write wins over count, clear or reload; the direction may also change while running. On start, COUNT begins at ZERO or TOP by direction unless written, or unless stopped elsewhere than ZERO. Settings take effect after synchronization. Normal operation must be used when the counter is the time base for capture.

Stop (CTRLBSET.CMD=0x2) loads the start value (ZERO or TOP by direction), clears all waveforms and sets STATUS.STOP. Re-trigger, by command (CTRLBSET.CMD=0x1) or event (EVCTRL.EVACT=0x1), reloads or clears the counter while counting, or resumes from COUNT when stopped; with the re-trigger event action, enabling the TC does not start it, and the first event starts it and each later one restarts it. Count (EVCTRL.EVACT=0x2) steps the counter up or down on each event. Start (EVCTRL.EVACT=0x3) starts a stopped counter on an event and does nothing while it counts; once enabled, counting begins on the event or a re-trigger command.

Channels default to compare. COUNT is compared with each CCx continuously, for timing or waveforms. CCBUFx double buffers CCx, copying at UPDATE or on a forced update (CTRLBSET.CMD=UPDATE), which avoids odd-length pulses and glitches. To put a waveform on a pin: choose WAVE.WAVEGEN, optionally invert WO[x] with DRVCTRL.INVENx, and assign the pin in PORT. A match sets INTFLAG.MCx on the next rising edge of CLK_TC_CNT and can raise an interrupt, event and DMA request. WAVE.WAVEGEN offers NFRQ, MFRQ, NPWM and MPWM. In NFRQ and NPWM, TOP is PER in 8-bit mode and MAX in 16- and 32-bit modes.

NFRQ: the period is set by PER (8-bit) or MAX (16- and 32-bit), and WO[x] toggles on each match of COUNT with CCx, setting INTFLAG.MCx. MFRQ: CC0 sets the period instead, and WO[0] toggles on each update.

NPWM: TOP sets the period and CCx the duty cycle. Counting up, WO[x] is set at start or at TOP and cleared at the CCx match; counting down, it is cleared at start or at ZERO and set at the CCx match. MPWM: CC0 is TOP and WO[1] follows CC1, while WO[0] gives a one-clock negative pulse at each overflow or underflow.

CCx, and PER in 8-bit mode, are double buffered, with valid bits CCBUFVx and PERBUFV in STATUS. While a valid bit is 1 the matching SYNCBUSY bit is set, writing that register or its buffer gives a PAC error, and the register itself cannot be accessed. With a valid bit set and CTRLB.LUPD=0 (cleared by writing CTRLBCLR.LUPD=1), the buffer is copied into the register at the hardware UPDATE and the valid bit clears. The software update command (CTRLBSET.CMD=0x3) works whatever LUPD is. Buffering is optional: both registers are in the map, and CTRLBSET.LUPD=1 turns it off. Counting down in NFRQ, MFRQ or PWM with buffering on, PERBUF is copied to PER continuously, whatever the update condition.

A new TOP (PER or CC0 by mode) takes effect after the synchronization delay, buffered or not. Unbuffered and counting up, a new TOP below the current COUNT makes the counter run on to wrap before it can match. With buffering software may write the buffer whenever it likes and PER changes only at the update, so no wrap or odd waveform occurs.

CTRLA.CAPTENx=1 makes channel x capture. The trigger is the TC_EV input event (EVCTRL.TCEI=1) or the channel's WO[x] pin (CTRLA.COPENx=1), one or the other per channel, so one channel can use a pin while the other uses an event. Pin capture works only in the event and time-stamp capture actions; other actions need internal events, so a pin is routed through an event first. Event System capture works in the event, time-stamp and PPW/PWP/PW actions, and its channels must be asynchronous. Capture is on the rising edge by default; for the falling edge set DRVCTRL.INVENx on a pin or EVCTRL.TCINV on an event. CCBUFx and CCx work as a FIFO: once CCx is read or empty, CCBUFx moves into it and the valid flag sets the channel interrupt flag, with optional interrupt, event or DMA request; CCBUFx cannot be read, so all captures are read from CCx.
