With EVCTRL.EVACT set to OFF, RETRIGGER, COUNT or START, the channels time-stamp events from EVSYS or their pins. A new capture arriving while INTFLAG.MCx is still set is not stored and sets INTFLAG.ERR.

PPW and PWP capture on both edges and restart the counter on one, giving period T and pulse width tp, hence frequency and duty cycle. PWP puts T in CC1 and tp in CC0; PPW puts T in CC0 and tp in CC1. EVCTRL.TCINV=1 moves the restart to the falling edge. Both channels need CTRLA.CAPTENx=1 to capture both values. A capture arriving while INTFLAG.MCx is set is lost and sets INTFLAG.ERR.

PW captures on the falling edge of the input, clearing the counter and stopping it there, and restarts counting on the rising edge. Inverting the input (DRVCTRL.INVENx or EVCTRL.TCINV) swaps the edges. A capture arriving while INTFLAG.MCx is set is lost and sets INTFLAG.ERR.

With CTRLBSET.ONESHOT=1 (cleared through CTRLBCLR.ONESHOT) the counter stops at the next overflow or underflow, sets STATUS.STOP and drives the waveform outputs to zero. A re-trigger command, re-trigger event or start event restarts it and clears STATUS.STOP.

With the STAMP event action, and TOP below MAX, each capture event copies COUNT into CCx, or MAX if the counter overflowed, and sets INTFLAG.MCx. A capture arriving while MCx is set is lost and sets INTFLAG.ERR.

CTRLA.CAPTMODEn=CAPTMIN keeps the lowest captured value in CCx: a capture is stored only if COUNT is below the last one, and MCx sets when COUNT is at or above the previous capture, marking a new absolute minimum. CCx must start non-zero, or nothing is captured. CAPTMAX keeps the highest: stored only if COUNT is above the last capture, MCx set when COUNT is at or below the previous one; CCx must start below TOP, or nothing is captured.

OVF is raised on an update (overflow, underflow or re-trigger) and cleared by the DMA acknowledge. MCx, for a compare channel, is raised on each match and cleared by the acknowledge; for a capture channel it is raised while CCx holds valid data and cleared by reading CCx.

Interrupt sources OVF, MCx and ERR (capture overflow), each with a flag in INTFLAG, enabled through INTENSET and disabled through INTENCLR; a request lasts until its flag clears, the source is disabled or the TC resets, and one NVIC line serves all. Output events are OVF and MCx; EVCTRL.MCEOx=1 enables an output event and 0 disables it. EVCTRL.EVACT picks one input action: OFF, START, RETRIGGER, COUNT, STAMP, PPW/PWP or PW; EVCTRL.TCEI enables the input event, which must come over an asynchronous path.

The TC works in any sleep mode; in Standby it needs CTRLA.RUNSTDBY=1. It wakes the device by interrupt or acts through EVSYS. With CTRLA.ONDEMAND=1 it stops requesting its clock while STATUS.STOP=1 and asks for it again on a re-trigger or start, before counting resumes.

Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, STATUS.CCBUFVx, CTRLBCLR, CTRLBSET, COUNT, PER, PERBUF, CCx and CCBUFx. COUNT is synchronized for reading on demand by the READSYNC command in CTRLBSET.CMD.

Three TCC instances, TCC0 to TCC2. Each is built from a counter with its prescaler, compare/capture channels and control logic; counts clock pulses or events, time-stamps input events to measure frequency and pulse width, and generates frequencies and PWM. Waveform extensions aimed at motor control, ballasts, LEDs, H-bridges and power converters give low- and high-side outputs with optional dead time and synchronized bit patterns across the outputs, and the fault inputs shut external drivers down in a safe, predictable way.

Up to four compare/capture channels with double-buffered period, double-buffered compare or capture, and circular buffers on period and compare; frequency generation, single-slope PWM and dual-slope PWM with half-cycle reload; event, frequency and pulse-width capture; output matrix routing channels to pins, low- and high-side outputs with programmable dead time, double-buffered swap and pattern generation, dithering; two recoverable and two non-recoverable fault sources, the debugger able to act as a non-recoverable fault; two counter input events and one per channel; output events for count, re-trigger and overflow plus one per channel; interrupts on overflow and re-trigger, compare match or capture, and faults; DMA requests and triggers.

Pins are assigned in PORT. The TCC runs in any sleep mode whose clock runs; interrupts wake the device and events act on other peripherals without waking it. CLK_TCCx_APB is on after reset and gated in MCLK. GCLK_TCCx must be set up in GCLK first; TCC0 and TCC1 share one generic clock generator. GCLK_TCCx is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes are synchronized. DMA requests go to the DMAC, the interrupt line to the NVIC, events to EVSYS. The TCC halts while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL keeps it running.

The PAC can write-protect every writable register except INTFLAG, STATUS, PER, PERBUF, CCx, CCBUFx, WAVE, PATT and PATTBUF. While the CPU is halted in debug, all write protection is off, and debugger accesses are never protected.

Each TCC has up to four channels CCx. COUNT, PER/PERBUF and CCx/CCBUFx are 16 or 24 bits wide depending on the instance, each buffer with a valid flag. The counter is compared with TOP and ZERO, and on reaching either the TCC can raise interrupts, DMA requests or events; in waveform modes the comparisons set period and pulse width. A prescaled GCLK_TCCx and EVSYS events drive the counter, and events also trigger capture.

Acting directly on the channel outputs, the recoverable fault unit lets events restart or halt the period, shorten the active pulse, or disable the output while the fault lasts, for uses such as current-sense regulation and zero-crossing or demagnetization re-triggering. It shares the MCE0 and MCE1 event inputs and uses only asynchronous events when enabled. Fault inputs can be filtered, blanked and qualified to reject glitches.

Some instances add stages after the fault unit. The output matrix (OTMX) routes channel outputs to the pins in several arrangements. Dead-time insertion (DTI) splits each of the four lower OTMX outputs into a non-inverted low side (LS) and an inverted high side (HS) with optional dead time between them. SWAP exchanges LS and HS, for example for fast-decay motor control. Pattern generation forces outputs to fixed levels, changed at UPDATE, for stepper and full-bridge drive. The non-recoverable fault unit forces the outputs to a preset safe state on a fault, for immediate shutdown of high-current or high-voltage drives; it shares the TCE0 and TCE1 count events, which may be filtered, and unfiltered it acts asynchronously even with no clock running.

Enable-protected: CTRLA (except RUNSTDBY, ENABLE and SWRST), FCTRLA, FCTRLB, WEXCTRL, DRVCTRL and EVCTRL. Protected CTRLA bits may be written in the write that sets ENABLE, not the one that clears it. Required: enable CLK_TCCx_APB, and for capture set CTRLA.CPTEN for the channel. Optional: CTRLA.PRESCALER, CTRLA.PRESCSYNC, CTRLBSET.DIR=1 for down-counting, WAVE.WAVEGEN, WAVE.POL, and DRVCTRL.INVEN per channel.

CTRLA.ENABLE turns the TCC on and off. CTRLA.SWRST=1 resets every register but DBGCTRL and disables it; disable first or the result is undefined. The prescaler divides GCLK_TCCx by 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 256 or 1024; above 1, the counter can act on the next GCLK_TCC edge or the next prescaled edge (CTRLA.PRESYNC). Counting events bypasses the prescaler. Prescaled ticks and event ticks together form CLK_TCC_COUNT.

Each CLK_TCC_COUNT tick clears, reloads, increments or decrements the counter. CTRLB.DIR=0 counts up and 1 down. Counting up, the tick after TOP sets zero (overflow); counting down, ZERO reloads TOP (underflow); either sets INTFLAG.OVF, usable for an interrupt, DMA request or event, and stops the counter in one-shot mode (CTRLBSET.ONESHOT). COUNT may be written while running, the write winning over count, clear or reload, and the direction may change while running. On start, COUNT begins at ZERO or TOP by direction unless written, or unless stopped elsewhere than ZERO.

Stop (CTRLBSET.CMD=0x2) holds COUNT and, with waveform generation, drives the outputs to the state in DRVCTRL.NREx/NRVx and sets STATUS.STOP. Pause (EVCTRL.EVACT1=0x3, STOP) holds COUNT and the outputs until a start event (EVCTRL.EVACT0=0x3, START). Re-trigger, by command (CTRLBSET.CMD=0x1) or event (EVCTRL.EVACTn=0x1), reloads or clears the counter while counting and sets INTFLAG.TRG, with an event if EVCTRL.TRGEO=1; when stopped it resumes from COUNT; with the re-trigger event action enabling does not start the counter, the first event starts it and each later one restarts it. Start (EVCTRL.EVACT0=0x3) starts a stopped counter and is ignored while counting; with it, enabling does not start the counter and later events do not restart it. Count (EVCTRL.EVACT0=0x5) steps up or down by direction on each event. Direction (EVCTRL.EVACT1=0x2) sets the direction from the event level, over an asynchronous path, overriding CTRLB.DIR. Increment (EVCTRL.EVACT0=0x4) counts up on each TCE0 event and decrement (EVCTRL.EVACT1=0x4) counts down on each TCE1 event, whatever the direction. Non-recoverable fault (EVCTRL.EVACTn=0x7) stops the counter and overrides the outputs per DRVCTRL.NREx/NRVx; TCE0 and TCE1 must then be asynchronous. With the action off (0x0) enabling the TCC also starts it.

Channels default to compare and must be reconfigured to capture. COUNT is compared with each CCx continuously. CCBUFx double buffers CCx, copied at UPDATE or on a forced update (CTRLBSET.CMD=0x3), avoiding odd-length pulses and glitches. For a pin output: choose WAVE.WAVEGEN, optionally invert with DRVCTRL.INVENx, assign the pin in PORT. A match sets INTFLAG.MCx on the next rising edge of CLK_TCC_COUNT, and can raise an interrupt (INTENSET.MCx), an event (EVCTRL.MCEOx), both, and a DMA request. WAVE.WAVEGEN offers NFRQ, MFRQ, NPWM, DSTOP, DSBOTTOM, DSBOTH and DSCRITICAL. TOP is CC0 in MFRQ and PER in all others. Dual-slope modes update when the counter reaches ZERO; the others update on wraparound: overflow, underflow or re-trigger.
NFRQ: PER sets the period and WO[x] toggles on each match of COUNT with CCx, setting the channel match flag. MFRQ: CC0 sets the period instead and WO[0] toggles at each update.
NPWM: TOP sets the period and CCx the duty cycle. Counting up, WO[x] is set at start or at TOP and cleared at the CCx match; counting down, cleared at start or at ZERO and set at the CCx match.

PER sets TOP and CCx the duty cycle; the counter runs ZERO to PER and back. WO[x] is set on the match while counting up and cleared on the match while counting down. Interrupts and events come at TOP, ZERO or both, by mode; in DSBOTH a second update at TOP occurs when the circular buffer is on. Dual slope reaches a lower top frequency than single slope. TOP sets the resolution, at least 1 bit (TOP=0x00000001), and with TOP=0x00000001 and no prescaler the output reaches half of fGCLK_TCC. In DSTOP, DSBOTTOM and DSBOTH with TOP below MAX/2, the MSB of CCx picks the ramp on which the match interrupt or event fires: rising for CCx[MSB]=0, falling for 1.
DSCRITICAL makes centred pulses that need not be aligned: PER sets the period, CCx sets the output edge while counting up and CC(x+CC_NUM/2) the edge while counting down.

WAVE.POLx works in every waveform mode. In single- and dual-slope PWM it flips the edge alignment of each channel to the start or end of the cycle. In NFRQ and MFRQ it sets the output's initial state.

PATT, WAVE, PER and CCx are double buffered, with valid bits PATTBUFV, WAVEBUFV, PERBUFV and CCBUFVx in STATUS. While a valid bit is 1 the matching SYNCBUSY bit is set, writing that register or its buffer gives a PAC error, and reading the register is invalid. With a valid bit set and CTRLB.LUPD=0 (cleared by writing CTRLBCLR.LUPD=1), the buffer is copied at the hardware UPDATE and the valid bit clears. The software update command (CTRLBSET.CMD=0x3) works whatever LUPD is. Buffering is optional and CTRLBSET.LUPD=1 turns it off. Counting down in NFRQ, MFRQ or PWM with buffering on, PERBUF is copied to PER continuously.

A new TOP (PER or CC0 by mode) takes effect after the synchronization delay, buffered or not. Unbuffered and counting up, in any mode, a new TOP below the current COUNT makes the counter run on to wrap before it can match. With buffering, PERBUF can be written at any time and PER changes only at the update, so no wrap or odd waveform occurs.

Capture needs EVCTRL.MCEIx=1 and CTRLA.CPTENx=1 for the channel. Channels time-stamp EVSYS events. CCBUFx and CCx work as a FIFO: once CCx is read or empty, CCBUFx moves into it and sets the channel flag, with optional interrupt, event or DMA request; CCBUFx cannot be read, so captures are read from CCx. A capture arriving while STATUS.CCBUFV is still set is not stored and sets INTFLAG.ERR.

PPW or PWP in EVCTRL.EVACT1 captures on both edges and restarts the counter on one, giving period T and pulse width tp: PPW puts T in CC0 and tp in CC1, PWP the reverse. EVCTRL.TCEINVx=1 moves the restart to the falling edge for event source x. A channel captures only with CTRLA.CPTENx=1; otherwise it ignores the capture and stays a compare channel, free for other use. A capture arriving while INTFLAG.MCx is set is lost and sets INTFLAG.ERR. Counting up, CAPTMIN capture (FCTRLn.CAPTURE=CAPTMIN) cannot record values below 1; counting down covers the full range down to 0. In dual-slope PWM with TOP below MAX/2, the MSB of CCx records CTRLB.DIR: 0 for a capture on the rising ramp, 1 on the falling ramp.

With CTRLBSET.ONESHOT=1 (cleared through CTRLBCLR.ONESHOT) the counter stops at the next overflow or underflow, sets STATUS.STOP and drives the outputs to the DRVCTRL.NREx/NRVx values. A re-trigger command, re-trigger event or start event restarts it and clears STATUS.STOP.
PER and CC0 to CC3 can run as circular buffers: at each update the register value is copied back into its buffer. Circular buffering is meant for RAMP2, RAMP2A and DSBOTH.

Dithering adds extra clock cycles to some compare matches across a frame of 16, 32 or 64 PWM cycles, one at a time in a blue-noise sequence that keeps flicker low, refining the average pulse width or period. CTRLA.RESOLUTION selects DITH4 (16-cycle frame), DITH5 (32) or DITH6 (64). The low DITHERCY bits of COUNT, PER and CCx give the number of extra cycles in the frame and the remaining bits the value itself; in DITH4 the four least significant bits are DITHERCY. A cycle gets an extra clock when, with MASK = 0x0F, 0x1F or 0x3F for DITH4, DITH5 or DITH6 and value = cycle × DITHERCY, (value AND MASK) + DITHERCY exceeds MASK. Dithering CCx leaves the period unchanged.

WAVE.RAMP picks one of three ramp modes, all on single-slope PWM. RAMP1 is ordinary single-slope PWM. RAMP2 serves power factor correction, half-bridge and push-pull SMPS: two timer cycles alternate, A with the odd channel output off and B with the even one off; the ramp index advances at each update and can be set by CTRLBSET.IDXCMD. In standard RAMP2, PER sets both ramp periods, different per ramp with WAVE.CIPEREN=1; two channels give two outputs, or one output and one capture channel. In RAMP2A, with the circular buffer on, CC0 drives both WO[0] and WO[1] with the same polarity, and channel 1 is free for capture. RAMP2C gives RAMP2 behaviour without the circular-buffer update constraint: CC0 sets ramp A's period and PER ramp B's; with more than two channels WO[0] is set by CC2 and cleared by CC0, and on a two-channel TCC a pulse on WO[0] lasts all of ramp A when WAVE.POL0=0.

Fault A and Fault B act on channels CC0 and CC1, restarting or halting the counter and holding the outputs inactive either while the fault lasts or from the first valid fault to the end of the cycle. The inputs are the first two channel events, TCCxMC0 (A) and TCCxMC1 (B), over asynchronous EVSYS channels, and the TCC must run a PWM mode.

FCTRLA and FCTRLB each set three filters, usable alone or together. Input filter: detection is normally asynchronous, acting at once even with no clock; FCTRLn.FILTERVAL drops events shorter than that many clocks and delays valid ones by the same. Blanking: FCTRLn.BLANK picks an output edge after which faults are ignored for a time set by FCTRLn.BLANKVAL, against switching bounce; FCTRLn.BLANKPRESC=1 divides the blanking clock by 64. With BLANKVAL=255 the longest blanking is 2.67 µs unprescaled or 170 µs prescaled at fGCLK_TCCx = 96 MHz, and 170 µs or 10.9 ms at 1 MHz. Qualification: FCTRLn.QUAL=1 ignores the fault input whenever its channel output is inactive.

Fault A and B actions are set separately and most can be combined. Keep (FCTRLn.KEEP=1): the output is clamped to zero while the fault lasts and released at the start of the first cycle after it ends. Restart (FCTRLn.RESTART=1): the fault ends the cycle and starts a new one; in RAMP1 the outputs stay inactive while the fault lasts; in RAMP2 the cycle index advances, and Fault A counts only in cycle A, Fault B only in cycle B. Hardware halt (FCTRLn.HALT=0x1): the counter halts and the cycle stretches while the fault lasts, with the output inactive, and counting resumes when it ends (restarting if Restart is also set); in RAMP2 and RAMP2A a new cycle advances the index. Software halt (FCTRLn.HALT=0x2): as hardware halt, but resuming also needs software to clear STATUS.FAULTn after the fault ends.

FCTRLn.CAPTURE captures the counter when the fault occurs. CAPT is an ordinary capture, flagging each one. CAPTMIN and CAPTMAX keep the absolute minimum or maximum in CCx, storing only a lower or higher value and flagging each new extreme; CCx must start non-zero for CAPTMIN and below TOP for CAPTMAX, or nothing is captured. LOCMIN, LOCMAX and DERIV0 let CCx follow the counter at each fault and flag a local minimum, local maximum, or either (DERIV0 is LOCMIN OR LOCMAX). In CAPT an interrupt comes with every filtered fault and channel capture; in the other modes only on an extreme value.

A non-recoverable fault drives every compare output to the level set in DRVCTRL.NRE and DRVCTRL.NRV; the EV0 and EV1 inputs are enabled as faults in EVCTRL.EVACT0 and EVACT1. DRVCTRL.FILTERVALn adds a digital filter, making detection synchronous and delaying the action by the filter length. With DBGCTRL.FDDBD=1, entering debug raises a Debug Fault State and its DFS interrupt. In RAMP2, RAMP2A or DSBOTH with CTRLBSET.LUPD=1, a change of ramp index or direction raises an Update Fault State and its UFS interrupt.

With the STAMP event action, and TOP below MAX, each capture event copies COUNT into CCx, or MAX after an overflow, and sets INTFLAG.MCx. A capture arriving while MCx is set is lost and sets INTFLAG.ERR.
After the recoverable fault stage come OTMX, DTI, SWAP and pattern generation. DTI and SWAP work on pin pairs: slice x acts on WO[x] and WO[WO_NUM/2 + x].

0x0, the default, puts channel n on OTMX[n] and, with more outputs than channels, repeats the channels modulo their number (channel 0 again on OTMX[CC_NUM], and so on). 0x1 repeats them modulo half their number, giving the lower channels twice the outputs, for example four full-bridge transistors from two channels, with pattern generation overriding outputs for any quadrant. 0x2 puts CC0 on every output, for a stepper with pattern generation. 0x3 puts CC0 on the first output and CC1 on all others, which with pattern generation and the fault extension can drive as many as seven boosted LED strings.

Dead time is an off period in which both the non-inverted low side and the inverted high side are held low, so the two never switch together. There are four identical generators, one per lower channel, sharing one dead-time register, with separate low- and high-side values. An 8-bit counter counts down one per peripheral clock to zero and holds both outputs off while non-zero. A rising OTMX edge reloads it from DTLS and a falling edge from DTHS.

The pattern generator drives a synchronized bit pattern on its pins, for BLDC commutation, steppers and full bridges. PATT.PGE enables the pattern per output and PATT.PGV gives its level; their buffers update at UPDATE like other double-buffered registers, and software may write PATT directly when no synchronization is needed.
Two TCCs on the same GCLK_TCC can be linked for more synchronized channels: CTRLA.MSYNC=1 in the slave makes its channels follow the master's counter.

OVF: with CTRLA.DMAOS=0 a request comes on every update (overflow, underflow or re-trigger); with DMAOS=1 a trigger comes on the update following a DMA one-shot command (CTRLBSET.CMD=DMAOS); either is cleared by the acknowledge. MCx on a compare channel: a request on each match with DMAOS=0, none with DMAOS=1, cleared by the acknowledge. MCx on a capture channel: raised while CCx holds valid data and cleared by reading CCx, whatever DMAOS is.

Circular buffers, meant only for RAMP2, RAMP2A and DSBOTH, must be rewritten in order and in step with the timer, which the DMA triggers ensure. In RAMP2 and RAMP2A, a channel's request comes at the start of ramp B instead of on its match, and with any circular buffer on the overflow request waits for the start of ramp A after a DMA transfer in the previous ramp B; one DMA channel on the MC trigger updates ramp A values and a second on the overflow request updates ramp B values. In DSBOTH the channel request comes at the start of down-counting and the overflow request at the start of up-counting after a transfer in the previous down-count, again split over two DMA channels.

Sources OVF, TRG, CNT (selected by EVCTRL.CNTSEL), ERR, UFS, DFS, the recoverable faults FAULTn, the non-recoverable faults FAULTx and MCx. All are asynchronous wake-up sources. Flags in INTFLAG, enable through INTENSET, disable through INTENCLR; a request lasts until its flag clears, the source is disabled or the TCC resets; one NVIC line serves all.

Output events OVF, TRG, CNT (selected by EVCTRL.CNTSEL) and MCx, each enabled by its EVCTRL.xxEO bit. A channel input event (MCx) can capture or raise a recoverable or non-recoverable fault. Event 1 (TCCx EV1) can re-trigger, set the direction, stop, decrement, capture period and pulse width, or raise a non-recoverable fault. Event 0 (TCCx EV0) can re-trigger, count by direction, start (counting on from the rising edge to TOP or ZERO, unaffected by later events), increment regardless of direction, count by direction on each prescaled clock while the asynchronous event is active, or raise a non-recoverable fault. EVCTRL.EVACT0 and EVACT1 choose the actions and EVCTRL.MCEIx and TCEIx enable the inputs; with several events wired to the TCC, the action applies to each of them.
The TCC works in any sleep mode; in Standby it needs CTRLA.RUNSTDBY=1. It wakes the device by interrupt or acts through EVSYS.

Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLBCLR, CTRLBSET, STATUS, PATT, PATTBUF, WAVE, COUNT, PER, PERBUF, CCx and CCBUFx. Synchronized on read: CTRLBCLR, CTRLBSET, PATT, PATTBUF, WAVE, PER, PERBUF, CCx, CCBUFx, and COUNT on demand through the READSYNC command in CTRLBSET.CMD.

The true random number generator delivers numbers that come from a physical entropy source, not from an algorithm. Its output passes the NIST SP 800-22 and Diehard test suites, and it can seed a NIST-approved deterministic generator as FIPS PUB 140-2 and 140-3 call for. A fresh 32-bit value is ready every 84 clock cycles. It has no pins, no DMA and no analog connections.

Clocked by CLK_TRNG_APB, gated in MCLK. The TRNG keeps running in any sleep mode while its clock runs; its interrupt can wake the device and its event can act through EVSYS without waking it. It keeps running when the CPU is halted by a debugger. All writable registers except INTFLAG can be write-protected by the PAC.

Once CTRLA.ENABLE is 1 the TRNG produces a new 32-bit number in DATA every 84 CLK_TRNG_APB cycles, flagging each with an optional interrupt or event; writing CTRLA.ENABLE to 0 stops it. EVCTRL can be written only while the TRNG is disabled. No register needs synchronization.

Interrupt source DATARDY, set when DATA holds a new number; it is a synchronous wake-up source. Flag in INTFLAG, enabled through INTENSET, disabled through INTENCLR, one combined line to the NVIC. Output event DATARDY, enabled by EVCTRL.DATARDYEO. In standby, CTRLA.RUNSTDBY=0 stops the TRNG while keeping its settings; RUNSTDBY=1 keeps it running so an enabled interrupt can wake the CPU.

The AES module encrypts and decrypts 128-bit blocks with one shared symmetric key, following FIPS 197. Key lengths of 128, 192 and 256 bits run 10, 12 and 14 rounds, and one block takes 57, 67 or 77 cycles. It supports the five NIST SP 800-38A confidentiality modes (ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR), CCM and CCM* for authenticated encryption, CFB data segments of 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits, and optionally GCM encryption with authentication.

Clocked entirely by CLK_AES_APB, gated in MCLK. The module draws clock only during an APB access to its registers or while it is enabled and processing. It works in any sleep mode while its clock runs, and all its interrupts are synchronous wake-up sources. The DMAC serves it through two request lines, an input-data request and an output-data request. It keeps running under a debugger halt but can be made to halt. Every writable register but INTFLAG can be PAC write-protected; debugger accesses are not protected.

Round keys come from the cipher key by the Rijndael key schedule. An initial AddRoundKey XORs the state with the round key; each full round then applies SubBytes (table substitution of each byte), ShiftRows (cyclic shift of each row), MixColumns (mixing the four bytes of each column) and AddRoundKey; the final round leaves out MixColumns.

CTRLA is enable-protected. CTRLA.ENABLE turns the module on and off and CTRLA.SWRST resets it. CTRLA.CIPHER picks encryption or decryption and CTRLA.KEYSIZE the 128, 192 or 256-bit key held in KEYWORD; with CTRLA.XORKEY set, a write to KEYWORD stores the XOR of the new and old key. Input and output share a buffer of four 32-bit words reached through the DATA address; DATABUFPTR names the word the next access uses, steps by one and wraps after each access, and can be written directly. CBC, CFB and OFB need a 128-bit initialization vector in INTVECT, which also holds the counter in CTR mode; GCM also needs its 128-bit authentication data. Writing CTRLB.NEWMSG marks the next block as the start of a message. CTRLA.AESMODE selects the mode and CTRLA.CFBS the CFB segment size. The CTR block counter is 16 bits wide, so it rolls over after 1 MB of data. When a block is done INTFLAG.ENCCMP sets and can interrupt; it clears once the relevant output words have been read.

CTRLA.STARTMODE selects how processing starts. Manual: load the key into KEYWORD, the IV or counter into INTVECT (every mode but ECB), enable interrupts in INTENSET if wanted, write the data to DATA, then set CTRLB.START; INTFLAG.ENCCMP sets at the end and clears when DATA is read. Auto: processing begins by itself once the needed number of input words is written, with no START bit; DMA transfers use this mode. Last Output Data (LOD): used for the MAC in CCM. With LOD off in CCM the input is counter-mode encrypted; with LOD on, CBC-MAC is computed from an all-zero IV, and ENCCMP clears on the next write to DATA instead of on a read, so only the final result of a chain of blocks has to be read. Building the message for a CCM* security level is left to software.

The expanded key holds 4(Nr + 1) 32-bit words, of which the first Nk (4, 6 or 8 for 128, 192 or 256-bit keys) are the user key. Encryption walks it forward four words a round; decryption walks it backward, starting from the last four words. The module computes each round key on the fly instead of storing the whole schedule, so decryption needs the last Nk words first. Writing CTRLA.KEYGEN computes them ahead in Nr clock cycles; otherwise they are computed automatically at the first decryption, adding Nr cycles of latency to it.

Four hardware countermeasures against differential power analysis: type 1 and type 2 each randomly add one cycle to processing (two variants); type 3 adds a random number of cycles, at most 11, 13 or 15 for 128, 192 or 256-bit keys; type 4 adds random spurious current draw. All are enabled by default but take effect only after a seed is written to the DRNGSEED register; CTRLA.CTYPE disables any of them. They draw on a deterministic random generator inside the module seeded through RANDSEED, and a new seed is needed after a key-size change. More countermeasures mean better protection and lower throughput; throughput is highest with all of them off.

GCM pairs the AES engine in CTR mode, which gives confidentiality, with a GHASH universal hash over a binary Galois field, which runs after the AES step on each packet and yields the authentication tag (NIST SP 800-38D).

Set CTRLA with STARTMODE manual (auto when the DMAC feeds it), CIPHER encryption, KEYSIZE to suit the key, AESMODE ECB and CTYPE as wanted; set CTRLA.ENABLE; write 0 to CIPLEN; write the key to KEYWORD; write zeros to DATA; set CTRLB.START; wait for INTFLAG.ENCCMP. The hash subkey then sits in HASHKEY.

Set CTRLA with STARTMODE manual, CIPHER encryption, KEYSIZE to suit, AESMODE GCM and CTYPE as wanted; set CTRLA.ENABLE; write the key to KEYWORD; set CTRLB.GFMUL; write a block of authentication data to DATA; set CTRLB.START; wait for INTFLAG.GFMCMP; the result is in GHASH. Repeat the data, start and wait steps for each further header block. Authentication data shorter than 128 bits is zero-padded to a full block.

Set CTRLB.NEWMSG; load CIPLEN; load J0 + 1 into INTVECT, where J0 = IV || 0^31 || 1 for a 96-bit IV and otherwise J0 = GHASH_H(IV || 0^(s+64) || [len(IV)]64), s being the fewest zeros that pad the IV to a multiple of 128 bits. For each block: load plaintext into DATA, set CTRLB.START, wait for INTFLAG.ENCCMP; the ciphertext is in DATA and the running hash in GHASH. Before the last block set CTRLB.EOM, then write it, start and wait as before; GHASH then holds the final hash of the data. Finally load [len(A)]64 || [len(C)]64 into DATA, set CTRLB.GFMUL and CTRLB.START, and wait for INTFLAG.GFMCMP; GHASH holds the final value. With the DMAC feeding the module the sequence is the same without the START writes for the data blocks.

Write CTRLA.ENABLE to 0, set CTRLA.AESMODE to CTR, write CTRLA.ENABLE to 1; load J0 into the initialization vector register and the GHASH value into DATA; set CTRLB.NEWMSG and CTRLB.START; wait for INTFLAG.ENCCMP. The GCM tag is then in DATA. No AES register needs synchronization.

A USB 2.1 full-speed (12 Mbit/s) and low-speed (1.5 Mbit/s) controller that works as a device or as an embedded host, with on-chip transceivers, built-in pull-ups, pull-downs and series resistors, Link Power Management (LPM-L1), and a 1 kHz SOF clock that can be brought out on a pin. As a device it has 8 endpoint addresses, each with an IN and an OUT endpoint (16 in all), each set to control, interrupt, bulk or isochronous; payloads up to 1023 bytes; no endpoint size limit; feedback endpoints; crystal-less operation. As a host it has 8 physical pipes with no size limit, virtual pipes multiplexed on one physical pipe so the tree is unlimited, and phase-locked SOFs.

Endpoint and pipe descriptors and data buffers live in system SRAM, placed wherever software likes and sized by how many endpoints are used. The controller's own AHB master moves the data during each transaction, using neither the CPU nor the DMAC. Ping-pong mode uses the IN and OUT banks of one address in one direction, so software handles one buffer while the controller uses the other. Multi-packet transfers send a payload larger than the endpoint size as several packets without software help. When the bus is idle and suspended the device can sleep in any mode, and bus resume wakes it from any mode.

Bus clock CLK_USB_AHB, gated in the power manager; generic clock GCLK_USB, which must be configured in GCLK first and is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some register writes are synchronized. GCLK_USB must be 48 MHz ± 0.25% for low and full speed, and CLK_USB_AHB at least 8 MHz to keep up with 12 Mbit/s. A digital PLL in the module recovers the bus clock within the USB jitter limits; crystal-less device operation uses the USB clock recovery module.

The USB runs in any sleep mode while its clock runs and its interrupts can wake the device. It has no events. It keeps running under a debugger halt. Writable registers can be PAC-protected except the device INTFLAG and EPINTFLAG and the host INTFLAG and PINTFLAG; protection is lifted while the CPU is halted in debug and never applies to debugger accesses.
The DP/DM driver strength is trimmed by production values that software must copy from the NVM software calibration area into PADCAL before enabling the USB, or the specified accuracy is not reached.

After a hardware reset the USB is idle: disabled, its clock stopped, device and host state reset. CTRLA.MODE (device 0, host 1) and CTRLB.SPDCONF are set before writing CTRLA.ENABLE=1, which enters the chosen mode; writing 0 disables it at any time, back to idle. CTRLA.SWRST resets every USB register and disables the module.

Writing CTRLB.DETACH=0 attaches the device and 1 detaches it. The host first reads the descriptor at address 0, resets the bus and assigns an address; software writes it to DADD.DADD and sets DADD.ADDEN to answer at it. ADDEN clears on every bus reset.

DESCADD holds the base address of the endpoint descriptor table. Before using an endpoint, set its direction and type in EPCFG.EPTYPE0/1 and initialize its descriptor so the controller does not fetch random RAM; set PCKSIZE.SIZE to the size reported to the host and ADDR to the data buffer. INTFLAG.RAMACER sets on a RAM access underflow during an IN data stage. Disabling an endpoint clears its EPINTENCLR/SET, EPINTFLAG and EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0/1.

A bus reset comes from the host and is handled by hardware. It clears EPCFG of every endpoint but 0, FNUM, DADD, EPINTENCLR/SET, EPINTFLAG, EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0/1, EPINTSMRY and CTRLB.UPRSM, and sets INTFLAG.EORST at its end.
On each SOF token the frame number goes to FNUM.FNUM and INTFLAG.SOF sets; a CRC or bit-stuff error in the token sets FNUM.FNCERR.

A SETUP token is dropped unless its address matches DADD.DADD, the endpoint is enabled and EPTYPE0 is control. The controller then fetches ADDR and waits for DATA0, giving up on any other PID. If EPINTFLAG.RXSTP is 0 the data is written to the buffer whatever EPSTATUS.BK0RDY says; bytes beyond PCKSIZE.SIZE are thrown away but the packet is still checked for CRC and bit-stuff errors, and an error sends the controller back to idle. Software must never report an endpoint size above PCKSIZE.SIZE. On success it sends ACK and writes the byte count (CRC excluded) to PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT. A packet of exactly SIZE bytes stores no CRC bytes, SIZE - 1 stores the first CRC byte, and SIZE - 2 or fewer stores both. EPSTATUS.DTGLOUT, DTGLIN, CURRBK and BK0RDY are set, BK1RDY and STALLRQ0/1 cleared, and RXSTP sets, interrupting if EPINTENSET.RXSTP is set.

An OUT token is dropped unless the address matches, the endpoint is enabled and EPTYPE0 is OUT. The controller fetches ADDR and waits for DATA0 or DATA1. With EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0 set the data is dropped and, except on isochronous endpoints, STALL is returned and EPINTFLAG.STALL0 sets. Isochronous endpoints accept both PIDs; others compare the PID with EPSTATUS.DTGLOUT and on a mismatch drop the data but still ACK. With EPSTATUS.BK0RDY already set the data is dropped, EPINTFLAG.TRFAIL0 and STATUS_BK.ERRORFLOW set, and a non-isochronous endpoint answers NAK. Otherwise the data is stored at ADDR, truncated at PCKSIZE.SIZE, and checked for CRC and bit-stuff errors. On an isochronous endpoint with an error the byte count is still written and TRFAIL0 and STATUS_BK.CRCERR set. On success the endpoint ACKs (unless isochronous), writes BYTE_COUNT, stores CRC bytes as for SETUP, sets BK0RDY, toggles DTGLOUT (unless isochronous) and sets EPINTFLAG.TRCPT0.

PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT counts the bytes received and must be zeroed before a new transfer; the total expected goes in PCKSIZE.MULTI_PACKET_SIZE and must be a whole multiple of PCKSIZE.SIZE, or excess data may overwrite other SRAM. Each full-size packet adds SIZE to BYTE_COUNT and toggles DTGLOUT (unless isochronous); when BYTE_COUNT reaches MULTI_PACKET_SIZE the bank ready bit and TRCPT flag are set.

An IN token is dropped unless the address matches, the endpoint is enabled and EPTYPE1 is IN. With EPSTATUS.STALLRQ1 set a non-isochronous endpoint answers STALL and EPINTFLAG.STALL1 sets. With EPSTATUS.BK1RDY clear EPINTFLAG.TRFAIL1 sets and a non-isochronous endpoint answers NAK. Otherwise the controller sends PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT bytes from ADDR plus CRC, as DATA0 on isochronous endpoints and by EPSTATUS.DTGLIN otherwise. Isochronous endpoints then clear BK1RDY and set TRCPT1 at once; others wait up to 16 bit times for an ACK and, if it comes, clear BK1RDY, set TRCPT1 and toggle DTGLIN, or else return to idle.

PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT holds the total to send and PCKSIZE.MULTI_PACKET_SIZE counts what has been sent, zeroed before each transfer. Each IN token sends SIZE bytes, or the remainder if less than SIZE is left; a total that is a multiple of SIZE ends with a zero-length packet when AUTOZLP is set. A full packet adds SIZE to MULTI_PACKET_SIZE and toggles DTGLIN (unless isochronous); the short last packet adds its length, clears the bank ready bit and sets TRCPT.

One direction is enabled in EPCFG.EPTYPE0/1 and the other set to Dual Bank. The enabled endpoint's buffer, address and byte count serve as bank 0, the disabled one's as bank 1. EPSTATUS.CURBK shows the bank for the next transaction and updates after each; the TRCPT/TRFAIL flags and BK0RDY/BK1RDY follow it, and DTGLOUT/DTGLIN update for the enabled direction only.

A feedback endpoint shares its number with the first (lower) of the data endpoints it serves and runs the opposite direction, as in explicit feedback for USB audio. It is made by giving the IN and OUT halves of one address different PCKSIZE.SIZE and EPTYPE values, for example Interrupt IN with SIZE 64 and Isochronous OUT with SIZE 512.

operation.topic: USB device suspend and pad states
operation.text: The pad is in a low-power Idle state when the USB is disabled, CTRLB.DETACH is 1 or a suspend has been detected, and Active when CTRLA.ENABLE is 1, DETACH is 0 and no suspend is flagged. A suspend on the bus sets INTFLAG.SUSPEND and idles the pad; any non-idle bus state sets INTFLAG.WAKEUP and wakes the pad.

Upstream resume is the only signalling a device starts itself, and it needs a prior DEVICE_REMOTE_WAKEUP request from the host and INTFLAG.SUSPEND set. Writing CTRLB.UPRSM sends it; the controller sends it automatically after 5 ms of bus inactivity; INTFLAG.WAKEUP then sets, SUSPEND clears, and UPRSM clears when the resume has been sent. After a host-driven resume INTFLAG.EORSM sets. Setting UPRSM while a host resume is already under way is ignored and the bit clears.

CTRLB.LPMHDSK selects the handshake to an LPM transaction. When one arrives on an enabled endpoint, normally endpoint 0, the EXTREG field of that endpoint's bank 0 descriptor receives BESL, bRemoteWake and bLinkState. An ACK sets INTFLAG.LPMSUSP and the transceiver suspends 9 µs later; stopping the USB clock then saves more, and the MCU may sleep in any mode whose wake-up latency meets the host's BESL. Leaving L1 works like ordinary suspend except that a device-started wakeup is shorter. A NYET answer sets INTFLAG.LPMNYET (interrupting if enabled); STALL or no handshake sets nothing and the transaction is ignored.

Per endpoint, EPINTFLAGn holds STALL0/STALL1, TRFAIL0, TRFAIL1, RXSTP, TRCPT0 and TRCPT1, each gated by EPINTENSETn; EPINTSMRY shows which endpoints have one pending. Device-level flags in INTFLAG are LPMSUSP, LPMNYET, RAMACER, UPRSM, EORSM, WAKEUP, EORST, SOF and SUSPEND, each gated by INTENSET. Endpoint and device sources combine into one USB interrupt. WAKEUP is asynchronous and wakes the device from any sleep mode.

Software sets CTRLB.VBUSOK once VBUS is present; while it is 0 host operation is halted even if configured and enabled. Device connection is seen as DP or DM pulled high (by speed) and disconnection as both pulled low, read through STATUS.LINESTATE; INTFLAG.DCONN and INTFLAG.DDISC flag them. In host mode an endpoint is called a pipe.

Writing CTRLB.BUSRESET sends a bus reset; INTFLAG.RST then sets and all pipes are disabled. If the bus was suspended (CTRLB.SOFE 0) it is first resumed, setting INTFLAG.WAKEUP, and SOFE is set so SOFs follow the reset at once. The reset clears every PCFG, FNUM, BINTERVAL, HSOFC, PINTENCLR/SET, PINTFLAG and PSTATUS.FREEZE. STATUS.SPEED then gives the negotiated speed.

operation.topic: USB host pipe configuration and activation
operation.text: DESCADD holds the base of the pipe descriptor table. Set each pipe's type and direction in PCFG.PTYPE, initialize its descriptor, set PCKSIZE.SIZE to the device endpoint size and ADDR to its buffer; PCFG.BK=1 gives two banks, which control pipes cannot use. INTFLAG.RAMACER sets on a RAM underflow in an OUT stage. A pipe is enabled by a non-zero PCFG.PTYPE, which also sets PSTATUS.FREEZE so it can be finished before any transfer; disabling it resets its registers and clears BINTERVAL, PINTENCLR/SET, PINTFLAG and FREEZE. During enumeration the default control pipe is resized to the device's bMaxPacketSize0. After SET_ADDRESS completes, the new address goes in CTRL_PIPE.PDADDR of the pipe descriptor.

Clearing CTRLB.SOFE stops SOFs and suspends the bus; the device suspends 3 ms later. Freeze active pipes first and wait at least one full frame to avoid losing data. A non-idle bus state sets INTFLAG.WAKEUP; an upstream resume (K state) also sets INTFLAG.UPRSM, and the host must answer with a downstream resume, started by writing CTRLB.RESUME, within 1 ms and lasting at least 20 ms. The host can also resume on its own by CTRLB.RESUME. When the downstream resume ends SOFE sets again and the bus is active.

For synchronous endpoints the SOF period is kept through active, idle, suspend and resume states (not through disconnect, connect or reset): 1 ms while active and a whole number of milliseconds otherwise. GCLK_USB must keep running or the SOF period becomes erratic.

operation.topic: USB host control, IN and OUT pipes
operation.text: A control transfer has SETUP, data and status stages, and software changes PCFG.PTOKEN for each; the initial toggles are DATA0 for SETUP and DATA1 for IN and OUT. IN pipe: clearing PSTATUS.BK0/1RDY offers the bank, and IN requests run while the pipe is unfrozen (PSTATUS.PFREEZE 0). A full bank sets PINTFLAG.TRCPT0/1 and BK0/1RDY; software clears TRCPT by writing 1, reads PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT bytes from ADDR and clears BKnRDY to free the bank. With two banks each good transaction moves to the next; PSTATUS.CURBK and DTGLIN show progress. A single-bank pipe uses only TRCPT0 and BK0. OUT pipe: software writes data at ADDR and sets PSTATUS.BK0/1RDY to send it (switching bank in dual-bank mode), clearing PINTFLAG.TRCPT0/1 beforehand so no completion is missed.

Several logical pipes can run in turn on one physical pipe, reaching any endpoint of any attached device; software saves the pipe registers and descriptor before switching and restores them, PCFG and PSTATUS in particular, afterwards.

Data flow error, isochronous and interrupt pipes only: PINTFLAG.TRFAIL sets (interrupting if enabled); PINTSMRY names the pipe and STATUS_BK.ERRORFLOW the bank. On an OUT pipe it is an underflow (sending from an empty bank); on an IN pipe an overflow (a packet arriving while the bank is full, so its data is lost). The next good transaction clears ERRORFLOW. CRC error, isochronous IN pipes only: TRFAIL sets and STATUS_BK.CRCERR marks the bank; the corrupted packet stays in the bank and TRCPT0/1 sets. PERR, all pipes: set when an error field in the descriptor's STATUS_PIPE is set and STATUS_PIPE.ERCNT exceeds CTRL_PIPE.PERMAX; below that limit ERCNT just counts up.

Any enabled pipe with PCFG.PTYPE set to EXTENDED sends an EXTENDED token then an LPM token, using EXTREG.VARIABLE from the descriptor; PTOKEN, BK and SIZE do not matter. ACK: the host enters L1 sleep at once, sets PINTFLAG.TRCPT0 and clears CTRLB.SOFE; L1 lasts at least TL1RetryAndResidency of the USB 2.0 LPM addendum. NYET sets TRFAIL; STALL sets STALL. No or corrupt handshake: the token pair is retried up to CTRL_PIPE.PERMAX times, then PERR sets and STATUS_BK is updated. Each outcome freezes the pipe (PSTATUS.PFREEZE) until software unfreezes it. L1 is left by CTRLB.RESUME (downstream resume) or CTRLB.L1RESUME, whose K state lasts the BESL time in EXTREG.VARIABLE; a device upstream resume sets INTFLAG.UPRSM and the host then does an L1 resume. On leaving L1 SOFE is set again.

Per pipe, PINTFLAGn holds STALL, PERR, TRFAIL, TXSTP, TRCPT0 and TRCPT1, each gated by PINTENSET; PINTSMRY shows which pipes have one pending. Host-level flags in INTFLAG are DDISC, DCONN, RAMACER, UPRSM, DNRSM, WAKEUP, RST and HSOF, each gated by INTENSET. All combine into one USB interrupt. DDISC, DCONN and WAKEUP are asynchronous, and WAKEUP wakes the device from any sleep mode.

The configurable custom logic replaces simple glue gates on the board. It has 4 lookup tables (LUTs), each with three inputs that can be masked one by one, an 8-entry truth table, and an optional synchronizer, filter and edge detector on its output. The inputs can come from pins, events, peripherals (AC, TC, TCC, SERCOM) or another LUT; the outputs go to pins or to the event system. Each LUT gives any 3-input function (AND, NAND, OR, NOR, XOR, XNOR, NOT and so on). Each adjacent pair (LUT0/LUT1, LUT2/LUT3) can drive a sequential element: a gated DFF, a JK flip-flop, a gated D-latch or an RS latch.

Bus clock CLK_CCL_APB, gated in the power manager. The generic clock GCLK_CCL, asynchronous to the bus clock, is needed whenever a LUT uses event inputs, filtering, edge detection or sequential logic. The CCL runs in any sleep mode while its clock runs, has no interrupts or DMA, and its events can act through EVSYS without waking the device. It keeps running under a debugger halt. All writable registers can be PAC-protected, except against debugger accesses.

SEQCTRLx.SEQSEL can be written only while the pair's even LUT is disabled, and LUTCTRLx (except ENABLE) only while that LUT is disabled; protected LUTCTRLx bits may be written together with ENABLE=1 but not with ENABLE=0. CTRL.ENABLE turns the CCL on and off, LUTCTRLx.ENABLE each LUT, and CTRL.SWRST resets every register and disables the CCL.
Each LUT outputs the TRUTH bit indexed by its three inputs IN[2:0], taken as a binary number with IN[2] most significant; TRUTH sits in LUTCTRLx.TRUTH.

LUTCTRLx.INSELy chooses the source of input y of LUT x. MASK ties it to 0. FEEDBACK takes the output of the pair's sequential element. LINK takes the output of the next LUT (LUT2 feeds LUT1, and so on). EVENT takes the LUT's one asynchronous event line, which can serve any of its inputs; the event system must be set up first. IO takes the LUT's pin. AC takes a comparator output: comparator 0 on even LUTs (LUT0, LUT2) and comparator 1 on odd LUTs (LUT1, LUT3); the AC must be set up first. TC takes waveform output WO[0] of TC N or, as the alternative, of TC N+1 (TC0 and TC1 for LUT0, TC1 and TC2 for LUT1, and so on). TCC takes WO0, WO1 and WO2 on IN0, IN1 and IN2. SERCOM takes the transmitter output (TxD for USART, MOSI for SPI) of SERCOM N, which must be driven out on SERCOMn PAD[0].

An incoming event passes through an edge detector that makes a one-GCLK_CCL-cycle strobe on a rising edge. Set it up by enabling GCLK_CCL, routing the event asynchronously in EVSYS, selecting EVENT in LUTCTRLx.INSEL, setting LUTCTRLx.INVEI if the falling edge should strobe instead, and then setting LUTCTRLx.LUTEI.

A LUT's output is combinatorial by default and can glitch when inputs change. LUTCTRLx.FILTSEL adds a synchronizer or a digital filter clocked by GCLK_CCL, which delays OUT by two to five GCLK cycles and also filters event inputs. The filter is cleared one APB clock after its LUT is disabled.

LUTCTRLx.EDGESEL=1 turns the output into a pulse on each rising edge; for falling edges invert the truth table. A valid filter setting must be on with it, or behaviour is unpredictable. Its logic clears one APB cycle after its LUT is disabled.

SEQCTRLx.SEQSEL places one of four elements after each LUT pair (DFF, JK, DLATCH or RS); GCLK_CCL must run and, as wanted, the LUT filters or edge detectors be on. The even LUT (LUT2x) drives D, J or S and the odd LUT (LUT2x+1) drives G, K or R. Disabling the even LUT clears the element: the flip-flops are cleared asynchronously with reset held one APB cycle; the D latch holds G on and D at 0 for one more APB cycle; the RS latch holds R on and S at 0 for one more APB cycle. Otherwise the flip-flops update on rising GCLK_CCL edges.

Output event LUTOUTx, the LUT output, enabled by LUTCTRLx.LUTEO; input event INx feeds the truth table, enabled by LUTCTRLx.LUTEI. With CTRL.RUNSTDBY=1 GCLK_CCL stays on in every sleep mode. With RUNSTDBY=0 it stops in standby, and a LUT using its filter, edge detector or sequential element outputs 0 there; otherwise the truth table keeps working and its output follows the inputs.

The OPAMP controller runs three low-power general-purpose op amps with rail-to-rail inputs. Each can be used alone with external feedback on its pins, or with internal resistor ladders as a unity-gain buffer, inverting or non-inverting programmable gain amplifier (PGA), cascaded PGAs, instrumentation amplifier, transimpedance amplifier, or comparator with programmable hysteresis, with no external parts. Inputs can be pins, the DAC, ground, the ladder or another op amp's output; the output can go to a pin or to the ADC or AC. The DAC can give the reference for an inverting PGA or the instrumentation amplifier. Four bias settings trade speed against current. Options for low power: a voltage doubler that can be turned off, and starting only when the ADC or AC asks for it. With the ADC, the op amp offset and gain can be measured and corrected.

Bus clock CLK_OPAMP_APB, gated in the power manager. The voltage doubler needs CLK_ULP32K, the 32 kHz output of OSCULP32K in OSC32KCTRL, when VCC is below 2.5 V. Behaviour in idle and standby follows OPAMPCTRLx.RUNSTDBY, OPAMPCTRLx.ONDEMAND and CTRLA.ENABLE. No DMA, interrupts or events. It keeps running under a debugger halt. All writable registers can be PAC-protected, except against debugger accesses. Each op amp has two pins usable as analog inputs and one as analog output, all set to analog first; a DAC used as input must be configured and enabled first. The AC and ADC can switch an op amp on through the analog on-demand request.

Each op amp works standalone or with built-in feedback, chosen in OPAMPCTRLx. After it is enabled there is a start-up delay, measured internally so it tracks temperature and supply, before the output is valid; STATUS.READYx then sets. Below 2.5 V the start-up also waits for the voltage doubler; if the supply always stays above 2.5 V, CTRLA.LPMUX turns the doubler off. Configure an op amp fully before enabling it, and set up its clock in OSC32KCTRL first. CTRLA.ENABLE turns the controller on and off, OPAMPCTRLx.ENABLE each op amp, and CTRLA.SWRST resets all registers and disables it. No registers need synchronization.

Before starting an op amp, set in OPAMPCTRLx: MUXPOS (positive input), MUXNEG (negative input), RES1EN when the resistor ladder is used, RES1MUX (ladder input), POTMUX (ladder tap), RES2VCC (VCC on the ladder), RES2OUT (output to the ladder) and BIAS (speed against current). In standalone mode both inputs and the output are pins and feedback is external; op amps can be cascaded.

R1 and R2 are the two parts of the internal ladder on either side of the POTMUX tap. Voltage follower: the negative input takes the unity-gain path from the output. Inverting PGA example: R1 = 4R, R2 = 12R gives Vout = -3 × Vin. Non-inverting PGA example: R1 = 4R, R2 = 12R gives Vout = 4 × Vin. The three op amps can be cascaded as three inverting or three non-inverting PGAs (each with R1 = 4R, R2 = 12R in the examples), OPAMP0/OPAMP1 or OPAMP1/OPAMP2 can form a differential amplifier, and OPAMP0 and OPAMP1 as followers feed OPAMP2 in the instrumentation amplifier, whose reference is the DAC or GND chosen by OPAMPCTRL0.RES1MUX.
Any op amp can convert a current to a voltage: the positive input goes to ground and the negative input to the output through the resistor ladder.

Any op amp can act as an inverting or non-inverting comparator whose hysteresis keeps noise near the threshold from making the output chatter. The positive input always goes to the resistor ladder. Inverting: the signal goes to the negative input and RES1MUX to ground (the reference). Non-inverting: the signal goes to RES1MUX and the negative input to ground.

operation.topic: OPAMP as ADC and AC driver
operation.text: Any op amp can buffer or amplify a signal for the ADC or AC, alone or cascaded for more gain: set OPAMPCTRLx.ANAOUT=1 and select the op amp in the ADC or AC input multiplexer. The DAC can serve as reference through OPAMPCTRLx.MUXPOS and RES1MUX.

operation.topic: OPAMP offset and gain compensation with the ADC
operation.text: Configure the op amp as a voltage follower, route it to the ADC (ANAOUT=1 and the ADC input mux), then find offset before gain. Offset: with the positive input at ground, the ADC result is the value for OFFSETCORR. Gain: with the positive input close to but below VDD (0.8 × Vref, for example) so the ADC does not saturate, the expected result divided by the measured one is the value for GAINCORR.

The voltage doubler supplies only the analog multiplexer switches, so they work with the supply below 2.5 V; it switches on and off by itself with the supply level. With the supply sure to stay above 2.5 V, CTRLA.LPMUX disables it, which saves power and shortens start-up, since enabling op amps otherwise waits for the doubler to settle. OPAMPCTRLx.BIAS sets each amplifier's bias current, trading propagation delay against current, and changes start-up time too.

Two converters, ADC0 and ADC1, of 8, 10 or 12 bits, up to 1 MSPS, with single-ended or differential inputs and signed or unsigned results, left or right adjusted. Each ADC reaches as many as 20 analog inputs, 20 distinct channels overall, 28 positive and 10 negative selections counting internal ones. Internal inputs: temperature sensor, bandgap, the core, I/O and VBAT supplies each scaled down, DAC. Single, free-running and sequenced conversion; window monitor on a chosen channel; reference from 1.0 V to VDDANA, internal or external; one event input to start conversions; DMA of results or settings; hardware offset and gain correction; averaging and oversampling up to a 16-bit result; selectable sampling time.

Bus clock CLK_APB_ADCx, enabled in MCLK; generic clock GCLK_ADC, configured in GCLK before use and asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes are synchronized. The ADC runs in any sleep mode while its clock runs; RESRDY and WINMON can wake the device and its events can act without waking it. One DMA request line, one interrupt line, events to EVSYS. It halts under a debugger halt unless DBGCTRL keeps it running. Every writable register but INTFLAG can be PAC-protected, except against debugger accesses. AINx pins and VREFA/B are analog inputs; the AC and ADC can switch an op amp on through the analog on-demand request.
The BIAS and LINEARITY values from production must be copied by software from the NVM software calibration area into CALIB to reach the specified accuracy.

Results default to 12 bits; 8 or 10 bits shorten the conversion, and oversampling with decimation extends to 16 bits. CTRLB, REFCTRL, EVCTRL and CALIB can be written only while the ADC is disabled. CTRLA.ENABLE turns it on and off; CTRLA.SWRST resets all registers but DBGCTRL and disables it. INPUTCTRL picks the input. A conversion starts on SWTRIG.START=1 or a trigger event; in free-running mode only the first needs starting. Each result overwrites RESULT; with more than one channel in use it must be read as soon as INTFLAG.RESRDY sets, or INTFLAG.OVERRUN flags the lost result.

GCLK_ADC passes through a prescaler set by CTRLB.PRESCALER, dividing by 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 or 256 to give CLK_ADC; the smallest division is 2. REFCTRL.REFSEL selects the reference VREF; INTREF is the default, and external or other internal references can be chosen.

CTRLC.RESSEL selects 8, 10 or 12 bits (default 12), which changes the conversion time. Single-ended conversion gives the full 12 bits when the positive input stays positive; when it may go below the negative input, use differential mode (CTRLC.DIFFMODE). Either works single-shot or free-running, and in free-running each conversion sets INTFLAG.RESRDY.

A conversion begins once the software or event start is synchronized to GCLK_ADC; the input is sampled during the opening half-period of CLK_ADC, then one bit is resolved per CLK_ADC cycle from MSB to LSB. SAMPCTRL.SAMPLEN lengthens sampling (for example to six cycles). SAMPCTRL.OFFCOMP adds an offset compensation phase before sampling, and then the sampling time must be one CLK_ADC cycle. Example: 1 MSPS at 12 bits with four sampling cycles needs CLK_ADC = 1 MSPS × (4 + 12) = 16 MHz, so GCLK_ADC = 32 MHz with the minimum prescaler of 2.

AVGCTRL.SAMPLENUM sets how many consecutive results are summed. Beyond 16 samples the sum would overflow the 16-bit RESULT, so it is shifted right automatically. CTRLC.RESSEL must be set to accumulate two or more samples.

Averaging sums m samples and divides by m, improving accuracy in noisy conditions at the cost of sample rate; the division combines the automatic shift with a further shift set in AVGCTRL.ADJRES. CTRLC.RESSEL must be set. INTFLAG.RESRDY sets when the average is ready.

Resolution rises from 12 bits up to 16 bits, at a lower effective rate, by summing 4^n samples and shifting the sum right by n bits for n extra bits; the shift is the automatic shift plus AVGCTRL.ADJRES.

One start request can run a series of conversions over any of the 32 positive inputs marked in SEQCTRL, in rising MUXPOS order (AIN0, AIN1, AIN2 and on); in differential mode the MUXNEG input serves the whole sequence. SEQSTATUS.SEQBUSY is set while the sequence runs. After each conversion SEQSTATUS.SEQSTATE holds the input just converted, RESULT is written and INTFLAG.RESRDY sets, and the next input starts by itself. With no SEQCTRL bit set the ADC converts the MUXPOS input.

CTRLC.WINMODE compares each RESULT with WINLT (lower) and WINUT (upper) and sets INTFLAG.WINMON on a match. The thresholds are signed in differential mode and unsigned otherwise, and only as many bits as CTRLC.RESSEL gives are compared (in 8-bit mode the lower eight; in differential 8-bit mode the eighth bit is the sign even when the ninth is zero).

Offset error is how far the transfer function sits from the ideal line at zero input; gain error is how far the midpoint of the last output step sits from the ideal line once offset is removed. OFFSETCORR is subtracted from the conversion before it reaches RESULT, and GAINCORR scales it, when CTRLC.CORREN is set. Correction adds 13 CLK_ADC cycles of latency: on the first conversion only in free-running mode, on every conversion in single mode.

INPUTCTRL, CTRLC, AVGCTRL, SAMPCTRL, WINLT, WINUT, GAINCORR and OFFSETCORR are double buffered: a write is held in a buffer, with its SYNCBUSY bit set, so the running conversion is not disturbed, and passes to the ADC when the next RESULT is ready.

The temperature sensor sits in SUPC. To use it: set clocks per the electrical characteristics; set SUPC.VREF.TSEN and select the INTREF voltage in SUPC.VREF.SEL as the electrical characteristics require; select INTREF in ADC.REFCTRL.REFSEL; select TEMP on MUXPOS and GND on MUXNEG in ADC.INPUTCTRL; set the rest per the electrical characteristics; enable and convert, giving ADCm. The sensor is linear but depends on INTREF, which itself drifts with temperature, so each device carries a Temperature Log row measured in production at a room and a hot temperature: ROOM_TEMP_VAL_INT/DEC and HOT_TEMP_VAL_INT/DEC (tempR, tempH in °C, integer and decimal parts, e.g. 0x19 and 2 mean 25.2 °C), ROOM_ADC_VAL and HOT_ADC_VAL (12-bit readings ADCR, ADCH), and ROOM_INT1V_VAL and HOT_INT1V_VAL (INT1VR, INT1VH, the true 1 V reference in two's complement around 1 V in 0.001 V steps: 0 to 127 is 1 V down to 0.873 V, -1 to -127 is 1.001 V to 1.127 V). A coarse temperature uses INT1Vc = 1 V; interpolating the reference at that temperature and recomputing gives the fine value.

DMA request RESRDY: set when a result (or, with averaging, the finished average) is ready, cleared by reading RESULT. Interrupts RESRDY, WINMON and OVERRUN, flags in INTFLAG, enabled through INTENSET and disabled through INTENCLR, one combined NVIC line; RESRDY and WINMON are asynchronous wake-up sources. Output events RESRDY and WINMON, enabled by EVCTRL.xxEO. Input events START (start a conversion) and FLUSH (abandon it), enabled by EVCTRL.xxEI; FLUSH wins when both arrive together and any connected event triggers an enabled action. Events must use asynchronous EVSYS paths; the ADC reacts to rising edges, or to falling edges with EVCTRL.xINV=1.
Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, INPUTCTRL, CTRLC, AVGCTRL, SAMPCTRL, WINLT, WINUT, GAINCORR, OFFSETCORR and SWTRIG.

One pair of analog comparators, COMP0 and COMP1, identical but separately controlled; the pair can form a window comparator. Each compares two inputs and gives a digital output, with selectable propagation delay against current, hysteresis off or one of four levels, an optional digital filter, and an output that can go to a pin raw or synchronized. Inputs: four shared pins for either input, ground, the bandgap, a 64-level VDD scaler per comparator, the DAC and OPAMP2. Interrupts on rising edge, falling edge, toggle or end of comparison, and in window mode on above, inside, below or outside; events from each comparator output and the window state.

Bus clock CLK_AC_APB, gated in the power manager; generic clock GCLK_AC, configured in GCLK before use and asynchronous to the bus clock. The AC runs in any sleep mode while its clock runs; its interrupts can wake the device and its events act without waking it. No DMA. Under a debugger halt it stops after the comparison in progress unless DBGCTRL keeps it running. All writable registers but CTRLB and INTFLAG can be PAC-protected, except against debugger accesses. The four input pins are shared by the pair and must be set to analog; the bandgap, OPAMP2 or DAC must be configured and enabled before a comparator uses them.

The output is 1 when the positive input is above the negative one and 0 otherwise. The positive input is a pin; the negative input is a pin or an internal source. EVCTRL can be written only while the AC is disabled. CTRLA.ENABLE turns the AC on and off and CTRLA.SWRST resets it. Each comparator is set up in COMPCTRLx while disabled: SINGLE (measurement mode), HYSTEN and HYST, SPEED, INTSEL, MUXPOS and MUXNEG, FLEN and RUNSTDBY; then COMPCTRLx.ENABLE starts it. Clearing CTRLA.ENABLE stops all comparators without clearing their ENABLE bits.

After enabling, an automatically measured start-up time passes before the first result, and the output is not valid during it; the write takes effect 2-3 GCLK_AC cycles after it is made. Continuous (SINGLE=0): the comparator compares without pause, STATUSA.STATEx always holds the latest result, STATUSB.READYx sets after start-up, and edges are found by comparing successive samples at the GCLK_AC rate. In sleep, a continuous comparator can run without a clock: a toggle makes the power manager start GCLK_AC just long enough to register it unless it wakes the system. Single-shot (SINGLE=1): writing CTRLB.STARTx, or an input event with EVCTRL.COMPEIx=1, clears READYx, starts the comparator, and after start-up makes one comparison, updates STATUSA, raises events and interrupts, and sets READYx. Events follow the output state whether or not the interrupt is enabled.

COMPCTRLx.MUXPOS and COMPCTRLx.MUXNEG pick the inputs, and may be changed only with the comparator disabled. A pin used as input must have its digital input and output disabled in PORT. The multiplexers switch so as to keep crosstalk between channels low. For the CCL to use the comparison result internally the field must be 0x1 or 0x2.

WINCTRL.WEN0 pairs the comparators; both must use the same SINGLE setting and RUNSTDBY setting, and the same pin as positive input, with their negative inputs as the upper and lower limits (either way round). STATUS.WSTATE0 shows below, inside or above. WINCTRL.WINTSEL picks an interrupt on going above, inside, below or outside; events follow the inside/outside state. The single comparators keep their own outputs, interrupts and events. In single-shot window mode both compare together on either START bit or either event.
Each comparator has its own 64-level divider of the supply, on when COMPCTRLx.MUXNEG is 0x5 or MUXPOS is 0x4 and the comparator is enabled; SCALERx.VALUE sets the level.

COMPCTRLx.HYSTEN enables hysteresis and COMPCTRLx.HYST sets its level; it works only in continuous mode. COMPCTRLx.SPEED sets the bias current, trading propagation delay against current and changing the start-up time. COMPCTRLx.FLEN selects no filter or a 3-sample or 5-sample majority filter clocked at the GCLK_AC rate: an output change is accepted once N/2+1 of the last N samples agree, adding N-1 sample cycles of delay. In continuous mode the first valid output comes after N samples and then one every cycle; in single-shot the comparison ends on the Nth sample. In sleep, filtering works only for single-shot measurements; it must be off for continuous measurement in sleep or interrupts and events may be false.

COMPCTRLx.OUT sends the comparator to its CMP[x] pin, either raw and unsynchronized or synchronized to CLK_AC and filtered. COMPCTRLx.SWAP exchanges the two inputs and inverts the output, so the input offset can be measured or cancelled; it can be changed only with the comparator disabled.

Interrupt sources COMP0 and COMP1 (per COMPCTRLx.INTSEL) and WIN0 (per WINCTRL.WINTSEL0), flags in INTFLAG, enabled through INTENSET and disabled through INTENCLR, one combined NVIC line. Output events COMP0 and COMP1 (copy of the comparator state) and WIN0 (copy of the inside/outside state), enabled by EVCTRL.xxEO. Input events START0 and START1 start a comparison after the start-up time, enabled by EVCTRL.COMPEIx; in window mode either starts both comparators.

COMPCTRLx.RUNSTDBY=0 disables that comparator in standby, keeping its settings and powering its analog parts down, so it needs start-up time on return; RUNSTDBY=1 keeps it running and any enabled AC interrupt can wake the CPU. The AC also works with its clock stopped as long as it is powered (not in shutdown). Continuous mode in sleep: the comparator stays on and is watched asynchronously; a matching edge starts GCLK_AC to record the interrupt and make events, and wakes the device if the interrupt is enabled; no filtering. Single-shot in sleep: an event starts GCLK_AC and the comparator, one comparison (filtered if wanted) is made with its events and interrupts, and both turn off again unless set to wake the system.
Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, COMPCTRLn.ENABLE and WINCTRL.

Two 12-bit DACs, each up to 1 MSPS, used separately or together as one differential DAC; 16-bit resolution through hardware dithering; several trigger sources; high drive; DMA. DAC0's output can feed other peripherals internally. References: INTREF (default), VDDANA or the VREFA pin.

Bus clock CLK_DAC_APB, gated in MCLK; generic clock GCLK_DAC, configured in GCLK before use and asynchronous to the bus clock. The DAC runs in any sleep mode while its clock runs; its interrupts can wake the device and its events act without waking it. One DMA request line and one interrupt line. Under a debugger halt it stops after finishing the conversion in progress, unless set to keep running. All writable registers but INTFLAG and the DATABUFx registers can be PAC-protected, except against debugger accesses. VOUT0, VOUT1 and VREFA must be set up first, and an internal input enabled before the DAC.

CTRLB, EVCTRL, DACCTRL0 and DACCTRL1 can be written only while the controller is disabled. CTRLA.ENABLE turns it on and off and CTRLA.SWRST resets all registers and disables it. In DACCTRLx: ENABLE turns that DAC on; LEFTADJ=1 left-aligns the data in bits 31:20, 0 right-aligns it in bits 11:0; RUNSTDBY=1 keeps it converting in standby, 0 halts it; DITHER selects dithering; REFRESH above 1 selects automatic refresh; CCTRL[1:0] sets the output buffer current to suit the data rate. After enabling, each DAC needs a start-up time; STATUS.READYx=1 shows it is ready, and conversions started before that are ignored. VOUTx is tri-stated while its DAC is disabled.

Each DAC turns DATAx into a voltage between GND and VREF, chosen by CTRLB.REFSEL. A conversion starts whenever DATAx is loaded, by a CPU write, by DMA, or from DATABUFx on a STARTx event, independently for each DAC even on a shared GCLK. STATUS.EOCx=1 marks VOUTx settled. The conversion is pipelined, so a new one can start 12 GCLK_DAC periods after the last; a write during a conversion waits until the DAC can take it. DAC0's output is available to the AC, ADC and OPAMP while DAC0 is enabled, and its pin is then reserved for that and cannot take another function. CCTRL lowers buffer current for lower conversion rates.

A DAC holds its output within one LSB for only about 100 µs, so a static level or a rate below 20 kSPS needs periodic refresh. DACCTRLx.REFRESH lets OSCULP32K restart the conversion of DATAx after each period, its accuracy set by that oscillator's tolerance; REFRESH=0 turns refresh off and 1 is reserved. Refresh keeps going in standby if RUNSTDBY=1. A write to DATAx during a refresh waits for the next slot.

CTRLB.DIFF=1 makes DAC0 and DAC1 convert DATA0 together, as a two's-complement value with bit 11 as sign (range -2047 to 2047). VOUT0 is the positive and VOUT1 the negative output, balanced around VREF/2; DACCTRL0 configures both, and DACCTRL1 need not be written.

DATAx is then a signed 16-bit value: bits 15:4 are the 12-bit code and bits 3:0 the dither. Each value is converted as 16 sub-conversions of either DATAx[15:4] or DATAx[15:4] + 1, whose average gives the 16-bit result. The STARTx event must fire 16 times per value and DATABUFx be reloaded every 16 conversions; the EMPTYx event and DMA request come every 16 transfers, while STATUS.EOCx still marks each sub-conversion.
The DAC reference must stay below VDDANA. 1 MSPS is reached only with VDDANA above 2.4 V. GCLK_DAC must be 12 MHz or less, which corresponds to 1 MSPS.

Single mode DMA requests: EMPTY0 and EMPTY1, set when DATABUFx or DATAx moves into the DAC's internal buffer and cleared by writing DATA or DATABUF or by writing 1 to INTFLAG.EMPTYx. In differential mode only EMPTY0, for the transfer into DAC1's buffer. If the CPU touches the registers that set or clear a request, the request can be lost or the transfer corrupted. Interrupts EMPTY0, EMPTY1 (internal buffer empty), UNDERRUN0 and UNDERRUN1 (buffer empty when a start event arrives), all asynchronous wake-up sources, with INTFLAG, INTENSET and INTENCLR and one combined NVIC line. Output events EMPTY0 and EMPTY1, enabled by EVCTRL.EMPTYEOx. Input events START0 and START1 move DATABUFx into DATAx as soon as the DAC can convert and start it, resynchronized to GCLK_DAC; enabled by EVCTRL.STARTEIx, rising edge by default or falling with EVCTRL.INVEIx. With a start event in use, write only DATABUFx. An event before start-up ends loads DATAx but starts nothing. Any connected event triggers the enabled action.

With DACCTRLx.RUNSTDBY=1 a DAC keeps converting in standby, and a STARTx event in sleep makes it request GCLK_DAC to finish the conversion (SleepWalking); with RUNSTDBY=0 it stops and is disabled in standby and needs its start-up time on waking. Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, DATA0, DATA1, DATABUF0 and DATABUF1. PCHCTRLm.CHEN must be read back after a change to be sure synchronization has finished.

The peripheral touch controller measures capacitive sensors on the board through the pins: self-capacitance with one Y pin per sensor, or mutual-capacitance matrices (including ITO grids) with one pin per X line and one per Y line. Which pins can be X or Y depends on package and configuration. Buttons, sliders, wheels and proximity; as low as 8 µA at a 200 ms scan rate; wake-up on touch from standby; self and mutual sensors mixed. Button counts: 6/10/16 self-capacitance and 60/120/256 mutual-capacitance for 32/48/64-pin packages; further stated counts are 2/6 self-capacitance and 12/48 mutual-capacitance buttons for 32/48 pins, 144 mutual-capacitance buttons and 24 self-capacitance buttons. One pin per electrode with no external parts, load-compensating charge sensing with parasitic capacitance compensation and adjustable gain, zero drift over temperature and VDD with automatic calibration, single-shot and free-running measurement, hardware noise filtering and de-synchronization, driven shield, selectable channel settling delay, start by command or auto-trigger, and an acquisition-complete interrupt (about 5% CPU scanning 10 channels every 50 ms). Conversion uses the ADC.

A mutual-capacitance sensor is the capacitance between an X electrode that transmits and a Y electrode that senses; a self-capacitance sensor is one Y electrode whose own capacitance is measured. No external parts are needed, but a series resistor of 1 kΩ or more on X and Y lines improves EMC.

Clocked by GCLK_PTC, asynchronous to the system and bus clocks, from a source chosen in GCLK and enabled in the power manager first (off by default); 400 kHz to 4 MHz. The ADC must be enabled and set up for the PTC to work. The PTC is driven through the QTouch Library, configured with QTouch Composer and linked into the application.
Typical figures are at 25 °C unless stated otherwise; minimum and maximum figures hold over the whole operating temperature and supply range unless stated otherwise.

Measured with VDDIN 3.3 V or 1.8 V; at 1.8 V the CPU runs from Flash with 3 wait states, at 3.3 V with 1 wait state in PL0 and 2 in PL2; low-power cache on; BOD33 off; XOSC stopped; XOSC32K running on an external 32 kHz crystal; in PL2 the DFLL48M runs at 48 MHz referenced to XOSC32K and is the main clock; in PL0 OSC16M runs at 4, 8 or 12 MHz; all AHB and APB clocks on, CPUDIV = 1, BUPDIV = 8, LPDIV = 1; I/Os with digital functionality disabled.

Wake-up times are measured at VDDIN 3.3 V, LDO regulation, CPU on OSC16M at 12 MHz with 1 wait state, cache on, Flash fast wake-up on (NVMCTRL.CTRLB.FWUP=1) and Flash in WAKEUPINSTANT mode (NVMCTRL.CTRLB.SLEEPPRM=1). From IDLE and STANDBY the CPU sets an I/O by writing PORT->IOBUS with PRIMASK=1 (no interrupt handler entered); the time runs from the wake-up input edge to the GPIO edge. From BACKUP the exit is an RTC wake-up, timed from the RTC pin toggle to the I/O set by the first instructions after reset. From OFF the exit is the reset pin, timed from the rising edge of RESETN to the I/O set by the first instructions after reset.

There are three pin types, each with its own speed: Backup, Normal and High Sink; PORT.PINCFG.DRVSTR selects drive strength. High Sink pins: PA08, PA09, PA16, PA17, PA22, PA23, PA27, PA31. Backup pins: PA00, PA01, PB00, PB01, PB02, PB03. Pins with an I2C function meet the I2C standard in Standard, Fast, Fast-plus and High-speed (up to 3.4 MHz) modes; on PA12, PA13, PB12, PB13, PB16, PB17, PB30 and PB31 the output low current in Standard and Fast modes is limited to 2.5 mA instead of 3 mA at VOL = 0.4 V, and to 3 mA instead of 6 mA at VOL = 0.6 V.

At power-up the device is held in POR reset until VDDIN passes the POR rising threshold, then in BOD reset until VDDIN passes the default BOD33 level (about 1.6 V), during which the BOD33 level from the user row is loaded; then it runs. When VDDIN falls below the user-defined BOD level the device goes back into BOD reset until VDDIN rises above that level again, and runs once it does. If VDDIN falls further, below the POR falling threshold, the device goes into POR reset, the BOD returns to its default level, and on the next rise it passes through BOD reset and the user-row load again before running. The internal reset is asserted for the whole time the device is in POR or BOD reset.

Seen from an AINx pin, the ADC input is the series sampling switch resistance RSAMPLE into the sampling capacitor CSAMPLE, whose other plate sits at VDDANA/2; the signal source and its resistance RSOURCE drive the pin. The sampling time must let CSAMPLE settle through RSOURCE + RSAMPLE.

In host mode SCK is driven by the device; MOSI changes within tMOS before and is held tMOH after the sampling edge, and MISO must be set up tMIS before and held tMIH after it. In client mode SS falls at least tSSS before the first SCK edge and rises tSSH after the last; MOSI must be set up tSIS before and held tSIH after the sampling edge; MISO is valid within tSOSS after SS falls, changes tSOS before and is held tSOH after the SCK edge, and is held tSOSH after SS rises.

With the same frequency equations as in PL0: in host mode, a non-volatile memory with tvalid = 12 ns max allows 9.8 MHz at VDDIO > 2.7 V; in client mode an ideal host (tsu = 0) allows 16.3 MHz at VDDIO > 2.7 V.

The USB pad buffers meet USB 2.0; their AC parameters are those of the USB 2.0 electrical specification. The interface is USB-IF certified as a low/full-speed peripheral silicon building block (TID 40001709) and as a full-speed embedded host (TID 120000459). To be USB-compliant: performance level PL2 only; CPU clock above 8 MHz while USB is active (no limit in USB suspend); supply 3.3 V (3.0 V min, 3.6 V max); GCLK_USB accurate to 48 MHz ±0.25% in device mode and 48 MHz ±0.05% in host mode.

Devices for -40 °C to 105 °C differ from the standard range only in the parameters listed for 105 °C; every other characteristic is as for the standard range. Typical figures are at 25 °C; minimum and maximum hold over the full temperature and supply range unless stated otherwise.

Measured with VDDIN 3.3 V or 1.8 V; at 1.8 V the CPU runs from Flash with 3 wait states, at 3.3 V with 1 wait state in PL0 and 2 in PL2; low-power cache on; BOD33 off; XOSC stopped; XOSC32K running on an external 32 kHz crystal; in PL2 the DFLL48M runs at 48 MHz referenced to XOSC32K and is the main clock; in PL0 OSC16M runs at 4, 8 or 12 MHz; all AHB and APB clocks on, CPUDIV = 1, BUPDIV = 8, LPDIV = 1; I/Os with digital functionality disabled.

There are three pin types, each with its own speed: Backup, Normal and High Sink; PORT.PINCFG.DRVSTR selects drive strength. High Sink pins: PA08, PA09, PA16, PA17, PA22, PA23, PA27, PA31. Backup pins: PA00, PA01, PB00, PB01, PB02, PB03. Pins with an I2C function meet the I2C standard in Standard, Fast, Fast-plus and High-speed (up to 3.4 MHz) modes; on PA12, PA13, PB12, PB13, PB16, PB17, PB30 and PB31 the output low current in Standard and Fast modes is limited to 2.5 mA instead of 3 mA at VOL = 0.4 V, and to 3 mA instead of 6 mA at VOL = 0.6 V.
The POR and BOD reset sequence at start-up and on a falling supply is the same as for the standard range.

Host mode, from fSCKmax = 1 / (2 × (tMIS + tvalid)): a non-volatile memory with tvalid = 12 ns max allows 9.8 MHz at VDDIO > 2.7 V. Client mode, from fSCKmax = 1 / (2 × (tSOV + tsu)): an ideal host (tsu = 0) allows 16.3 MHz at VDDIO > 2.7 V.

Some ordering codes (suffix -SLL) are IEC 61508 SIL 2-enabled and can use the SIL 2 certified self-test library (STL), which Microchip supplies on request with its user's manual and an integration checklist.

Where electromagnetic noise is high, three things matter most for reliable running: decoupling capacitors placed tight against each supply pin, an RC network filtering RESET, and a pull-up resistor holding SWCLK. Noise should also be kept from reaching supply pins, I/O pins and crystals.

One supply or two, each 1.62 V to 3.63 V; VDDIN and VDDANA must get the same voltage. The core regulator has four modes: linear (no inductor; the default while running), switching buck (the most efficient while running), low-power (the default in Standby) and shutdown (in Backup). Software can swap between linear and switching mode at any time, but the board must be built for the mode that will be used: switching needs the inductor from VSW to VDDCORE.
On the QFN packages the exposed pad must be connected to GND.
The VREFA/VREFB decoupling is needed only when an external analog reference is used; with the internal references it can be left off.

The reset network is needed only if something on the board drives RESET low; the push-button can be left off if no manual reset is wanted. RESET has an internal pull-up, so the external pull-up is optional; it keeps the pin from dipping low and resetting the device by accident. The resistor in series with the button lets the filter capacitor discharge gently, avoiding a current surge and the noise spike it would cause.
Unused pins leak least in their default state, so they need no set-up to save power.
Internal oscillators, external ones, or both together can clock the device, for example OSC16M as the system clock and a 32.768 kHz watch crystal on XOSC32K for the RTC.
Keep the crystal next to its pins: long traces load the crystal too heavily to oscillate and couple noise into the rest of the system.

XOSC32K is tuned for a 32.768 kHz watch crystal and for very low power, so the crystal's load capacitance and ESR (both from the crystal maker) need care. With the pin parasitics and PCB capacitance, a crystal of under 12.5 pF load can run with no external capacitors; the crystal maker may call for external capacitors to improve accuracy and safety factor. Keep the pins next to XIN32/XOUT32 as quiet as possible to minimise cycle-to-cycle jitter.

Programming and debugging use the Serial Wire Debug (SWD) interface, supported by tools such as Atmel-ICE, SAM-ICE, JTAGICE3 and the embedded debugger of the SAM L21 Xplained Pro kit. A pull-up on SWCLK is critical for reliable operation. JTAGICE3 does not take the 10-pin Cortex debug connector directly; a 10-pin header with the JTAGICE3 pinout (also usable with the Atmel-ICE AVR port) or the JTAGICE3 squid cable connects it.

The USB port is a D+/D- pair plus VBUS and GND, usable only at the supply voltages the USB electrical requirements allow. Dedicated transient suppressors on D+, D- and VBUS, as close to the connector as possible, improve ESD robustness. The cable shield should not be tied straight to board ground, which would make the cable an antenna; join shield and ground through an RC filter instead.
